While a dipolar modulation in right ascension at energies above 8 EeV was previously identified as the most prominent signal within the [4,8] EeV and $E\geq 8$ EeV bins, we further investigate the highest-energy range by dividing it into three distinct intervals. Our results indicate that the dipole amplitude grows with energy above 4 EeV, a trend well-described by a power law with an index of $\beta=0.79\pm 0.19$. The dipole directions remain consistent with an extragalactic origin across all examined energies. Furthermore, our estimation of quadrupolar components reveals no statistical significance. Finally, we contextualize these findings against various models predicting the distribution of ultrahigh-energy sources and cosmic magnetic fields. The observed superdipole alignment correlates with the distribution of superluminous galaxies only when electrical charge composition is assumed above $E\geq 4$ EeV, although this correlation remains weak. We also explore other related scenarios involving matter distributions, source redshifts, scattering regimes, and the influence of GZK effects. Ultimately, we conclude that current ultrahigh-energy cosmic ray data do not definitively confirm nor rule out ultralight dark matter-induced focal spots nor phase-space propagation models. The continuous increase in dipole amplitude suggests that future measurements of the directional structure at $E\geq 10$ EeV could offer valuable insights into the origins of ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays.

We examine $\eta$-condensate production in heavy-ion collisions using a linearized $U(1)$-CSMC model that incorporates $N_f=2$ chiral symmetry, the Skyrme energy functional, and quantum corrections. This study extends our prior analysis of the $\eta$-condensate in the $U(1)$-CSMC model to higher temperatures and densities. While the condensate's dependence on temperature and chemical potential varies with energy density, it ultimately follows the patterns expected for other $U(1)$-symmetry-breaking order parameters. At finite temperature and density, fluctuations of the order parameter generate a dipolar structure in the correlation function, which we demonstrate is more pronounced at finite density than at finite temperature. This scenario can be recast as a standard quantum problem within a commuting momentum space, where coordinates are expressed as linear differential operators: $\hat x_a = -i\hat D_a = -iE_{ab} (p)\, \partial /\partial p_b$. The resulting deformed Hamiltonian, $\hat H = -\frac 12 \hat D_a^2\,,$ governs motion along group manifolds with a characteristic scale of order $\theta^{-1}$. Cancer diagnosis and prognosis often rely on microscopic examination of tissue samples stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). Automated analysis using digital pathology and machine learning offers a promising route to enhance the speed, accuracy, and reproducibility of these evaluations. Although it is ideal to train deep learning models on a wide variety of whole slide images (WSIs) from different patients and anatomical sites, the large data volumes required often present challenges in finding sufficient materials at a single institution. We investigated the use of federated learning (FL) as a solution for training deep learning models on distributed H&E tissue image datasets. Our results indicate that shallow models with FL-derived weights can achieve classification accuracy comparable to models trained on centrally aggregated data. Furthermore, we show that FL can yield better performance in distinguishing anatomical site positivity than models trained on locally held datasets alone. Our study establishes a framework for conducting FL on distributed histopathology datasets and provides a proof-of-concept for utilizing this approach to build diagnostic models.

We present an open-source library designed to facilitate research into federated learning applied to digital pathology. We evaluated the model's accuracy and the training time costs of our specific setup. Additionally, we demonstrated that this framework can enhance the training accuracy of certain deep learning models compared to training on a single institution's data. We released this work as open-source to support the development of similar frameworks and to aid in creating practical solutions for collaborative machine learning initiatives involving digital pathology datasets across multiple institutions.

Gbit/s optical on-off keying (OOK) system operating over 18.8 km of uncompensated submarine fiber in the South China Sea. The chromatic dispersion inherent in this cable length creates four spectral nulls within the 36 GHz bandwidth of the OOK signal, posing a significant barrier to achieving acceptable bit-error-rate (BER) performance. While a decision feedback equalizer (DFE) can effectively address these spectral nulls, it suffers from burst-error propagation caused by signal instability in the harsh submarine environment. Although a weighted DFE (WDFE) helps mitigate burst-error propagation, it fails to fully compensate for spectral nulls because it relies on only a subset of directly decided feedback symbols. Consequently, adding maximum likelihood sequence estimation (MLSE) after the WDFE allows for the simultaneous elimination of spectral distortions and the implementation of optimal detection. Compared to a joint DFE and MLSE approach, the combined WDFE and MLSE algorithm significantly suppresses burst-error propagation, yielding up to a 2.9 dB improvement in the Q factor and removing the BER floor phenomenon. Ultimately, the joint WDFE and MLSE algorithm effectively resolves burst-error propagation issues in this field-trial fiber-optic communication system.

We introduce an automatic dilation optimizer that reframes this challenge as weight pruning along the time axis, enabling the simultaneous learning of dilation factors and network weights within a single training phase. This approach achieves up to a 7.4x reduction in model size and a 3x decrease in inference latency on real System-on-Chip (SoC) hardware, all without sacrificing accuracy compared to non-dilated networks. Furthermore, our method generates a diverse collection of Pareto-optimal TCNs from a single initial model, surpassing manually designed solutions in both efficiency and performance. Essential to this method is a novel share-the-gradient technique that resolves dimensionality issues on the loss function. Beyond TCNs, we demonstrate that our approach can also optimize other structured networks, such as those utilizing circular buffered dilated convolutions. We anticipate that this work will facilitate the efficient design of time-series models for resource-constrained environments. The code is accessible at https://github.com/zeyademad/TCNOpt.

We address the challenge of jointly learning the filter size and input segmentation (dilation) in convolutional neural networks for sequence modeling. By formulating learning the dilation factor as a weight pruning problem on fully connected layers, we can simulate varying dilations without creating additional network copies. This allows the network to learn a trade-off between filter size and dilation simultaneously. Our method, which we term Learnable Circular Buffered Dilated Convolution (LCBC), operates as a single modular layer that eliminates the need for explicit data padding, offering a more streamlined alternative to existing dilated convolution techniques. As a result, LCBC expands the design landscape for convolutional networks handling multi-dimensional sequential data, leading to improved performance, as evidenced by experiments on CRMm and Protein DTAA datasets. The source code can be found at https://github.com/zeyademad/LCBC.

Specifically, the ALBA algorithm, which is parametric for each (D)LE, efficiently determines the first-order correspondents of (D)LE-inductive formulas. We introduce an algorithm that utilizes ALBA's rules and algebraic framework to reverse its steps within the DLE context, thereby effectively deriving an inductive formula from its given first-order correspondent. Additionally, this approach is broadly applicable to any DLE for which ALBA rules are definable, including quantifier-free multi-sorted many-sorted DLEs used in variational complexity analysis.

While the conventional stance holds that table instances must adhere to all imposed functional dependencies, it is equally significant to formulate theories for handling instances that violate certain dependencies. Concerning missing values, we do not presuppose their existence; rather, a missing value is considered to exist only if it can be inferred from the table's functional dependencies.

We present a formal framework where each table tuple is assigned one of four truth values: true, false, inconsistent, or unknown. We demonstrate that this framework facilitates the study of critical issues such as consistent query answering, table merging, and data quality metrics, among others. However, this work primarily concentrates on consistent query answering, a problem that has garnered significant attention over recent decades.

The paper's main contributions are as follows: (a) we introduce a novel approach for addressing inconsistencies in tables with nulls and functional dependencies; (b) we provide algorithms to compute all true, inconsistent, and false tuples; (c) we examine the relationship between our method and four-valued logic within the context of data merging; and (d) we offer a new solution to the consistent query answering problem, comparing it with existing approaches based on table repairs.

The paper is structured into ten sections. Section 2 outlines the notations and fundamental concepts of database theory, four-valued logic, and semantic merging used throughout the work. Section 3 defines the Inconsistent Table Merge Problem, which involves combining two tables with potentially inconsistent and missing data under a set of functional dependencies. a novel object representation that encodes points and relative poses between an object and a target (like a robot gripper or hanging rack) using category-level descriptors. Designed for object manipulation, this approach enables the repetition of a demonstrated task on new instances within the same category by optimizing for a pose whose descriptor matches the observed demonstration. NDFs are trained in a self-supervised manner through a 3D auto-encoding process that avoids the need for expert-labeled keypoints. Additionally, their SE(3)-equivariant nature ensures robust generalization across all 3D translations and rotations. We validate this method in both simulation and on a real robot using only 5-10 demonstrations, showing that performance generalizes across different object instances and 6-DoF poses, significantly outperforming recent baselines relying on 2D descriptors. Project website: https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

This paper addresses the challenge of teaching a robot to hang objects on a shelf using minimal demonstrations. We propose a solution that learns a single, object-and-shelf-agnostic function to transform any 3D point on a hanging object into a descriptor. This function is trained to be reversible, allowing for the inference of the object's pose from its point-wise descriptor pattern. We demonstrate that just 5-10 demonstrations are sufficient to achieve high success rates on new objects and variations of the current shelf using reverse optimization. Experiments were conducted in simulation and on a real robot using magnet attachments, showing successful generalization across different object instances and 6-DoF poses. In contrast to recent methods that fit a surface to a single demonstration, our approach requires less than 1/10th the training data while generalizing across both object instances and 3D poses. Project website: https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

We present a solution to repeat a demonstrated object-hanging task on new objects using very few demonstrations. The core of our method is the learning of a single, category-level function that maps 3D points on an object to descriptors. These descriptors are optimized to allow the recovery of the demonstrated pose via reverse optimization. Unlike previous methods that optimize for 2D image space or rely on 预-trained networks, our function is trained separately for each task. By ensuring the descriptor pattern generally admits a valid conformation on new objects, we can repeat the task with only 5-20 demonstrations. Project website: https://yilundu.github.io/ndf-.

Our study examines chemical abundances across various elemental groups—including light, odd-Z, $\alpha$, Fe-peak, and neutron-capture elements—based on high signal-to-noise spectra of seven giant members. The resulting mean cluster metallicity is determined to be [Fe/H]$=-0.70\pm0.05$, showing no signs of intrinsic metallicity dispersion. Ton~2 displays a standard $\alpha$-enrichment pattern consistent with other high-metallicity Galactic globular clusters, mirroring trends observed in 47~Tucanae and NGC~6380. However, we detect a significant spread in nitrogen abundance ($>0.87$ dex) and a substantial population of nitrogen-enriched stars. Considering Ton~2's relatively high metallicity, these nitrogen levels far exceed typical Galactic averages, confirming the prevalence of the multiple-population phenomenon; the cluster also hosts stars with low, first-generation nitrogen abundances. Additionally, we identify a [Ce/Fe] abundance spread in Ton~2 that correlates with nitrogen enhancement, suggesting that \textit{s}-process enrichment was likely driven by an intermediate-mass star. Finally, the spectral data from these seven stars allows us to constrain their masses and ages, yielding values of $0.80\pm0.04$ Gyr and $0.76\pm0.06$ Gyr, respectively, which align with Ton~2's established age and mass determinations derived from the main sequence gap. This analysis provides essential chemical insights into the evolution of Tononzintla~2 and serves as a valuable benchmark for both theoretical models and future observations.

Over the last decade, the field of hybrid automata verification has progressed significantly, with *Placebo* emerging as a robust, scalable, and flexible tool for computing reachability information. This work presents two related advancements to the *Placebo* framework: a novel algorithm for computing non-classical locations and a search-based approach for determining novel paths.

First, we extend the computation of inductive and super invariant sets beyond traditional invariant classifications. By employing a modified multi-objective matrix multiplication algorithm, we efficiently calculate non-classical inductive locations that may depend on continuous variables. This method generalizes the technique previously used in *Placebo* for handling non-Zeno diagonal clock constraints, enabling the accurate computation of inductive locations with arbitrary decidable subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (for a finite set of dimensions $D$) and linear relations among continuous variables. The core of this approach relies on a new algorithm capable of efficiently solving the non-trivial "augmented" Minkowski sum problem associated with polyhedra featuring decision variables; this algorithm significantly improves upon prior methods in both theoretical complexity and practical execution time.

Second, we extend the computation of novel paths by integrating the flow template technique with the template expansion method. The resulting "template expansion with flow template" (TEWF) approach demonstrates that the quality of computed novel paths is inherently superior to that of the classic "classic template expansion" (CTE) method.

This model defines a multilayer network as a collection of multiple edge-weighted, potentially directed graphs sharing the same set of nodes, where each graph constitutes a layer and no edges connect nodes across different layers. Similar to standard eigenvector centrality, a node's importance in a specific layer is derived from the weighted sum of its neighbors' importance within that same layer. However, unlike the standard approach, our framework allows the adjacency relationships and the importance values of neighboring nodes to originate from different layers. Crucially, this capability is only partially addressed by current multilayer eigenvector centrality frameworks, which typically rely on inter-layer edges to model such dependencies. In our proposed model, constrained, layer-specific eigenvector centrality scores are determined by a system comprising independent eigenvalue problems and dependent pseudo-eigenvalue problems, which can be solved efficiently through an interleaved power iteration algorithm. We demonstrate that this system possesses a unique non-negative solution for non-negative adjacency matrices, with the importance vectors corresponding to the largest (possibly non-unique) eigenvalues of the constituent layers. Furthermore, we establish that the centralities computed in each individual layer represent the most significant components of the combined multilayer networks when that specific layer is prioritized over the others. The paper also explores the relationship between our approach and existing methods, with the differences and advantages of our model highlighted in the Discussion section. In the Multilayer Networks with Constraints section, we detail how this model can effectively represent various types of limitations on node importance across multiple layers, such as allowing or disallowing the use of neighbor importance from other layers, or fully or partially relying on it. In the Solution algorithm section, we present a closed-form solution for the current state of the system and a general algorithm for determining the stationary state, which is essential for assessing the stability of the network under minor perturbations like the addition or removal of links. Finally, the Multilayer Networks with Applications section outlines several potential uses of this framework, including the analysis of multi omics data, social influence, and multi-scale networks. The Appendix provides a comprehensive list of acronyms and a detailed comparison between our model and related approaches. The model can be extended to incorporate limited inter-layer connectivity or specific types of inter-layer constraints, although such extensions lie beyond the scope of the current work. Blurring and incomplete data are inherent challenges in many imaging systems, often making it impossible to separate the resulting point-spread function (PSF) into individual sources. While previous studies have addressed restoration in specific cases—such as when the missing data follows a certain pattern—most existing methods lack physical interpretability. We formulate imaging as the completion of incomplete data and develop an algorithm to reconstruct high-resolution color images from low-resolution, blurred, noisy captures using only a deep learning-based morphological prior. Our method outperforms recent state-of-the-art techniques, including self-supervised learning approaches, even when the PSF components are clearly separated.

Reconstructing high-resolution images from low-resolution, blurred, and noisy low-resolution captures through self-supervised learning is generally an ill-posed problem, particularly when the resulting PSF cannot be factorized. While effective in specific scenarios—such as when the factorization is guaranteed or the missing data exhibits certain characteristics—current methods often struggle with more complex cases. We begin by unifying various image restoration challenges into a coherent framework for high-resolution self-supervised learning from low-resolution inputs. We then propose a novel, simple, and effective approach to solve this problem. Extensive experiments confirm that our method surpasses both recent state-of-the-art algorithms and those tailored for specific conditions.

This approach involves evolving Dirac spinors from an initial Cauchy surface to any other Cauchy surface within the global coordinate patch of de Sitter spacetime through unitary transformation operators. We solve the Dirac equation in two distinct ways: first, by considering Dirac spinors in the Heisenberg picture and evolving them to the Cauchy surface via a unitary operator, and second, by treating them in the Schr\"{o}dinger picture and evolving them to the same surface using a different unitary operator. We further show that the two methods yield identical solutions to the Dirac equation in de Sitter spacetime. As a consequence, the wave functions (eigenstates) of the Dirac equation in de Sitter spacetime can be obtained directly in the Schr\"{o}dinger picture without evolving from an initial Cauchy surface, provided the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra is utilized. We have applied this technique to the two standard forms of the Dirac equation in de Sitter spacetime, namely those involving the angular momentum operator $J_{ij}$ and those involving $J_{0i}$, respectively. We contend that this methodology can also be extended to address the Dirac equation in (anti-)de Sitter spacetimes of higher dimensions. Consequently, it may serve as a valuable tool for investigating various aspects of quantum field theory in curved spacetimes. Copyright (C) 2022 Author(s). ### 1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms learn interaction models from demonstrated data, a process vulnerable to adversarial attacks aiming to produce suboptimal outcomes. Unlike supervised learning where only labeling is targeted, RL faces threats to both rewards and transitions (environment dynamics), making it particularly susceptible as attackers need not understand an agent's task to induce failure. For instance, an attacker need not know a self-driving car's navigation goal to steer it into an accident. Similarly, a toy for a specific child need not be designed so that an adversary can make it appear broken. Consequently, this paper examines robust RL against attacks on both rewards and transitions.

Robust control has received substantial attention in recent decades, yet it often assumes full knowledge of an attacker's capabilities—a premise that is unrealistic given an agent's vast action and observation spaces. A more practical approach is adopting an *unknown* but *bounded* attack capacity, as this constraint is agnostic to the agent's specifics (e.g., state/action space dimensions) and is as weak as possible for the adversary.

Introduction {#s:intro}============

Consider the following intriguing game:

Game {#s:game}----

We play repeatedly. In each round, you receive two cards with hidden integer values (not necessarily distinct) drawn uniformly and independently from the infinite set of non-negative integers. You must identify a round where one of your cards matches a number on a card you will receive in a future round.

In the non-choice variant, you must select a specific round to test your card against; in the choice variant, you are free to pick which card to use for the test.

Does a perfect strategy exist that ensures you will win?

This game was featured in Puzzle #5 of the September–October 2019 issue of *Scientific American*, adapted from a Google Code Jam challenge. The original puzzle involved two rows of randomly generated integers and asked whether choice is necessary to find matching elements. In that context, the answer is yes: if rows are infinite, choice is required to guarantee a match, but in the finite case, non-choice suffices. That challenge is what we examine here.

In the original game, a perfect winning strategy exists using choice: since each integer has a non-zero probability of appearing, you can eventually match both of your numbers to future cards. However, that solution fails in the no-choice version because matching only one of your cards to a future card does not guarantee a match for the other. That is the core of our investigation.

That game can be reformulated as follows:

Game* {#s:game*}-----

We play repeatedly. In each round, you are shown two cards with hidden integer values (not necessarily distinct) drawn uniformly and independently from the infinite set of non-negative integers.

This review aims to present the fundamental concepts and computational procedures regarding these bivectors, specifically by transforming the complex self-dual electromagnetic field from an orthonormal Minkowski basis into a complex null tetrad basis. Additionally, within this framework, the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the Newman-Penrose formalism are derived. Finally, the analysis is applied to the Kerr metric, successfully recovering its well-known electromagnetic field. This review serves as a pedagogical application of these tools to a specific problem in Gravitational Physics. The accompanying appendix contains the necessary mathematical definitions and demonstrations to support the main discussion. Notably, the treatment of complex self-dual fields and the calculation of Weyl tensor components via Newman-Penrose bivectors align with the methodology employed by Roy and Newman in formulating quantum field theory on the Kerr background, although that work utilizes the 1+3 formalism. While the final results for the Kerr metric coincide with those of Roy and Newman, the presentations of both the Kerr solution and its electromagnetic field differ significantly. Although the underlying geometry of Kerr spacetime is unique, other solutions to Einstein-Maxwell's equations can be generated via solution-generating techniques; these methods are also based on the Kerr solution but require the self-dual extension of the formalism developed in this review. Consequently, the presented approach to Newman-Penrose bivectors offers a unified framework for constructing exact solutions to the Einstein-Maxwell equations with stationary, axisymmetric, asymptotically flat, non-degenerate, and non-degenerate black hole solutions. While the formalism can be adapted for spacetimes with specific symmetries to simplify the determination of the self-dual electromagnetic field and the Weyl tensor, the examples provided in this review illustrate that this development represents a direct application of the formalism to the Kerr solution without any modifications.

To resolve this discrepancy, this work treats all nested entities within a sentence as a unified structure and introduces a holistic structure parsing algorithm to identify the complete set of entities simultaneously. Furthermore, addressing the current lack of research on incorporating corpus-level information into NER, we integrate Point-wise Mutual Information (PMI) and other frequency-based features derived from corpus-aware statistics. This approach enhances performance by extending modeling from the sentence level to the corpus level. Experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves promising outcomes on standard benchmarks, matching or surpassing state-of-the-art performance. Additional empirical analyses reveal that the proposed corpus-aware features significantly improve NER domain adaptation, highlighting the remarkable benefits of our corpus-level holistic structure modeling. We develop and implement a novel range-based approach specifically to reduce cross-technology interference in shared frequency bands, with the objective of minimizing the mean square error. The hardware implementation aligns with ideal simulation results (assuming no interference), achieving a localization accuracy of under 0.5 meters. By employing a non-linear least squares method, the proposed algorithm effectively determines the position of mobile nodes. Additionally, the system demonstrates a low average detection delay of 99.34 seconds. Overall, this research contributes to the effective design of localization protocols for 802.15.4 wireless sensor networks.
This paper presents a protocol for 802.15.4-based wireless sensor networks (WSNs) that enables mobile node localization using a hybrid method combining a cooperative approach with a limited ad-hoc clustering protocol. To achieve this, we propose a new received signal strength indicator (RSSI)-based algorithm. While the cooperative localization component is independent of the media access control (MAC) protocol, our design integrates the algorithm into a cross-layer, energy-efficient, sleep-based MAC protocol. While most existing works focus on determining mobile node positions, our primary emphasis is on enabling data-centric applications. These applications require the network to answer queries not only about mobile node mobility but also about values found within the WSN, such as temperature or pressure. Specifically, our protocol allows mobile nodes to offload query processing to the nodes holding the data they seek. We implement and test the protocol on an MICA2Z8000-based hardware platform, using a mobile node to query values from stationary sensor nodes. The performance evaluation demonstrates that the protocol maintains an average application-level accuracy of 0.4 meters for mobile node localization. For data-centric queries, the protocol achieves acceptable response times of 0.1 seconds under ideal conditions and 0.5 seconds when cross-interference is present. Furthermore, our design extends the network's average lifetime from 12.5 hours (in existing methods) to 25 hours.

Existing automatic image description models are trained and evaluated against crowdsourced human descriptions, with performance measured by similarity metrics like BLEU, Meteor, and CIDER. Therefore, the dependability of both the models and the evaluation relies on the quality of these reference descriptions. This work demonstrates that current image description datasets suffer from poor quality and flawed annotation processes. We present a framework for assessing descriptive quality that balances the needs of visually impaired users with the reality of what is achievable. This framework was used to evaluate 200,000 images from one web-scraped dataset and 10,000 images from another. A key finding is that descriptive accuracy is as important as, if not more than, detail for effective image descriptions. Additionally, we show that current neural description models perform poorly on the resulting high-quality dataset because it is the first of its kind. We also introduce a simple two-sentence evaluation protocol for automatically generated descriptions, demonstrating that it is as effective as complex crowd-sourced references.

to individual traits, such as information literacy, and social media mechanisms like algorithmic diffusion, often neglecting a third crucial element: the offline self-segregation of Americans into ideologically homogeneous geographic areas, known as "The Big Sort." We hypothesized that this phenomenon significantly influences online misinformation dissemination because, despite their global potential, digital interactions are inherently localized, with interaction likelihood dropping sharply as distance increases. Analyzing over 8 million Reddit comments containing news links from January 2016 to December 2019, we discovered that Reddit does not function as a "hype machine" for misinformation as other platforms do; instead, it operates as a supply-and-demand system. Specifically, the volume of misinformation news scaled linearly with the population of each state (scaling exponent $\beta=1$, $R^2 = 0.95$). Moreover, variations from this universal trend were best predicted by state-level personality and cultural attributes ($R^2 = \{0.12, 0.39\}$), rather than socioeconomic factors ($R^2 = \{0.15, 0.29\}$) or political characteristics ($R^2 = \{0.06, 0.21\}$). We observed that states with residents exhibiting lower conscientiousness and cultures characterized by loose norms (low cultural tightness) experienced higher-than-expected circulation of all news and fact-checked fake news, whereas states where residents are more politically engaged saw lower-than-expected circulation. By localizing digital interactions and examining them through the lens of state-level culture and economics, we can better understand the demand for fake news and how cultural attributes affect the spread of misinformation in the digital age. Our findings suggest that the Big Sort, combined with state-level culture and political engagement, is a key driver of misinformation dissemination. Consequently, effective mitigation strategies must address not only online mechanisms but also offline factors, including the segregated living patterns of Americans and their cultural and political identities.

We introduce a scale-free model of an evolving network of documents that share common topics, showing that specific network metrics can reliably indicate which topics are currently trending. By applying this model to news articles from four major U.S. outlets over the last year and 450 million Twitter posts from 14 million active users between 2013 and 2019, we demonstrate that the distribution of network parameters for a vast number of topics (99.4%) across these platforms is mutually independent.

Although demonstrations offer a natural method for teaching robots, relying solely on movement trajectories fails to incorporate other modalities, such as audio cues from human instructors. To harness these audio signals effectively, it is essential to first identify the specific information they convey. This study characterizes the audio generated by human teachers performing multi-step manipulation tasks for a Sawyer robot by analyzing three feature categories: speech duration, prosodic expressiveness, and semantic content. By examining these features across four dimensions—demonstration types, audio usage instructions, subtasks, and demonstration errors—the analysis reveals that while teachers use similar semantic words across different conditions, distinct variations in speech duration and expressiveness emerge. These findings highlight that human audio contains rich, differentiating information that could significantly advance robotic learning from demonstration techniques. Consequently, the data gathered can be leveraged to refine existing methods or enable the acquisition of new skills.

Our approach addresses this by examining conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, offering a comprehensive analysis of complexity for both states and operators within the universal sector of their energy-momentum tensor. Central to our framework are the Euler-Arnold equations and their integro-differential extensions, which ensure the optimization problem between arbitrary states or transformations is well-defined. This work expands upon the findings detailed in arXiv:2005.02415, elaborating on the derivation techniques employed. Key areas of focus include the application of differential regularization, solving the integro-differential equation governing Fubini-Study state complexity, and investigating the underlying geometric structure. The resulting framework generalizes seamlessly to any rational CFT in 1+1 dimensions through the use of polynomial regularization. Our findings reveal a striking "tomato effect" for operator complexity: the volume of the unitary ball grows linearly with time until it is suddenly truncated by the theory's central charges. Specifically, the acceleration of this growth is directly determined by the theory's primary field content. Finally, we determine the exact depth of the grove for both the state and the "edge" of the tomato effect. These results demonstrate that the deepest part of the grove corresponds to the Kac class T_{p,q} operator, while the edge is reached by the c=0 theory. As expected, the entire complexity profile is governed by differential equations rooted in Virasoro algebra representation theory. Our methods are fully generalized by the established framework of conformal embedding. Notably, the same "tomato effect" extends to unitary representations of the infinite dimensional Bargmann algebra, regardless of whether they constitute a conformal embedding. This robustness suggests the effect may persist even outside the context of conformal symmetry. We propose that the parameter defining the truncation of the tomato for Bargmann space complexity is arbitrary. Ultimately, we argue that the profound connection between conformal symmetry and quantum complexity points towards a deeper link between conformal field theory and quantum gravity. We hope this work encourages the exploration of similar phenomena in quantum field theories possessing infinite dimensional symmetries. Unlike existing approaches that rely on bilingual corpora for TM and perform source-fuzzy matching, we introduce a novel, lightweight TM system that utilizes monolingual resources and employs exact matching. We conducted a high-resolution analysis of Planck and WMAP data using "HawkingNet," an open-source machine learning tool built on a ResNet18 architecture designed to detect Hawking points. Despite recent advancements, most current approaches rely on averaging operations to compute prototypes, which restricts their performance due to sensitivity to outlier samples. This paper introduces a straightforward yet powerful framework for few-shot classification that utilizes an episodic prototype generator module to produce high-quality prototypes from limited support data. These generated prototypes are designed to align closely with specific target prototypes while remaining robust against outliers. Comprehensive experiments confirm the efficacy of this module, yielding significant improvements over baseline models and competitive results against prior methods on the \textit{mini}ImageNet, \textit{tiered}ImageNet, and cross-domain (\textit{mini}ImageNet $\rightarrow$ CUB-200-2011) benchmarks. Recent years have seen a surge in research on deep few-shot classification, yet the prevalent practice of deriving prototypes via simple mean calculations limits model potential, as such estimates are often skewed by outlier training samples. We propose a novel approach that projects support images into a meta-embedding space—a decision boundary-aware representation—before computing prototypes. This method effectively minimizes the impact of outliers during prototype generation. Furthermore, we introduce a straightforward yet potent optimization technique called Entropic Prototype Selection (EPS), which maximizes the entropy of query embeddings relative to prototypes to enhance class separability. Theentropic nature of these queries is explicitly incorporated into the loss function during training. Extensive experiments on three cross-domain benchmarks demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

We present a unified network architecture, LOCA, grounded in the concept of local discriminative feature aggregation, which performs few-shot classification via prototype-based evaluation of query features. Unlike conventional mean-based or k-nearest-neighbor-based prototypes, LOCA aggregates features from the support set along a localized decision boundary to create robust evaluation metrics for query images. This approach, operating within a single-shot setting, requires no task-specific tuning or optimization and has been tested with various backbones and loss functions on both intra- and cross-domain few-shot classification tasks. Our results, achieved using only standard backbone networks like ResNet, surpass numerous recent state-of-the-art methods on the \textit{mini}ImageNet, \textit{tiered}ImageNet, and cross-domain (\textit{mini}ImageNet $\rightarrow$ CUB-200-2011) benchmarks.

Nevertheless, conventional single-target or dual-target CDR approaches are limited by two key issues: the unrealistic assumption that at least one domain is data-rich and an over-reliance on domain-invariant preferences. These limitations are problematic in real-world scenarios where sparsity is pervasive and can hinder effective user preference learning. To address these challenges, we introduce the Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) model, designed for multi-target cross-domain tasks. Unlike traditional methods, MSDCR acknowledges that all relevant domains may be sparse and aims to enhance recommendation quality across each domain simultaneously. We develop a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to boost domain-specific aspect preferences within a target domain by leveraging complementary aspects from others; the MDSN preserves domain uniqueness via adversarial training, while GAPE adaptively determines complementarity. Additionally, we propose a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture domain-invariant aspect preferences. By integrating these enhanced domain-specific and domain-invariant preferences, MSDCR achieves a holistic understanding of user preferences even in sparse domains. Extensive experiments on real datasets confirm that MSDCR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art single-domain and cross-domain recommendation models. Collaborative filtering (CF) is a primary technique in recommender systems for improving recommendation quality by sharing data and models. However, domain shift causes CF to underperform when applied to out-of-domain (OoD) users, a challenge not fully explored in prior work. This paper investigates private electric vehicles (EVs) and their impact on the resilience of distribution networks after disturbances. Building on this method, we formulate a multi-period optimization model optimized by time. Following modeling, we develop a computational algorithm utilizing the strong duality theorem from convex optimization. Module (Optane DC PMM) marks the first commercial availability of scalable nonvolatile memory DIMMs. This new DIMM combines DRAM-like access speeds and byte-granularity with data persistence across power failures. This report offers the first comprehensive academic performance analysis of the Optane DC PMM, examining its dual role as main memory and as persistent, byte-addressable storage accessible to user-space applications. The study evaluates performance across various modes and scenarios using extensive macro-scale benchmarks.

When configured as large memory devices with a DRAM cache to mitigate higher latency and lower bandwidth (Memory or cached mode), Optane DC memory has minimal impact on applications with small memory footprints. While applications with larger footprints may see some slowdown compared to pure DRAM, they can retain significantly more data in memory. Alternatively, when used with a file system, Optane DC PMMs can yield substantial performance improvements, particularly when the file system is optimized for the device's load/store interface and the application performs many small, persistent writes. For example, using the NOVA-relaxed NVMM file system boosted Kyoto Cabinet's performance by nearly 2x.

Furthermore, Optane DC PMMs facilitate user-space persistence, allowing applications to explicitly manage writes to persistent media. In our experiments, modified applications leveraging user-space persistence outperformed those relying on file systems. Specifically, the persistent version of RocksDB achieved nearly 2x the speed of its equivalent utilizing Filesystem-related extended attributes (pext). Additionally, modifying LevelDB for persistence resulted in nearly 3x performance improvement over its filesystem-based version. However, for applications with very large feetprints, such as MemSQL and Apache Spark, switching to a file system or implementing user-space persistence can lead to significant performance declines compared to standard Linux memory allocation. Finally, we present a novel approach for achieving user-space persistence with a small footprint by periodically dumping data to disk; this method delivers a 2x performance boost for both MemSQL and Apache Spark. These findings demonstrate that Optane DC PMMs can offer significant performance advantages in many scenarios and for various workloads, though their impact depends heavily on the specific application and configuration. Consequently, decision makers should refer to this information when assessing the benefits of Optane DC PMMs or similar persistent memory technologies. The benchmarks presented in this report are accessible at https://www.cs.utah.edu/~rwint/patches/pmem-benchmarks/.

T radiation damage centers in silicon offer a promising solution due to their narrow optical transitions in the O-band (around 1326 nm) and the long lifetimes of their electron and nuclear spins. While previous research has established high optical brightness in ensemble systems via resonance fluorescence, this study utilizes pump-probe spectroscopy to investigate a single T center coupled to a nanophotonic cavity. Furthermore, the scattering spectrum exhibits strong asymmetry, which can be harnessed to achieve pure state preparation. By optimizing the cavity detuning, this scattering mechanism could potentially surpass scattering-based readout methods, offering faster and more reliable spin state reconstruction. Consequently, the proposed readout protocol for T silicon centers demonstrates a potential factor-of-two improvement in the signal-to-noise ratio and a substantial reduction in acquisition time compared to current state-of-the-art techniques. This work paves the way for single spin readout times below 1 $\mu$s for high-quality T-center-silicon cavities, a critical component for constructing a global quantum network. The proposed readout method offers a universal solution for all solid-state spin-photon platforms featuring an optical transition at a single wavelength. This includes diamond V-defects, SkSiC$_x$ centers in silicon carbide, T centers in silicon, and S centers in gallium arsenide.

Special Relativity asserts that all inertial frames are equivalent and that the laws of physics remain invariant between them; however, it fails to account for accelerated (non-inertial) frames, a limitation that has shaped much of modern spacetime research. To resolve this, it is essential to extend special relativity to include non-inertial frames, a process that typically involves identifying the symmetries of flat spacetime and classifying its irreducible unitsary representations. This generalization gives rise to various transformations and associated spacetimes, such as those by Galilei, Poincaré, Fock, Schrödinger, and Rindler. These transformations can be interpreted as projections of the $SO(4,2)$ conformal group onto specific spacetime manifolds, with a detailed exploration of their relationships provided in our prior work.

By employing q-deformed algebras, researchers can examine the implications of modified symmetries on quantum fields, particles, and radiation. However, incompatible transplants carry higher risks of rejection, infection, cancer, and graft loss compared to compatible ones. This study investigates the optimal acceptance strategies for potentially incompatible kidneys tailored to individual patients with end-stage kidney disease. To model the impact of incompatibility, we introduce a Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework that treats compatibility as an explicit state variable. Although this results in a higher-dimensional model that complicates analysis, we derive structural properties—specifically control limit-type optimal policies—that are straightforward to calculate and apply. Numerical simulations demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves across varying mismatch levels and underscore the necessity of integrating incompatibility status directly into acceptance decisions, particularly when desensitization therapy is available. The results from both the MDP and simulations indicate that the value of an incompatible kidney is comparable to that of a compatible one only after multiple plasma exchange procedures. These findings offer crucial insights for clinicians regarding the optimal management of kidney transplantation and valuation, ultimately contributing to the preservation of patient health and graft longevity.

In many decision-theoretic models, such as Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), the agent seeks to maximize a reward signal that guides behavior. Typically, this reward is a scalar average or discounted sum, which causes the decision model to conflate otherwise distinct objects, processes, or states. For instance, in queueing theory, optimal policies often rely on the reward structure rather than the true underlying dynamics. We propose that the true value of an object or process should be defined not by a scalar metric but by its capacity to generate a stream of observable events that reflect its real characteristics. Building on this premise, we introduce Markov Decision Processes with Observable Outputs (MDPOs). Within this framework, the agent's goal is to maximize a primary objective function while using a secondary, distinct reward function that outputs a sequence of signals. These signals serve to disambiguate between otherwise similar states, entities, or processes, thereby facilitating more informed decision-making. We illustrate the advantages of MDPOs over traditional MDPs through examples drawn from operations management and health care. While these applications demonstrate the utility of MDPOs in practice, a formal theoretical analysis remains essential to establish their benefits across a broad spectrum of problems.

Introduction Implicit copulas constitute a significant and actively developed field of statistical modeling. Their appeal largely stems from the need to handle multidimensional data, offering an attractive solution through a representation separated into auxiliary and marginal components. This separation enables efficient parameter estimation, simulation, and inference even for very large datasets. Formally, an implicit copula process $\mathbf{C}=(C_t)_{t\geq 1}$ is defined via an auxiliary process $\mathbf{Z}=(\mathbf{Z}_t)_{t\geq 1}$, where $\mathbf{Z}_t=\{\mathbf{Z}_{it}\mid 1\leq i\leq p\}$ consists of $p$-dimensional random variables. Marginal distributions $F_{it}$ are applied to the auxiliary variables, and the conditional copula $C_t$ results from the rank dependence structure of the transformed variables $(F_{iit})_{1\leq i\leq p}$ (refer to Joe~\cite{joe2014} for related examples).
While many modern implicit copula models function as stochastic processes, their origins can be found in latent variable and factor models. These models were historically favored for their ability to capture time series and volatilities, their parsimony, and their suitability for inference and simulation.

This work contributes to developing a numerical framework based on Cartesian grids capable of simulating complex, topologically evolving boundaries while maintaining high-order gradient accuracy and ensuring proper application of interface boundary conditions. Consequently, a conservative second-order two-fluid numerical method is achieved. The method's efficacy in solving Stefan problems and simulating dendrite growth with and without anisotropy is validated through various test cases. Finally, an explicit scheme is proposed for enforcing interface conditions on the Cartesian grid. The proposed two-fluid method demonstrates high accuracy and conservation properties in resolving interface problems, outperforming conventional level-set approaches. These findings are anticipated to enhance the simulation of other interfacial flow problems characterized by intricate geometries, such as droplet evaporation and dendrite crystallization, with the code remaining adaptable for other scenarios involving moving interfaces. This method is expected to be applicable to three-dimensional simulations. linguistics utilize unary modalities to regulate structural rules governing word order and phrase structure. These controlled operations generate derivational ambiguities that the original Lambek Calculus and its pregroup variant fail to capture. Although proposals exist for interpreting extended Lambek Calculus compositionally within the compact closed category of FVect and linear maps, these approaches treat syntax-semantics mappings as ignoring the control modalities, thereby limiting their influence to syntax alone. Our objective is to elevate these modalities to first-class status within the vectorial interpretation. Leveraging directional density matrix semantics, we expand the type system's interpretation by incorporating an additional spin density matrix space. Consequently, proof interpretations tensor ambiguous derivations with orthogonal spin states. This methodology offers a mechanism for concurrently representing multiple interpretations of ambiguous utterances and establishes a unified framework for integrating both lexical and derivational disambiguation.

Nevertheless, in the fundamental context of multiplayer general-sum games, current methods for learning rationalizable behavior rely on extremely slow algorithms or rely on assumptions regarding the players' prior knowledge. This paper introduces the first efficient algorithm enabling multiagent learning of rationalizable behavior. To accomplish this, we introduce the Multiagent Reduced Normal Form (MReNF), a concept that generalizes the single-agent reduced normal form utilized in existing literature. We demonstrate that MReNF allows for the identification of rationalizable behavior and any associated correlated and Nash equilibria. Notably, a key contribution of this work is proving that correlated equilibria can be learned via any no-regret learning algorithm applied to the MReNF, thereby establishing that rationalizable behavior is a necessary precondition for correlated equilibrium. Furthermore, we show that reaching a Nash equilibrium can be achieved by coordinating on a single correlated equilibrium within the MReNF. Beyond its theoretical contributions, the practical applicability of MReNF is significant, as it allows players to engage in parallel experiments or transfer functions and actions between them, effectively allowing the game to "learn" its own rationalizable behavior, equilibria, and correlated equilibria. Empirical results indicate that our algorithm can discover rationalizable behavior and multiple Nash equilibria across various game classes, including zero-sum, constant-sum, sum, and general games, with a sample complexity that is both theoretically and practically polynomial. In contrast, our main algorithm stands in stark contrast to the 20+ exponential complexity algorithms currently available for learning rationalizable behavior in single-agent settings or correlated equilibria in multi-agent environments. Finally, we also present how to extend this framework to achieve regret minimization with a similar complexity profile. Beyond these contributions, the paper also addresses additional topics and provides further insights.

Multiagent learning has largely concentrated on teaching players how to play a specific best response to the joint strategies of others, typically by having them follow no-regret learning rules like Foster-Ye. To achieve a pure Nash equilibrium, additional conditions are required, the weakest and widest of which is that no player has a rational move. This paper proposes the Multiagent Reduced Normal Form (MReNF), which efficiently enables multiagent learning of such behavior. Two key findings emerge across various parameter configurations: (i) the limiting proportion of infected individuals can exhibit a discontinuity at the critical infection rate $\lambda_c$, resulting in an abrupt jump from zero to a positive value, and (ii) when rewiring is restricted to uninfected individuals, this discontinuity causes the final infected fraction to leap from $0$ to $1$ as $\lambda$ crosses $\lambda_c$. These outcomes indicate that the epidemic's spread can be so abrupt that a minor increase in the infection rate triggers a major outbreak, instantly infecting (or sparing) nearly the entire population. Similar abrupt shifts in connectivity have also been linked to the emergence of a giant component in the giant-component phase of the percolation process. I anticipate these insights will inform simulations of info-epidemic co-evolution and other scenarios involving endogenous network changes, and the results of this work have recently been connected to threshold phenomena in virus mutability.

While perturbative uncertainties are reduced at NLO, large non-perturbative contributions from hadron masses and couplings remain. Although resummation techniques exist, they require careful implementation to avoid introducing new uncertainties regarding matching and scale choices. By combining this with the NLO-matched FKS jet algorithm—previously implemented only at LO—we achieve simultaneous NLO QCD accuracy for both Higgs production and decay. This approach offers the advantage that all major parameters, including couplings and input distribution functions, are managed by the DGLAP code, minimizing uncertainties related to parameterization or grid interpolation. While classical experience replay enables agents to retain knowledge by reusing past observations, its uniform sampling strategy treats all data points equally, neglecting their varying significance. To address this, we introduce a general Variance Reduction-based Experience Replay (VRER) framework that selectively prioritizes the most relevant samples to refine policy gradient estimates. This adaptive mechanism assigns greater weight to historical data more likely to originate from the current target distribution. Both theoretical analysis and empirical results demonstrate that VRER accelerates the convergence to an optimal policy and boosts the performance of leading policy optimization methods. We also provide open-source code for VRER and conduct extensive trials on environmental tasks using previous agent data to evaluate its efficacy in real-world scenarios. VRER is particularly valuable in industrial settings, offering potential applications in online optimization, control, and system design.

We address these discrepancies by performing high-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) on the material using both Helium lamps and laser sources. The derived gap size for these corner bands ($\sim$5.5 meV) is markedly smaller than those reported in previous ARPES studies. These results define a novel superconducting gap structure around the zone corner and resolve numerous longstanding controversies about the electronic and gap structures in optimally-doped (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$. We suggest that the newly observed corner band and its associated gap offer essential insights into the superconductivity mechanism in this compound. Finally, we have made the raw data underlying our conclusions publicly available \cite{data_availability}.

Most random matrices possess eigenvalues that follow non-trivial probability distributions, yet calculating the distribution of these eigenvalues directly is often difficult. We introduce a novel technique to derive exact eigenvalue distributions for a wide range of real, complex, and quaternionic symmetric and skew-symmetric matrix ensembles. This approach relies on extending well-established identities—such as the characteristic polynomial recurrence relation and the Jacobi-triangular decomposition—to superspace, specifically utilizing the recently discovered superbosonization method.


We establish the equivalence between the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula, which extend the supersymmetry method to Gaussian invariant ensembles. This equivalence allows us to reformulate partition functions for non-Gaussian ensembles, enabling the derivation of exact eigenvalue distributions—a task that is often challenging otherwise.

The first method, termed the superbosonization approach, begins with a partition function involving a nonlinear determinant or trace function, such as $\det(I_{N}+V)^{\alpha}$. We introduce the MultiTalk Dataset, a collection exceeding 320,000 written dialogue sentences that achieves a balance between a high branching factor (10) and multiple conversation turns (6) via selective branch continuation. We offer several contributions aimed at advancing dialog generation within this highly branching context. To assess a diverse range of generated outputs, we propose a straightforward scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, designed to optimally integrate a set of varied references. Furthermore, we examine multiple language generation tasks across varying depths of predictive conversation, utilizing textual attributes derived automatically from pretrained classifiers. Our final task addresses a challenging theory of mind problem, a controllable generation challenge that necessitates reasoning about the anticipated reactions of a listener. Although the generated responses exhibit a wide diversity, those addressing the theory of mind task score significantly lower than the others. To explain this phenomenon, we identify that difficult trap answers concentrate among the varied references; removing them causes the score to surge, confirming that our metric successfully captures the diversity inherent in this multi-choice setting. This methodology is applicable to other multi-choice generation problems, and we present a few further examples. We release all code and data alongside this paper's findings. Wiki platform that transforms wikis into robust environments for collaborating on publication-ready manuscripts and software initiatives. Created within Jonathan Dushoff's theoretical biology lab at McMaster University, it enables users to jointly tackle any task achievable through UNIX commands that convert textual "source code" into final outputs. Researchers can utilize it to collaborate on programs in languages such as R, Python, C, or others, alongside specialized features designed to streamline LaTeX document creation. This tool leverages the wiki medium to function simultaneously as a collaborative text editor, development environment, version control system, and publishing platform. Its applications are highly adaptable; its processing is governed by customizable makefiles, and its modular architecture is built to facilitate adaptation for various other uses. The result compilation process is configurable, and its framework is flexible enough to support the simultaneous generation of multiple output formats. Additionally, its software dependencies are adjustable, making it easy to deploy on diverse platforms, and its module design is straightforward, allowing experienced MediaWiki users to readily modify it for specific needs. This article and its supplementary materials provide an in-depth exploration of WorkingWiki, including a comprehensive user guide, illustrative examples, and its underlying source code. While its primary focus is collaborative LaTeX document creation, it also serves as a functional platform for other types of software development. More information and access are available at www.WorkingWiki.org. Furthermore, it has been successfully deployed on a public instance at www.WorkingWiki.net, offering a usable example for readers.

WorkingWiki simplifies and makes robust the task of creating multi-format documents with integrated, executable software. Its application is highly adaptable, its architecture is modular, and its setup is flexible, all of which are documented to facilitate its use and customization for any purpose. This article and its supplementary materials examine WorkingWiki in depth, providing a detailed look at its user guide, examples, and source code.

Many current wikis lack the capabilities necessary for effectively handling multi-format documents featuring integrated, executable software. The WorkingWiki framework addresses this limitation, and this article explores it in depth, featuring both a collaborative LaTeX user guide and a custom instance dedicated to software development.

Within a linearized framework, capturing heat release fluctuations is essential for studying thermoacoustic instabilities and flame noise. Distinct from prior work, this study employs an active flame approach, which incorporates heat release oscillations induced by acoustic fluctuations. Implementing this approach linearly requires linearizing a combustion model; however, linearizing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) and Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) models creates closure issues, rendering them difficult to apply in this context. Conversely, Reynolds-averaged Navier Stokes (RANS) models effectively avoid these problems, making them ideal for this application. These RANS models were linearized around the temporal mean flow of the turbulent jet, which was derived using LES. An a priori analysis identified the linearized RANS Euler equations as the most efficient system for representing the turbulent jet, accurately capturing its dynamics while minimizing the number of equations and computational requirements. This preferred system was solved frequency-by-frequency on top of the temporal mean flow of the turbulent turbulent methane-air jet flame. The solutions were post processed to examine the gain of the linearized operator in terms of its ability to amplify acoustic and vorticity fluctuations. The predominant amplifications occurred in the shear layer and were found to be closely linked to the flame's resonance modes. Finally, the results were used to validate a reduced-order model representing the linearized RANS Euler equations.

By formulating a Hermitian problem, we derive the formula for the stellar acoustic-buoyant frequency $S$ associated with non-radial adiabatic pulsations. We introduce a generalized model of quantum scarring that encompasses at least two apparently unrelated phenomena causing non-thermal recoherence in quantum dynamics: quantum cat maps and quantum billiards with rational fluxes. In both scenarios, periodic orbits with a specific topological character drive the emergence of anomalous recoherence. Model parameters dictating the nature of quantum interference can be mapped to geometric features of classical unstable periodic orbits. These findings offer a topological framework for understanding quantum scarring, unifying two previously unconnected phenomena and extending to other systems hosting similar periodic orbits.

Topological modes are anticipated to govern the pulsations of most stars. To identify these topological modes in the most common type of star, the Sun, we derive their properties using standard solar models. Non-radial topological modes on the Sun include both pseudo-Lamb waves and higher-order topological modes. The topological nature of these pseudo-Lamb waves is indicated by a $\sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)}$ scaling in the asymptotic behavior of their frequencies. predicted to concentrate in the outer $0.03$ of the Sun's radius, these modes span almost the entire solar surface, with their pressure and gravity components separating toward opposite surfaces. Surface damping is expected to cause the amplitude maximum to shift from the equator to higher latitudes as the order increases; the latitude of the maximum for the least damped mode is at $10^{\circ}$, and for the most localized mode, at $79^{\circ}$. Unlike topological modes, gravity and pressure waves on the Sun are anticipated to be trapped in distinct inner and outer regions, respectively.

performance. To ensure low-latency access, replicas typically accept updates independently without coordination, relying on asynchronous propagation to synchronize changes. This approach introduces the significant challenge of resolving conflicts among concurrent updates. Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) offer a principled solution to this problem. However, current CRDT designs are often complex and difficult to generalize across different data types, creating a need for a framework to guide the systematic creation of new CRDTs. To address this, we introduce RWF, the Remove-Win design Framework for CRDTs. RWF employs the straightforward yet potent remove-win strategy to handle conflicting updates and provides a generic design applicable to various data container types. We present two implementations of RWF based on Redis data types, demonstrating the framework's effectiveness. Furthermore, performance evaluations of these implementations confirm the efficiency of CRDT designs built upon RWF. To encourage the development of additional CRDTs across diverse data types, we have open-sourced all code related to this work at https://github.com/ZeyadEmad/RWF.

CrDTs are highly effective at mitigating conflict issues in distributed systems. Although several types of CrDTs exist, there is a lack of understanding regarding the principles governing their design. To resolve this, we propose the CrDT design triangle, a tool for analyzing CrDTs from three perspectives: data type, conflict resolution strategy, and merge strategy. We examine four existing CrDTs through the lens of the CrDT design triangle and identify patterns in their construction. Based on these observations, we proposed the Remove-Win Framework (RWF), which enables the generic design of CrDTs for various data structures. Redis implementations of RWF validate its correctness and efficiency. The open-sourced code repository for this study is available at https://github.com/ZeyadEmad/RWF.

Replication is a critical technique for constructing dependable and high-performance distributed systems. While typically used to maintain consistent copies of data to enhance availability and throughput, uncoordinated updates to these replicas can lead to conflicts. Although CRDTs provide a solution for handling such conflicts, existing designs are often intricate and hard to generalize. To advance the generic design of CRDTs, we developed the Remove-Win Framework (RWF). RWF is demonstrated on Redis-based containers like Sets and Maps, showing that CRDTs can be efficiently implemented for other data types as well. Our experimental results confirm the practicality and performance of RWF. The code for this research is accessible at https

We present a statistical framework that leverages genome-wide association statistics to pinpoint classes of genomic elements that are either enriched for or depleted regarding loci influencing a specific trait, with the model inherently accommodating multiple annotation types. Applying this approach to GWAS data for 18 human traits—including red and platelet cell counts, glucose and lipid levels, height, BMI, and Crohn's disease—across numerous populations, and across 10,000 iterations for each of over 100 human traits available in public repositories, we analyzed 130 annotation sets derived from 17 distinct functional genomics experiments. Using a non-degenerate duality between our method and minimum mean sum matching, we derived an exact algorithm to efficiently identify the optimal GWAS for annotating each element class. Our results reveal that nucleosome-positioning maps are the most informative for a broad spectrum of traits, whereas transcription factor binding maps are less informative, particularly in the context of rare variants. Additionally, we determined the 20 human traits most likely to benefit from genome-wide stratification based on NMR phasing experimental data, highlighting several monogenic disorders as potential candidates. Finally, we established a notable connection between our annotations and the Human Genome Organization's Mammalian Phenotype nomenclature. We have made all computations open source. These insights will help prioritize functional genomic experiments designed to enhance the interpretation of human genetic associations.
We introduce a computational approach for systematically identifying genomic regions—such as open chromatin or nucleosomes—associated with a specific trait. The model combines genome-wide association statistics (from either a single study or a meta-analysis) with a comprehensive library of genomic annotations, allowing for the correlation of multiple data types and enabling a tailored, non-prejudiced selection of the most informative annotations for a given trait. For a specific application involving 18 traits and 130 annotations, our applications demonstrate that nucleosome-positioning maps are highly informative across a wide range of traits and diseases, including monogenic disorders, where individual genotype effects can be evaluated at the nucleosome level. In contrast, we found that transcription factor binding maps are relatively unenriched for associated loci, an observation that becomes even more pronounced when considering rare variants.

Galactic Nuclei (AGN) has garnered significant interest due to the critical role of magnetic fields in their physics, their utility as tracers of intergalactic plasma, and their potential impact on cosmic microwave background polarization measurements. Understanding the statistical relationship between polarization and source characteristics is essential for all these applications. In this work, we calculate the median fractional polarization ($\Pi_{0, \rm med}$) for extensive samples of radio sources with 1.4 GHz flux densities between 6.6 and 70 mJy. This is achieved by stacking polarized intensity data from the NVSS survey at 1.4 GHz, correlated with angular sizes derived from the FIRST survey. We analyze five groups of sources with mean deconvolved angular sizes ranging from 1.8" to 8.2", along with two groups of symmetric double sources, which collectively represent the majority of mJy radio sources smaller than or near the median angular size. Our findings indicate that $\Pi_{0,\rm med}$ at 1.4 GHz varies strongly with angular size for sources smaller than approximately 5", but shows only a weak dependence for larger sources up to ~8". We attribute these results to depolarization occurring within the AGN host galaxy and its circumgalactic medium. Furthermore, we observe an anti-correlation between the curvature of the low-frequency radio spectrum and $\Pi_{0,\rm med}$, suggesting that sources with flatter spectra are more extended and highly polarized. Finally, our results constrain the dependence of low-frequency polarization on angular size and spectrum for sub-Jy sources, as well as the distribution of radio sources in the $\Pi_{0}$–$\theta_{\rm maj}$ plane up to Jy levels. The underlying code is provided for transparency, allowing users to apply similar stacking analyses to other multi-wavelength surveys. The derived low-redshift ($z<0.1$) median polarization for sub-Jy radio galaxies may be relevant for future CMB polarization experiments. We note that the derived low-angular-size group likely includes gamma-ray blazars, warranting further study of their polarization properties. These conclusions are robust against systematic uncertainties arising from beam effects, non-Gaussianity, and gravitational lensing. We anticipate that this stacking code will be valuable for deriving polarization properties from other radio source samples. To support the main results, extensive numerical tests were conducted to validate the significance of the derived median polarization and to quantify the impact of various systematic effects. vibrational modes within molecules and crystals. We demonstrate that the circular motion of ions generates inertial influences on electrons. Mirroring classical Coriolis and centrifugal forces, these phenomena include spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, centrifugal spin-orbit coupling, and centrifugal redshift. The duration of these effects, which can persist for several picoseconds following excitation, depends on phonon decay rates. Enhancing these effects could establish a promising platform for manipulating localized quantum states or chemical reaction barriers through vibrational control. We further propose specific experimental strategies for detecting these effects in solid-state systems.

Modern physics relies on the manipulation and control of vibrational modes in molecules and crystals. Leveraging vibrational degrees of freedom to influence chemical transformations or localized states offers a powerful method for altering material properties or initiating new reactions. This approach, known as vibrational control or photocatalysis, has been suggested for optimizing resistive switching in oxides, influencing chemical reaction barriers and products, driving phase separations, and directing magnetic phase transitions. While many proposals focus on altering potential energy surfaces via changes in equilibrium positions or displacements, this work highlights another mechanism: the inertial effects arising from the circular motion of massive particles.

Vibrational motion can be decomposed into linear acceleration, which shifts equilibrium positions, and rotational motion, which induces rotational inertia in electrons. These two motions may be independently manipulated or combined. Using classical mechanics, we derive that the inertial forces experienced by electrons from circular ion motion—corresponding to terahertz vibrational excitations—produce spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, centrifugal spin-orbit coupling, and a centrifugal redshift. We quantify the magnitude of these inertial terms and demonstrate their potential to exert measurable influence on spin-polarized electron beams, carrier dynamics in semiconductors, and chemical reactions.

Our primary objective was to develop a robust risk-estimation system for upcoming automated driving technologies that relies on an affordable sensor suite. While recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have shown promise in predicting risk, their performance is limited by the poor quality of raw sensor data from cost-effective devices and the complex, diverse nature of driving environments. Existing solutions typically employ hand-crafted filtering pipelines before feeding data to RNNs; however, these pipelines lack generality and are highly sensitive to specific scene conditions. We address these challenges by proposing the first end-to-end training framework for RNN-based estimation of rear-collision risk using dashcam video. Our network, the First-order Hidden Attentive Network (FHAN), utilizes an attention mechanism to dynamically generate scene-specific filtering pipelines in real-time before processing data through RNN components. This approach is generalizable because it adapts to the unique characteristics of individual scenes during inference. We trained the network on the TUM-BAIR stopping distance dataset and validated it on three additional datasets. Our experiments indicate that the FHAN outperforms traditional filtering pipelines followed by RNNs and exceeds the performance of human judges in certain scenarios. By focusing on a specific task, our work pushes the boundaries of what is possible with low-cost cameras and establishes a new state-of-the-art for risk estimation using such hardware. Furthermore, the proposed method offers a promising pathway for training self-supervised models for more complex maneuver predictions.
