We have numerically modeled these rotating objects to determine whether they can sustain nuclear fusion as their energy source, accounting for significant rotational deformation rather than assuming slow rotation. For various angular momentum values, we derived critical curves in the mass versus central degeneracy parameter space where nuclear energy generation equals surface luminosity. Our results indicate that when angular momentum surpasses a threshold of $J_0=8.85\times 10^{48}{\rm erg}~{\rm s}$, the critical curve splits into two branches representing lower and higher degeneracy due to the mass-shedding limit. Based on these findings, we simulated the mechano-thermal evolution of substellar objects under two simplified scenarios involving cooling and reductions in mass or angular momentum. In the first scenario, dominated by external braking mechanisms like magnetized winds or magnetic braking, the evolution is primarily governed by the spin-down timescale. In the second scenario, lacking external braking, gravitational contraction drives the object to the mass-shedding limit, after which it ejects mass to form a surrounding ring or disc and subsequently shrinks. The simulations reveal that under both conditions, the objects become significantly oblate and follow the same thermal evolution path as non-rotating objects of reduced mass. Additionally, we estimated the ejecta mass and its cooling trajectory in the case of mass or angular momentum loss. Comparing these outcomes with the well-established thermal evolution of non-rotating objects of equivalent mass and the properties of syzygy binaries (binary systems aligned in a straight line), we concluded that rotating substellar objects behave similarly to non-rotating objects with less mass or to syzygy binaries. This research offers new insights into rotation-induced phenomena such as the Apparent Mass Reduction Effect and the Syzygy Effect on substellar objects, suggesting that both can be interpreted as manifestations of the same underlying physical process.

These structures are frequently depicted in a two-tiered layout, where each entity set is shown as a collection of vertices aligned on one of two parallel horizontal lines, and their relationships are illustrated by edges linking corresponding vertices across the lines. A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings; however, minimizing crossings is computationally demanding and often yields drawings with so many intersections that they compromise readability. This work examines a recent method for eliminating crossings by splitting vertices, aiming to identify the minimum number of vertices that must be split to achieve a planar representation. Current research typically addresses these issues in isolation, despite their frequent co-occurrence in real-world scenarios. This study investigates incremental learning from imbalanced datasets, focusing on algorithms with constant model complexity and bounded memory for storing exemplars of previous classes. Due to limited memory, old classes receive fewer images than new ones, exacerbating the initial imbalance and creating a bias in score predictions toward newer classes. To mitigate this, we evaluate a comprehensive set of score calibration methods. Experiments were conducted across three datasets with varying imbalance configurations and memory constraints. Results indicate that most calibration methods improve performance, offering the greatest benefit in lower memory settings, which are more practical. Additionally, as a secondary contribution, we demonstrate that removing the standard distillation component from incremental learning loss functions yields superior results, showing that simpler vanilla fine-tuning serves as a stronger foundation for imbalanced incremental learning. To ensure these constraints are met, we develop an intermediary filter grounded in reference governors. Since modifications and impact events cause deviations from desired periodic orbits, we robustly guarantee hybrid invariance by employing predictive schemes within a brief time window during the gait cycle. We address the challenge of generating energy-efficient, nominal human joint trajectories that remain robust to variations in carrier dynamics. Building on prior research, we refine nominal trajectories using a genetic algorithm (GA) to minimize a cost function that captures both task performance and dynamic feasibility, accounting for changes in total system mass. Unlike many existing methods, we employ a filter to adjust the optimized energy costs, enabling the robot to walk at varying speeds. We experimentally validate these time-scaled, jointly-optimized trajectories on a 6-DOF humanoid robot (Shacrap@150) navigating flat surfaces at various nominal speeds. Our findings demonstrate a reduction in swing leg end-effector tracking errors compared to traditional space decomposition control structures. Additionally, the proposed optimization successfully accommodates variations in carrier masses of up to $0.5$ kg.

Based on collaboration structures, FL is categorized into Horizontal Federated Learning (HFL) and Vertical Federated Learning (VFL). In HFL, entities share identical feature spaces and data samples, whereas in VFL, they share common sample identifiers and collaborate on features. VFL offers a wider application scope and is particularly well-suited for joint model training among large enterprises.

This paper concentrates on VFL, examining potential privacy vulnerabilities within real-world frameworks. We developed and executed two practical privacy attacks: a reverse multiplication attack targeting the logistic regression VFL protocol and a reverse sum attack targeting the XGBoost VFL protocol. Our empirical analysis demonstrates that these attacks are (1) effective, allowing adversaries to extract private training data even when intermediate outputs are encrypted; (2) evasive, as they adhere strictly to protocol specifications and do not degrade the target model's accuracy; and (3) low-effort, requiring minimal prior knowledge of the target participant's data distribution. Furthermore, we show that the information leaked is as potent as the original training data for training alternative classifiers. Finally, we discuss potential countermeasures and their associated challenges, aiming to inspire future research directions.

In horizontal federated learning, a malicious node can exploit overlapping feature spaces to launch a transferable attack by reverse-engineering a user's data distribution. Vertical federated learning should mitigate this risk since its participants ideally possess disjoint data distributions. However, we demonstrate that an adversary with only a subset of features—such as image data attacking users who only hold text—can still infer the target user's complete data through machine learning-assisted reverse multiplication. We term this the "Reverse Multiplication Attack."

VFL protocols like difference privacy and secure multi-party computation were designed to prevent such attacks, yet they have significant drawbacks including poor privacy-utility trade-offs and high computational costs. Consequently, we propose that HFL's overlapping feature space is a more serious vulnerability, as a malicious node can reverse-multiply from that subset to attack the entire data distribution.

To overcome this, Random Fourier Features (RFF) were introduced to approximate kernel functions using randomized Fourier features, enabling scalability. This paper re-examines FPN within the detection framework to uncover the underlying reasons for its success from an optimization standpoint. We identify that the decline in large-object performance stems from improper back-propagation paths created when FPN is incorporated, which restricts each backbone level to processing objects only within specific scale ranges. Based on this analysis, we propose two viable strategies to ensure every backbone level can perceive objects across all scales in FPN-based architectures. The first strategy involves introducing auxiliary objective functions so that each backbone level directly receives back-propagation signals from objects of various scales during training. The second approach entails constructing the feature pyramid more rationally to eliminate illogical back-propagation routes. Extensive experiments on the COCO benchmark confirm the validity of our analysis and the efficacy of our proposed methods. Without relying on complex additions, we demonstrate that our approach yields substantial improvements (exceeding 2%) across diverse detection frameworks, including one-stage, two-stage, anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based detectors. Notably, on the ResNet-50 backbone, our technique achieves an additional 2.55% Gain in Average Precision (AP) for large objects (sizes > 9,600 pixels). In the continuous learning process of deep neural networks, different layers often specialize in recognizing patterns of varying frequencies, a phenomenon termed separation of concerns (SoC). While SoC has been thoroughly analyzed in single-classification tasks, its role in multi-object detection remains unclear, particularly regarding the interaction between backbone layers and the application of FPN. This paper re-examines SoC and its dynamics within FPN-based multi-object detection systems. By carefully analyzing the optimization behavior of these networks, we reveal that SoC in multi-object detection is not as explicit as in single-classification tasks; the backbone layers do not strictly separate by response frequency, instead focusing on objects of corresponding sizes. Furthermore, the introduction of FPN does not necessarily enhance SoC, as it may confine the responsibility of detecting objects of certain sizes to only one or a few intermediate backbone levels. Leveraging these insights, we propose a novel attention module designed to strengthen SoC within FPN-based detectors by explicitly enhancing the representation of objects at each scale through an economy-of-scale mechanism. In this study, we propose a sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, derived from a Michelson interferometer by optically linking the end mirrors to form an additional cavity. Sagnac interferometers can be derived from Michelson interferometers by optically connecting either the input or output end mirrors to create an extra cavity, resulting in a triply-coupled cavity system. This topology can be integrated with both power- and signal-recycling cavities to form advanced interferometer designs. We examine how the high-frequency (shot-noise) limit and the low-frequency (loss-noise) limit in sloshing-Sagnac interferometers are influenced by the optical losses in both the Sagnac and Michelson cavities. Furthermore, the low-frequency limit in these sloshing-Sagnac interferometers can be significantly lower than in signal-recycled Michelson interferometers, potentially by a factor of ten or more, due to the deeper quantum correlation of quadratures in the sloshing-Sagnac configuration.

Finally, the study confirms that the second derivative of the mass radius relation for GW190814 is negative, a critical feature for resolving the mass gap. The human brain continuously generates new representations for previously unseen objects, a process largely driven by attention to specific visual features. However, prior computational models have mainly relied on arbitrary, hand-crafted feature sets. We propose a framework that learns these essential features directly from data, mirroring human strategy by training a neural classifier on such hand-crafted features using a seen class distribution, then utilizing a universal approximator to estimate a distribution over the resulting residual errors. These estimated distributions allow us to learn new feature distributions for entirely unseen classes. When applied to ImageNet, our method achieves comparable performance to models trained on those specific classes.

In machine translation, neural models often struggle to generate rare words, frequently settling for generic synonyms like "x" or "other". This happens because the vast majority of training data consists of common words, causing neural models to over-rely on the training $N$-gram and under-explore other feature spaces. Our approach addresses this by applying a universal approximator to the residual matrix between a language model trained on a source language and its target counterpart. This enables the model to learn residual feature spaces specific to rare words in the source language, which are particularly discriminative for translation. On three English-to-foreign language tasks, our method consistently outperforms both standalone $N$-gram models and various neural models, including those trained on English-specific data.

Introducing a finite charge density modifies fracton mobility and creates a competition between the chemical potential and superfluid velocity in setting the dilaton gap. Furthermore, fracton mobility can be altered even at zero density by incorporating additional higher-derivative terms. Finally, we propose that fracton theory offers a robust theoretical framework for investigating the interplay between dilaton and spin-3/2 fields. This formal agreement suggests the potential for isolating immobile dilaton modes in experimental settings, potentially through analogies with the g-modes of neutron stars. Introduced in this work, this dilaton-spin-3/2 scenario extends the "patchy dilaton" model previously employed to explain the soft mode of charge-ordered organic insulators. Additionally, we provide a brief exploration of generalizing this theory to incorporate fermions. This generalization may aid in understanding the enigmatic behavior of certain superfluids and superconductors at quantum metal-fluidic transitions. Copyright (c) 2021 by the author(s). In this regime, cosmological perturbations are amplified significantly, leading to a breakdown characterized by an enhanced scalar power spectrum and substantial negative values for the Bardeen potential. This deep sub-horizon environment proves conducive to primordial black hole (PBH) formation. Working in the spatially flat gauge with $\delta\phi\neq 0$, we explicitly demonstrate how perturbations in both the inflaton field and the background gravitational field drive these enhancements and subsequent PBH generation. We compute the parameters $\sigma(M)$, $\beta(M)$, and $f_\mathrm{PBH}(M)$ near peaks in the density contrast profile to estimate the current dark matter fraction attributable to PBHs across specific mass scales. Our analysis indicates PBH formation within the wavenumber range $0.43\times 10^{13}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ to $9.8\times 10^{13}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, corresponding to masses between $1.35\times 10^{-13}M_\odot$ and $2.60\times 10^{-16}M_\odot$. These objects exhibit evaporation times ranging from $7.74\times 10^{33}$ sec down to $5.53\times 10^{29}$ sec, and we anticipate future constraints from gamma-ray telescopes. Finally, we propose that monitoring microlensing events using the JWST could help constrain both the mass and abundance of these PBHs.

The reliance on computer-based vote tabulation systems has increased globally since their introduction, offering clear benefits in speed and security while clearly addressing the drawbacks of manual counting. Despite these advantages, there is a concern that errors in vote tabulation can lead to significant mistakes in determining election winners, a phenomenon documented in studies regarding the 2000 US presidential election. Although previous research has explored OCR applications in vote tabulation, it has largely focused on digitizing ballots and converting ink marks to digits, a process that can generate errors requiring correction. Such errors can be categorized into two types: identification errors, where a mark is misidentified (e.g., a full circle being read as a half circle), and missing errors, where a mark is overlooked (e.g., a full circle being read as no mark). The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the effectiveness of iOCR in correcting missing errors in vote tabulation.

This study demonstrates that iOCR outperforms standard OCR in correcting missing errors caused by noise, achieves higher accuracy than human workers in identifying and correcting errors, and offers significant cost savings compared to manual labor.

The use of OCR in vote tabulation was introduced in prior work, along with the identification of two error types: missing and identification errors. That previous research estimated the distribution of missing error distributions based on ballots read by human workers. This study extends that work by measuring the performance of iOCR in correcting missing error distributions across various regular expressions, comparing its effectiveness against standard OCR and the error distributions of human voters and correction experts.

While previous research has examined over-parameterized linear models with non-sparse, high-dimensional data, those findings largely rely on the assumption of independent samples. This study investigates linear regression under over-parameterization with dependent time series data. We propose an interpolation-based estimator and establish a theoretical framework for its excess risk across various dependence structures. This approach accommodates infinite-dimensional data without requiring sparsity and unifies the handling of long-memory processes. Furthermore, we bound the risk using integrated covariance and the nondegeneracy of autocorrelation matrices. Our results indicate that convergence rates for short-memory processes match those of independent data, whereas long-memory processes decelerate convergence. Additionally, we provide examples of specific dependent processes applicable to this framework. Simulation results align with our theoretical predictions. The methods and outcomes presented here have broad applicability and extend to related problems. On the technical front, the innovations in this work address challenges that have historically been associated with non-i.i.d. learning.

Recent studies by Berend et al. (2019) and Khashabi et al. (2021) demonstrate that optimal sample complexity for proper learning of concept classes with polynomial growth functions requires exponential excess dimension. This paper extends those results to an improper learning setting, showing that exponential excess dimension is still necessary to achieve optimal sample complexity, even when the hypothesis class is unrestricted. This finding links the sample complexity of improper learning to the shattering dimension, a concept from VC theory applicable to non-i.i.d. learning. Additionally, we prove that certain concept classes with polynomial growth functions cannot be properly learned with more than a polynomial number of samples, regardless of the hypothesis class's size. These findings contrast with the work of Deming et al. (2019), which identifies limitations of double-descent phenomena in proper learning. Through both theoretical analysis and simulations, we illustrate that improper learning can achieve optimal sample complexity without incurring generalization gaps. Furthermore, we show that specific concept classes fulfill the conditions outlined by Tishby and Nagakarun (2020) for the presence of a generalization gap.

This paper presents a novel deep learning framework for speech enhancement that integrates a comprehensive attention mechanism into a bidirectional sequence-to-sequence approach. By leveraging latent information following each focal frame, this model extends earlier attention-driven recurrent neural network methods. For automatic speech recognition, obtaining high-quality input audio is crucial for accurate results. While existing deep learning architectures process input audio to generate output audio, they often fail to leverage the rich information contained in noisy signals. This paper introduces a new deep learning architecture for speech recognition capable of automatically utilizing latent information from noisy audio. Based on a sequence-to-sequence framework, the system employs a bidirectional long short-term memory network with a multi-layered structure. Each layer incorporates a multi-scale attention mechanism featuring a comprehensive component designed to capture latent info from noisy audio. Experimental data confirms that this multi-layered bidirectional LSTM structure with multi-scale attention yields more accurate automatic speech recognition results than single-layered or unidirectional alternatives. Additionally, the system demonstrates effective speech enhancement capabilities, producing clearer output audio even from heavily noisy sources. Finally, the paper shows that this bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory Network with multi-scale attention can be effectively applied to both speech enhancement and automatic speech recognition.

This work proposes a new deep learning approach for speech enhancement that integrates a multi-scale attention mechanism into a bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory network. The multi-scale attention utilizes latent info from noisy audio to generate weighted scores across various scales, which are then applied to the noisy signal. These applied scores contain latent info from the original clean speech, helping the system produce higher-quality enhanced speech. Based on a frame mapping scheme, a time-delay neural network predicts the next frame using these enhanced frames. critical component of Biosafety Levels (BSLs) in laboratories and infection-control hospitals, designed to contain deadly pathogens and prevent their escape. These rooms maintain internal pressure lower than the surrounding environment to ensure microbial containment. Currently, Building Management Systems (BMSs) rely on Differential Pressure Sensors (DPSs) to monitor and regulate this negative pressure. This paper presents a stealthy, non-invasive attack on NPRs by spoofing a DPS at its resonant frequency. Our key contributions are: (1) identifying that DPSs commonly used in NPRs possess resonant frequencies within the audible spectrum; (2) developing malicious music to induce resonance in these sensors, which causes their pressure readings to overshoot; and (3) demonstrating how this resonance can deceive BMSs into switching an NPR's negative pressure to positive, creating a risk of pathogen leakage. Through experiments on 8 DPSs from 5 manufacturers, we found resonance-induced reading errors ranged from 0.68 to 6.85 Pa, with a typical 30-second timing delay. Our attack was successfully executed using audible music, causing DPS reading errors of approximately 2.38 ± 1.03 Pa. This attack is particularly insidious because it induces resonance in the audible range and is maintainable via medium-volume music, making it a plausible, non-stealthy, and noisy threat to NPR safety. This research underscores the need for hardening industrial sensor electronics against resonant attacks. The code for this attack is available at https://github.com/AmirShakeri/Resonant-DPS-Attack.

Although this phenomenon is often blamed on forecasting inaccuracies or operational breakdowns, we argue it stems from risk-averse scheduling strategies. By applying a stochastic self-scheduling model to real-world data from the Australian National Electricity Market, we show that risk-averse storage units adopt a short-sighted operational approach. Specifically, they focus primarily on near-term price arbitrage, targeting only a limited number of extreme price peaks and valleys, which leaves them inactive during many periods characterized by significantly high or low prices. These findings carry significant policy weight, particularly given the lack of transparency surrounding unit-level risk aversion and the visible risks involved in intervention decisions. Our results offer concrete evidence to inform debates on the criteria for selecting storage facilities for government support and help clarify the strategic challenges inherent in storing energy. Methodologically, our study provides empirical validation for the recently proposed stochastic self-scheduling model.

We anticipate that this research will influence future studies on storage unit risk aversion, such as those employing cross-entropy methods to determine risk preferences from dispatch data. While we present the first empirical evidence of risk-averse behavior in a distributed optimization context, we expect to soon demonstrate how to solve equivalent problems through direct optimization in real-time. Furthermore, we aim to extend this work by using the self-scheduling model to investigate other concerns regarding storage, including market power, in both generic frameworks and specific market environments.

We expect storage to become essential for supporting low-carbon power grids; however, there is a notable lack of literature confirming that it can effectively provide reliability. While we have demonstrated the risk-averse nature of existing storage assets, we aim to use these insights to reevaluate storage's potential for reliability services and the necessity of government interventions to prevent market failures. We also plan to apply these findings to historical data from other markets, such as California and the Eastern Sebastian Market, to determine if the observed behaviors are location-specific or represent a broader trend. Additionally, we aim to explore how to elicit search radii from participants in our rolling horizon experiments, rather than relying on the default radius of one hour, to better understand the impact of limited look-ahead windows on risk-averse storage units. Finally, we plan to extend the current analysis by examining risk-averse behavior in the wholesale electricity market under the Uniform Price clearing mechanism, which is expected to yield distinct outcomes compared to the Pay-As-You-Clear mechanism

The model incorporates simplified linear boundary layer friction, Newtonian cooling, and dry convective adjustment. Through a series of controlled experiments, researchers varied the planetary rotation rate and the imposed equator-to-pole temperature gradient. These variables were converted into dimensionless parameters to define a parameter space where distinct circulation regimes are identified and categorized. Significant trends emerge when altering the planetary rotation rate alongside frictional and thermal relaxation timescales. Additionally, a regular baroclinic wave regime appears at intermediate thermal Rossby numbers, with its characteristics and dominant zonal wavenumber heavily influenced by radiative and frictional damping strengths. AL is particularly valuable in large-scale industrial applications where labeling expenses are high, prompting practitioners to utilize every available technique to enhance model accuracy. The recent achievements of self-supervised pretraining (SSP) underscore the significance of leveraging vast amounts of unlabeled data to improve model outcomes. In this study, we investigate the combination of AL and SSP using ImageNet. Through careful analysis, we attribute this limitation to a specific phase-transition-like phenomenon inherent to AL. We attribute these phenomena to the volume of data used for labeling. By elucidating the behavioral patterns of AL and its interaction with SSP, we provide essential insights for effectively applying AL to massive datasets.

To address these challenges, we introduce MixAL, a simple yet potent active learning framework that integrates global and local uncertainty with sample diversity. Evaluated on ImageNet, MixAL demonstrates a 5% improvement over strong baselines using only 10% of the data for labeling, surpassing 50+ existing AL methods. Additionally, we address several underserved issues in current literature, such as the impacts of scale, very small labeling budgets, and baseline comparisons. The source code for MixAL and our experiments is available open-source at: https://github.com/MingyeanDong/MixAL.

Concurrently, Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NOMA) has emerged as a promising technology for fifth-generation (5G) wireless systems. This paper introduces and evaluates an Adaptive Cooperative NOMA (ACN) protocol designed for vehicular communications at intersections. The system facilitates transmission between a source and two destinations, subject to interference from vehicles distributed on the roads according to a Poisson Point Process (PPP). First, we derive closed-form expressions for the outage probability of the ACN protocol. Subsequently, we compare these results with existing protocols in the literature. Our findings demonstrate that the ACN protocol achieves a substantial reduction in outage probability compared to current solutions, especially within intersection scenarios. Furthermore, the ACN protocol exhibits superior performance relative to other protocols at high data rates. These theoretical conclusions are validated through Monte-Carlo simulations.

Consequently, the combined problem of power allocation and scheduling becomes a mixed-integer non-convex challenge that is NP-hard. To address this, we introduce a low-complexity, decentralized framework that decouples power allocation from scheduling. In this approach, power is distributed centrally, while transmission modes are determined via a non-cooperative game aiming for a mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium. We evaluate two payoff calculation methods corresponding to different cross-interference power models and their associated communication overheads. Simulation results in a dense outdoor small-cell environment demonstrate that our proposed methods significantly outperform static TDD configurations. Furthermore, the optimal cross-interference power modeling approach yields a 33% increase in the probability of meeting rate requirements compared to the other method. Theoretical analysis of the cross-interference model is also presented.

Modern mobile data traffic volume has grown exponentially, necessitating higher spectral and temporal efficiency in wireless networks. While user density increases, distributed network optimization becomes difficult, and complex, centralized solutions often lack the scalability for real-time execution. This paper introduces a two-step decentralized framework consisting of a multi-access point coordinate descent algorithm for power allocation and a multi-access point game for uplink/sdownlink scheduling. We show that these components, when combined, enhance the overall system sum-rate and provide a clear division of responsibilities between the two steps. The power allocation requires only local channel state information (CSI) and a global rate target, making it suitable for mobile data environments. The scheduling step involves a message exchange protocol among access points that does not rely on channel knowledge. Simulations confirm that this two-step method achieves a solution quality comparable to jointly optimized problems but offers significantly better scalability and decentralization.

Access points (APs) in dense wireless local area networks (WLANs) utilize time-division multiple access (TDMA) to mitigate co-channel interference. We model the joint optimization of AP scheduling and user power control as a game-theoretic framework. Specifically, we define a stacked non-cooperative game where a mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium (NE) represents uplink/downlink scheduling, and a continuous best response represents power control. Because the resulting mixed-strategy game is high-dimensional, we employ a learning-based approach using multiagent reinforcement learning (RL). This learning process requires no information about the game's structure, such as dimensions or payoffs. Our evaluation shows that the learning-based solution outperforms heuristic methods

This study presents a quantitative analysis of magnetotransport data from BSCCO thin films reported by Zhao et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 122, 247001 (2019)], which supports a previously suggested vacancy mechanism [J. Phys. Condens. Matter. 10, L677 (1998)] enhanced by many-body vortex correlations. The model posits that the Hall anomaly arises from the movement of vacancies within pinned fragments of the vortex lattice. Initial validation explores vortex states near the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition within the vortex crystal. Subsequently, the measured activation energies are compared against the calculated creation energies for vortex-anti-vortex pairs and vacancies on the flux-line lattice without employing any adjustable parameters. This analysis clarifies the theoretical foundations and prerequisites of the vacancy model, notably revealing that vacancy activation energies are approximately one order of magnitude lower than those of an isolated vortex line. Ultimately, this proposed mechanism may offer a macro-theoretical framework applicable to other investigations.

Addressing the uncertainty surrounding the vortex core structure is essential for a comprehensive understanding of the Hall anomaly's source. While the vacancy model enhances stability when vortex cores are "fuzzy," the comparison of activation energies suggests that, in terms of an effective classical lattice, the "lattice constant" for an isolated vortex is roughly ten times larger than that for a vacancy. The absence of a rigorous theory for fuzzy vortex cores is one of several reasons the vacancy model remains unconfirmed. We advocate for the use of vortex-antivortex pairs as a complementary mechanism; however, its parameters require adjustment to fit the data, and it fails to account for activation energy comparisons. Consequently, we recommend revisiting the examination of vortex core structures, potentially utilizing the pair model with a focus on determining its microscopic parameters.

The vortex core structure remains an active area of debate. The vacancy model is viable when these cores are "fuzzy," yet the observation of a zero-crossing in the Hall anomaly at intermediate fields suggests otherwise. In contrast, the vortex-antivortex pair model applies when cores are well-defined; however, it does not explain the hallmark zero-crossing feature.

This study examines the temperature dependence of second- to fourth-order (factorial) cumulants of the order parameter by employing the parametric representation of the three-dimensional Ising model, which shares the same universality class as Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). Results indicate that at the critical temperature, normalized cumulants remain independent of the external magnetic field, establishing a fixed point in their temperature evolution. Monte Carlo simulations of finite-size systems confirm that this fixed point behavior persists at temperatures close to the critical value. Furthermore, this phenomenon is observed in the temperature dependence of normalized factorial cumulants starting from the fourth order. Through a mapping from the Ising model to QCD, a similar fixed point behavior is identified in the energy dependence of normalized cumulants (including fourth-order factorial cumulants) along various freeze-out curves. Although the correspondence between the lattice QCD energy scale and the Ising model temperature scale remains unquantified, the existence of this fixed point suggests that experimental data could be interpreted using the universal properties of the Ising universality class.

section0 Introduction

Semantic parsing converts natural language questions into executable query languages, a capability with wide-ranging applications in query generation, information extraction, and more. While existing research has primarily concentrated on generating syntactically correct queries, the recent rise in zero-shot semantic parsing has shifted focus to ensuring exact match accuracy. Although the recent transformer-based DNN approach by Huang et al.~\cite{huang2019learning} achieved high exact match results on the Wikipedia-QA task~\cite{hacker2016building} without training, our analysis reveals that many state-of-the-art methods still suffer from low execution accuracy in practical settings when database contents are absent. This discrepancy highlights the necessity of value filling, yet current models typically ignore it due to the lack of closed-form solutions for synthesizing complete queries.

We propose a novel semantic parsing framework designed to generate OpenSQL~\cite{shah2014comprehensive} that incorporates database contents via value filling, thereby achieving high execution accuracy even when contents are missing. Specifically, we tackle two key challenges in practical value filling: (1) handling closed-world assumptions where all relevant data exists within the provided databases, and (2) managing an excessive number of rows that could degrade execution accuracy if included.

### 1. Introduction

Music discovery involves helping users find new tracks or albums, while music recommendation aims to suggest existing items (like playlists) to users. Although these tasks appear distinct, they share the fundamental goal of enabling music discovery. There is a significant overlap between the information required for and the techniques used in discovery and recommendation. For instance, in a music player prototype developed for this work, each track's metadata is used to generate a description that highlights the track's main features (discovery), and users are suggested tracks based on the profiles of other users who have listened to those tracks (recommendation). Similarly, a playlist's description can be generated from the metadata of the included tracks, with the suggested playlists for a user created using the same underlying technique as the track descriptions.

However, recommending items without providing descriptions can make it difficult for users to discover new music. Consequently, a key objective of this work is to generate music playlist descriptions that assist in discovery. Although this task is comparable to other music information retrieval problems [1], it is unique because it necessitates combining audio content analysis with metadata. Specifically, the proposed method for generating these descriptions utilizes both the audio content and metadata of each track within the playlist.

Collision evasion maneuvers are formulated using dynamic vortex potential fields (PFs) and their negative gradients, creating a reciprocal, cooperative dynamic between the robots. The repulsive field depends on the relative velocity and position of a robot with respect to others, and the inclusion of vorticity in its definition ensures there are no local minima. Through an analysis of kinematics-based engagement dynamics in polar coordinates, the study demonstrates that a cooperative robot can successfully avoid collisions with non-cooperating entities, including stationary objects, constant-velocity robots, and those actively attempting to collide. Finally, a collision avoidance control system for a mobile robot is designed and implemented, illustrating the effective performance of the proposed methods. These results provide a foundation for developing packet loss-resilient inter-vehicle communication protocols to enable the collision avoidance of multiple robots with limited observability. Vortex potential fields and their gradients offer distinct advantages over traditional PFs for this domain, as they allow the field to pass through a finite distance known as the "eddy" surrounding a robot, regardless of the engagement dynamics. This property prevents the emergence of local minima and is crucial for enabling robots to actively seek out and investigate targets for applications like foraging and sensing. In this study, collision avoidance strategies for non-holonomic robots moving at constant linear speeds in a 2-D plane are investigated. Collisions are defined as the 2-D Cartesian coordinate-wise minimum of the relative position between two robots approaching each other along a trajectory, or the limit of the engagement range as linear speeds approach those of a pure pursuit dynamic. A dynamic vortex potential field (PF) is introduced to prevent collisions. The field's gradient remains finite along all trajectories except those resulting in a collision, and it approaches zero only asymptotically as the engagement range is reached.

In the context of the annealed large deviation principle (LDP) for the empirical process of these words, the rate function corresponds to the specific relative entropy between the observed and reference laws of words. Birkner, Greven, and den Hollander \cite{BGdH10} established the quenched LDP (conditional on a typical letter sequence) for scenarios where renewal times exhibit an algebraic tail; their derived rate function consists of two components: the annealed rate function and a second term proportional to the specific relative entropy between the observed and reference laws of letters, where the reference law is generated by concatenating words and randomizing the origin. This proportionality constant matches the tail exponent of the renewal process. The current paper aims to generalize both LDPs to cases where the underlying letter sequences are not i.i.d. It demonstrates that both principles remain valid when the letter sequence satisfies a mixing condition known as \emph{summable variation}. The resulting rate functions are still expressed as specific relative entropies with respect to the reference laws of words and letters, respectively. However, because neither reference law is i.i.d., the extension requires several approximation arguments. The paper also provides lower bounds that rely on coupling techniques applicable to the mixing condition and outlines upper bounds that hold for a broader class of letter sequences. Finally, lower bounds are given for a specific non-i.i.d. model featuring a drift; it is conjectured that the associated rate function aligns with the i.i.d. case.

Composed of passive reflective elements, an IRS can adjust the phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization of incident waveforms. These advantageous properties enable the control and optimization of wireless channel characteristics to meet specific signal design and processing requirements, thereby offering substantial potential for radar applications. This paper establishes the theoretical basis for integrating IRS into radar systems and examines the potential for enhancing target parameter estimation. Specifically, we analyze IRS deployment in scenarios where line-of-sight (LOS) links are weak or obstructed. We demonstrate that IRS can create a virtual or non-line-of-sight (NLOS) connection between the radar and the target, resulting in improved radar performance. The efficacy of this IRS-enabled virtual link in estimating moving target parameters is illustrated under both optimized and non-optimized conditions. Numerical simulations reveal that IRS enhances target parameter estimation when the LOS link's relative strength is weaker than approximately $10^{-1}$ compared to the NLOS link. Furthermore, if the NLOS link exhibits a favorable path loss exponent, IRS can significantly boost radar performance; otherwise, even a relatively strong LOS link can be substantially weakened by obstruction. Finally, we show that IRS can effectively extend the maximum detectable target distance. These findings provide fundamental insight into how IRS can establish a virtual link to moving targets for superior target parameter estimation. Additionally, we suggest that time modulation could be employed to multiplex multiple radar transmitters sharing an aperture via IRS for joint target observation. The proposed approach can be implemented in practical, often NLOS, environments and holds the promise of improving the performance of existing radar systems. Current limitations of IRS in radar, such as hardware hardware hardware hardware constraints, channel estimation, and signal optimization, are discussed to provide a comprehensive understanding of how IRS can enhance existing radar capabilities.

ing software vulnerabilities. Although significant advancements have been made recently, accurately measuring and comparing the efficacy of different fuzzers remains an unresolved research challenge. In software testing, mutation analysis stands as the gold standard for assessing test quality; it evaluates a test's capacity to identify synthetic bugs, operating on the principle that tests failing to catch these artificial faults will also miss real ones. By encompassing various coverage metrics and offering a vast, diverse array of faults that can be engineered to be difficult to trigger and detect, mutation analysis effectively avoids issues related to saturation and overfitting. However, traditional mutation analysis is prohibitively expensive for fuzzing because each mutation requires independent evaluation. This paper leverages modern mutation analysis techniques that pool multiple mutations, enabling the first-ever evaluation and comparison of fuzzers using this method. We introduce a dedicated benchmark for fuzzers, applying it to several popular tools and targets. Our comprehensive study demonstrates how this approach allows for the assessment of fuzzer performance and the measurement of improvements in specific techniques. Although our findings indicate that current fuzzers detect only a small fraction of mutations, we view this as a critical area for future research, specifically focusing on enhancing (1) the detection of failures beyond generic crashes and (2) the ability to trigger mutations (and consequently, faults).

Many of these methods rely on mechanisms applied to pre-trained representations, restricting or entirely avoiding updates to the backbone during continual training. In this paper, we challenge the necessity of such model complexity for achieving high performance by introducing a simple baseline for comparison. We contend that a pretrained feature extractor alone can deliver competitive or superior continual learning results on the Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 benchmarks. To test this, we developed a straightforward baseline that: 1) utilizes a frozen pretrained model to extract features for each class encountered, computing their mean on training data, and 2) classifies inputs using nearest neighbor distance to these class means, termed the Nearest Mean Classifier (NMC). This single-headed, exemplar-free, and potentially task-free baseline (via continual mean updates) achieved 88.53% accuracy on the 10-Split-CIFAR-100 dataset, outperforming most state-of-the-art methods initialized with the same pretrained transformer. We hope this work encourages future research into learning systems that can continuously enhance representation quality, even when starting from pretrained weights. Our code is available at https://github.com/Aniruddha-Debnath/Further思考.

64Ni nucleus has been significantly refined by integrating data from four experiments, which identified multiple 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV and determined their properties. The Monte Carlo shell model successfully reproduces these findings, revealing an unexpectedly intricate landscape of coexisting shapes. Notably, a prolate 0+ excitation was found at a surprisingly high energy of 3463 keV, with a collective 2+ state situated 286 keV above it; this marks the first such observation in Ni isotopes. Furthermore, the shift in the excitation energy of the prolate minimum across the neutron N = 40 subshell gap underscores the influence of the monopole interaction and its strength variations with N. The removal of the N = 40 gap's barrier effect and the associated coexistence of different shapes are also discussed, along with the impact of our updated level scheme on the inferred electric quadrupole moment and magnetic dipole moment of the low-spin low-energy state. Finally, the excited-state structure of 64Ni is contrasted with other N = 40 nucleon subshell states, and the newly identified long-lived 0+ state offers fresh insights into isomer decay pathways and the placement of 64Ni within the patellar region of the nuclear shell model. Ni-64, a key component of solar neutrino capture reactions, benefits from a more accurate weak interaction matrix element calculation following this updated level scheme. The precision of the fit to 64Ni data using the Monte Carlo shell model confirms its utility for predicting properties of long-lived excited states in nearby nickel isotopes, a finding that is indeed supported by recent experimental results for 62Ni.

Recent work by Jonsson et al. used high-resolution gamma-ray spectroscopy to revise the low-lying level scheme of 64Ni, detecting several previously unobserved or incomplete 0+ and 2+ states. They demonstrated that these games possess $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria under specific conditions for $\epsilon$ and $\lambda$, but they did not address the computational difficulty of locating such equilibria. This paper addresses that gap by constructing a query-efficient reduction from broader game classes to Lipschitz games. Utilizing this reduction, we establish an exponential query lower bound for any randomized algorithm seeking $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria in $n$-player, binary-action, $\lambda$-Lipschitz games, where the exponent scales with $\frac{n\lambda}{\epsilon}$. Furthermore, we propose "Multi-Lipschitz games," a generalization allowing player-specific Lipschitz constants, and demonstrate a reduction to standard Lipschitz games, revealing that the critical parameter is the sum of individual Lipschitz values. Finally, we derive an exponential lower bound on the deterministic query complexity required to find $\epsilon$-approximate correlated equilibria in $n$-player, $m$-action, $\lambda$-Lipschitz games for sufficiently large $\epsilon$, thereby highlighting the necessity of randomized approaches for the aforementioned results. Our proof methodology is notably more straightforward than prior techniques used to achieve similar findings. As a application, we achieve nearly optimal bounds for the query complexity of approximately solving median voting games. Specifically, we prove an exponential lower bound on the query complexity of $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria in $n$-player median voting games and demonstrate that the randomized "lift and round" algorithm by Daskalakis et al. \cite{Daskalakis2009} can be enhanced for this context to efficiently compute such equilibria. We also present a simpler lower bound of $3^n\epsilon$, improving upon the prior best bound of $2^n\epsilon$ established by Azrieli and Shmaya \cite{Azrieli2011}. Additionally, we show a lower bound of $\Omega(n^2/\epsilon^2)$ on the query complexity of *randomized* algorithms aiming to approximate pure Nash equilibria in mean payoff games, a problem previously regarded as solvable within polynomial query complexity. However, because CV relies on random data partitioning, the resulting performance estimates are stochastic and can exhibit significant variability, particularly in natural language processing (NLP). We show that such unstable estimates are unsuitable for effective parameter tuning; consequently, the selected parameters are highly sensitive to data splits, often leading to sub-optimal choices and severe reproducibility challenges.

To address this, we propose employing J-K-fold CV, which utilizes J independent K-fold cross-validations to assess performance. Our primary contributions involve extending J-K-fold CV to the domain of parameter tuning and exploring strategies for selecting optimal values for J and K. We argue that minimizing variability is more critical than reducing bias for successful tuning, advocating for lower-than-typical values of K in NLP literature. This allows computational resources to be redirected toward increasing J. To validate the broad applicability of our recommendations, we examine a diverse set of case studies, including sentiment classification (both general and target-specific), part-of-speech tagging, and document classification. Our empirical findings demonstrate that our proposed methods yield significant performance gains in these classification and tagging tasks, often surpassing the improvements achievable through extensive single K-fold CV with a large dataset. We further provide a comprehensive discussion on the implications of our work for researchers operating under limited computational constraints and varying data sizes.

In a related development, we explore techniques for reducing the high variance inherent in standard cross-validation when applied to sequence-labeling tasks like part-of-speech tagging. By analyzing the source of this variance, we develop a modified cross-validation approach for estimating model performance that demonstrates lower variance and requires considerably less computation. Extensive experiments on various datasets and models confirm that this new method produces more reliable estimates of generalization error than typical cross-validation schemes.

We characterize the variance of generalization error in cross-validation for sequence-labeling as stemming from fluctuations in training and validation loss as a function of data size. This variance can be significantly reduced by averaging performance metrics across a subset of parameters—such as the number of entities—within the sequences. This results in a modified cross-validation procedure that lowers training error variance and performs competitively against conventional methods on various part-of-speech tagging datasets. We note that while cross-validation variance can be mitigated by averaging over features or parameters, reducing bias remains an open challenge.

at addressing large-scale problems across numerous domains, their deployment in real-time systems is often hindered by the sheer volume of parameters involved. To overcome this challenge, Teacher-Student architectures were initially introduced in the context of knowledge distillation, enabling lightweight student networks to match the performance of complex teacher models. Recently, these architectures have been widely adopted for diverse knowledge learning tasks, including knowledge distillation, expansion, adaptation, and multi-task learning. Leveraging such frameworks, recent research has successfully achieved multiple learning objectives through efficient and compact student networks. Unlike previous surveys focused solely on knowledge distillation, this review comprehensively examines Teacher-Student architectures across a spectrum of knowledge learning goals. Furthermore, we systematically outline the processes of knowledge construction and optimization, analyze various architectural designs and learning strategies used to acquire representative and robust knowledge, and summarize recent applications in classification, recognition, and generation. Finally, we explore future research directions concerning architecture design, knowledge quality, and theoretical advancements in regression-based learning. By providing a thorough overview, this survey offers valuable insights and practical guidelines for both industry professionals and the academic community regarding Teacher-Student architectures in multi-objective knowledge learning.

The rapid advancement and widespread adoption of Deep Learning (DL) have sparked intense interest in creating models that are both highly accurate and computationally lightweight. While DL has delivered outstanding results in many fields, its heavy computational demands often create a discrepancy between promising offline performance and limited online performance due to hardware constraints. MnasNet addresses this by simultaneously optimizing for both accuracy and efficiency through a novel approach to architectural design that decouples accuracy from efficiency.

Although Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success across various domains, their high computational cost and memory usage often prevent real-time processing on hardware with strict space, power, and time limitations. Mini-batch spectral k-means (MB-SK) offers a solution by serving as a lightweight alternative to DNNs for data exploration and feature reduction, offering comparable performance with lower computational demands. This survey paper evaluates MB-SK against both classical and modern DNNs for classification and time-series forecasting, demonstrating that MB-SK can function as both a feature extractor and a classifier. Additionally, MB-SK serves as an effective training algorithm for DNNs in predicting time series data, with experimental results confirming its viability for constructing light-weight neural networks.

In many computational domains, data must conform to specific formats or structures to be processed or analyzed; for instance, source code requires a parser before analysis. Similarly, in graphical models, many current methods for most probable explanation (MPE) and constrained optimization (COP) rely on efficient algorithms for computing or sampling most probable explanations. This paper introduces a novel representation for graphical models that facilitates both MPE and COP while requiring significantly less memory than traditional formats. By enabling these tasks more readily and efficiently, we can now solve problems in margin inference and optimization that were previously too large for existing methods or lacked any feasible solution technique. Our experiments demonstrate that FABE outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives for most probable explanation (LibToppos, beam search) and constrained optimization (toulbar2, CP-SAT), achieving speedups of up to $10^5$.

We propose that these abrupt shear-thickening events serve as precursors to a rigidity transition and present a comprehensive theory of viscosity based on a universal crossover scaling function that bridges the frictionless jamming point with a rigidity transition induced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Experimental validation using two distinct systems—cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol—demonstrates that viscosity data collapse onto a single universal curve across a broad spectrum of stresses and volume fractions. This collapse identifies two separate scaling regimes characterized by different critical exponents, confirming that frictionless isotropic jamming and frictional shear jamming belong to distinct universality classes. By incorporating material-specific microscale interactions into a scaling variable that governs proximity to shear jamming (dependent on both stress and volume fraction), this reformulation enables the application of established theoretical frameworks for equilibrium critical phenomena to uncover the fundamental physics of the shear thickening transition. Furthermore, we derive an expression for the C1 bifurcation stress that aligns with the scaling variable, offering a novel perspective on high-stress viscosity plateaus observed in recent experiments. These findings provide a robust basis for developing constitutive models of strongly shear-thickening suspensions. Importantly, the principles of universal scaling and order parameters derived from this constitutive model can be adapted to address other complex materials, such as thickening blood or evaporating mineral dust aerosols.

Blood exhibits markedly higher viscosity under high shear conditions compared to stagnant states, a phenomenon attributed to red blood cell (RBC) aggregation that generates an internal network of weak bonds. We formulate a constitutive model for blood that extends the generalized Smoluchowski formalism to incorporate microstructural evolution governed by a Cahn-Hilliard equation. This approach captures both the formation and breakdown of RBC aggregates, enabling the model to reproduce the pronounced viscosity drops in blood flow curves reported in recent literature. By expressing constitutive parameters in terms of RBC properties, we demonstrate that the model remains valid across a wide range of suspensions, suggesting it could serve as a foundation for investigating the血流 dynamics of other high-concentration particle suspensions.

We establish the existence of a quantum phase transition in quantum Hall fluids at filling factor $\nu=1/2$ by linking the low-energy effective theory to the Hamiltonian of non-interacting spin-1/2 particles with on-site repulsion. A phase transition occurs between a non-ordered regime, where interactions are weak, and a quantum disordered phase, where strong interactions cause spin-singlet Roton condensation. This transition is mapped to the critical value $N_c$ of the number of spin-1/2 particles (Landau quasipairs) required to annihilate $N$ non-interacting electrons. While perturbation theory previously established a transition for any $N\ge 4$, we precisely determine the critical number $N_c=10$ for a system with one electron hole ($N=2g+2$ where $g$ denotes the genus). By computing the irreducible character degrees of the Weyl group $A_9$, we verify that no transition occurs for $N=8$, consistent with numerical findings in the literature. These methods are applicable to higher-order corrections and can be generalized to determine $N_c$ for any fixed electron hole number $h! \le 9!$. These findings offer deeper insight into the phases of quantum Hall fluids at $\nu = 1/2$ and the dynamical symmetry breaking patterns in $U(M)\times U(N)$ gauge theories with fundamental matter on non-simply laced lattices.

By employing cluster Gutzwiller mean-field theory, we find that Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions (DMI)—frequently present in various quantum magnets—stabilize these phases, distinguishing them from the pair hopping mechanisms required for ultracold atoms. The threshold DMI strength needed to transition into twisted superfluid and supersolid states relies on the magnitude of frustrated interlayer interactions, which can be adjusted through external pressure or shear forces applied between the layers. Additionally, we demonstrate that DMI strength can be precisely modulated via coupling to engineered circularly polarized light. These findings offer essential direction for the experimental pursuit of twisted superfluid and supersolid triplon phases in actual quantum magnets. Additionally, we discuss the potential for these phases to explain the unexpected behavior of the spiral magnetic phase recently reported in the copper oxide multilayer $\alpha$-(EDT)$$_2$ET.

We examine the probability distribution of WIMP incident velocity relative to the nuclear recoil angle within narrow recoil energy windows, across various WIMP masses and target nuclei. Our simulation results indicate that the scattering probability distribution for available incident velocity-recoil angle combinations within a specific energy window is influenced not only by the velocity distribution of incident halo WIMPs but also by the recoil angle factor. Consequently, the 1-D WIMP "effective" velocity distribution associated with a narrow energy window does not align with that derived simply from the generating velocity distribution of incident halo WIMPs. Therefore, the contribution to the differential WIMP-nucleus scattering event rate in the considered energy window cannot be accurately estimated merely by integrating over the 1-D theoretical velocity distribution of the entire halo WIMP population. As a result, the differential event rate and the corresponding WIMP mass limit derived from the zero-event limit of the 1-D "effective" velocity distribution may differ significantly from the actual event rate and the true WIMP mass limit. We propose that these findings are universally applicable to all direct detection experiments worldwide. Using polystyrene and hydrogel grains with diameter $d$, we examine materials exhibiting high and negligible contact friction, respectively. Drag forces were measured for orientations both perpendicular ($F_\perp$) and parallel ($F_\parallel$) to the cylinder's axis across a range of speeds $U$, spanning from quasi-static to rate-dependent regimes. Results indicate that the drag anisotropy ratio, $\xi = F_\perp/F_\parallel$, is not constant but rises substantially with both the driving rate and the aspect ratio $L/D$ in both granular media. Specifically, for $L/D = 40$, $\xi$ increases from 2.6 to 4.5 in high-friction beds and from 7.0 to 8.2 in low-friction beds as the nondimensional Froude number $Fr = U/\sqrt{g(D+d)}$ varies between $10^{-4}$ and $2 \times 10^{-2}$. On average, $\xi$ exhibits a logarithmic increase with $L/D$ when $L/D \gg 1$. Leveraging the index-matching properties of hydrogel grains in water, we demonstrate that sediment flow around the cylinder aligns with drag dominated by skin friction. Furthermore, by employing thin boundary layer approximations, we validate that the skin friction coefficient on the cylinder surface follows the Blasius solution for a flat plate. In the quasi-static limit, we find $F_\parallel$ scales as $(d/D)^2$, consistent with area friction, while $F_\perp$ scales as $(d/D)$, reflecting form friction. Our data also reveal a distinct tumbling regime for $\xi$ at intermediate Froude numbers. Finally, we discuss the implications of these drag anisotropy findings on the translation and rotation dynamics of cylinders within granular materials. This comprehensive analysis of anisotropic drag extends existing drag coefficients for long cylinders in water-saturated granular beds, offering new insights into the intermediate dynamics of marine organisms and the design of offshore foundations. Investigating drag anisotropy is also crucial for understanding the motion of elongated particles, varicose instabilities in jet impingement, and the spinning dynamics of rounder seeds.

We identify a nearly linear correlation between the outflow mass flux ($\dot{\Sigma}_{\rm out}$) and the star formation rate surface density ($\Sigma_{\rm SFR}$), expressed as $\dot{\Sigma}_{\rm out}\propto\Sigma_{\rm SFR}^{1.06\pm0.10}$, alongside a robust correlation between $\dot{\Sigma}_{\rm out}$ and the gas depletion time, where $\dot{\Sigma}_{\rm out} \propto t_{dep}^{-1.1\pm0.06}$. Assuming that ionized outflow mass scales with total outflow mass, our findings indicate that the areas with the highest $\Sigma_{\rm SFR}$ in IRAS08 are losing more gas through outflows than through stellar conversion. computer system configurations because of vast parameter spaces, intricate interdependencies, and expensive evaluation processes. Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO) has recently addressed these issues by employing probabilistic models; however, its adoption has been limited by the complexity of constructing these models. SBO typically accelerates convergence by decomposing the parameter space using contextual insights from system experts. We introduce BoAnon, an SBO framework that automatically infers system structure from logs. BoAnon offers an API that allows experts to encode domain knowledge as performance models or dependency components, which are then integrated into a probabilistic graph model derived from the learned structure. By applying this expert knowledge to contextualize system behavior within the graph, BoAnon enables the optimizer to discover efficient configurations more rapidly than competing methods. In evaluations using a hardware architecture search task, BoAnon achieved a 5-7x improvement in energy-latency objectives compared to default architectures. This novel pipeline for learning contextual structures makes SBO accessible for diverse computer systems, including databases and stream processors. BoAnon is open-sourced at https://github.com/IBM/BoAnon.

: In this brief, we present an algorithm for learning a Markov Automaton (MA) from observations of an unknown one. Our approach addresses three primary challenges: (1) formulating the learning task as a classification problem, (2) developing a algorithm to construct the underlying MA, and (3) solving the resulting system of inequalities. We evaluate the proposed algorithm across several benchmark systems and compare its performance against alternative learning methods. Our findings demonstrate that the algorithm efficiently accurately learns MAs from system traces, effectively capturing both transitions and probabilistic behaviors. While these Markov Abstractions are designed for model-based analysis, they also serve as a learnable representation for computer systems. Built upon this approach, BoAnon, a newly proposed Bayesian Optimization framework, utilizes the learned MA to contextually optimize system performances. BoAnon has already demonstrated remarkable results in energy-latency optimization for hardware architectures. BoAnon's underlying markov automaton was originally learned using the same algorithm described in this work.

However, the full potential of applications like data integration, search, and interlinking remains unmet when data quality is poor. Although some methods exist for assessing Linked Data quality, their performance suffers as data volumes increase, often exceeding the processing limits of a single machine. This paper introduces DistQualityAssessment, an open-source tool designed to evaluate the quality of large RDF datasets by scaling across a cluster of machines. It represents the first distributed, in-memory method for calculating various quality metrics for big RDF data using Apache Spark. Additionally, we propose a quality assessment pattern that facilitates the creation of new scalable metrics for big data. Integrated with the SANSA framework, this work has been successfully applied to at least three use cases outside the SANSA community. Results demonstrate that our approach is more generic, efficient, and scalable than previously proposed solutions. The software is accessible at https://github.com/SANSA-core/DistQualityAssessment.

The proliferation of software agents has created a demand for methods to automatically generate data models from existing datasets. Existing techniques for creating RDF datasets from relational and text-based data often rely on rule-based rules or language models derived from data examples. This study presents an extension to current software agent model creation methods for structured data, offering two main advancements for scalability on big data and for handling ambiguity. First, the approach leverages distributed, in-memory computing for efficient data model generation. Second, it employs a probabilistic approach for interpreting natural language annotations, using a random field model to interpret text without requiring pre-compiled knowledge. This has been implemented in PrSA, a tool for generating data models for big data. PrSA can process datasets containing billions of triples in under an hour on a mid-sized server cluster, a task impossible with out-of-core algorithms. PrSA also outperforms current software agents in handling ambiguity. The implementation and evaluations are available at https://github.com/SANSA-core/PrSA.

This paper introduces a novel, parameter-free technique for incrementally updating big data by adjusting its data distribution. This approach significantly enhances the performance of both data loading and query execution, including multi-join operations, without incurring high update costs. processes can be effectively modeled using specific parametric frameworks to facilitate statistical analysis. However, standard maximum likelihood (ML) estimation and inference techniques are often fragile, lacking robustness against minor model misspecifications or data contamination. While non-parametric alternatives offer robustness, they frequently suffer from a significant loss in efficiency. To address this, we propose a robust parameter estimation method for discretely observed data from parametric stochastic processes, leveraging the advantageous properties of the density power divergence within a minimum distance inference framework. Specifically, we introduce minimum density power divergence estimators (MDPDE) tailored for independent increment and Markov processes. We derive asymptotic consistency and distributional properties for these MDPDEs under dependent stochastic process settings and demonstrate their superiority over conventional ML estimators through examples such as Poisson processes, drifted Brownian motion, and autoregressive models. Furthermore, we display the practical utility of MDPDEs in change point detection. The findings of this paper are partially supported by the UGC-DSA Phase-2 grant.

In numerous practical contexts, data from stochastic processes can be accurately represented by simple parametric models, enabling robust parameter estimation and subsequent statistical inference. Although minimum density power divergence (MDPD) serves as a valuable measure of discrepancy between probability distributions, its application to estimate parameters of forward recurrence time distributions has not been explored. This paper extends MDPD to fill that gap. Based on this extension, we develop a minimum density power divergence estimator (MDPE) specifically for independently varying stochastic processes. We establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of this MDPE. The discussion includes applications to estimating parameters of Poisson processes and independent increment processes, as well as detecting shifts in the distribution of interarrival times. Although independent of particular processes, the derived asymptotic properties enable the use of a bootstrap procedure for calculating standard errors. Examples are provided to illustrate the efficacy of the proposed estimator. Previously, the author addressed related topics in *Robust Parameter Estimation and Inference For Stochastic Processes* (2021).

Many existing methods for estimating parameters of parametric models are highly sensitive to outliers. Although the minimum density power divergence estimator (MDPDE) offers robustness, it remains inefficient. This paper presents a novel approach to generate a robust estimator that improves upon the traditional MDPDE in terms of efficiency. Although independently valuable, this method also holds specific significance for its application to point process estimation.

Our analysis of electron temperature distributions in active galaxies reveals values ranging from 8,000 to over 30,000 K. In Mrk 79 and Mrk 348, gas outflows generate shocks that significantly influence the observed temperature patterns, whereas standard photoionization models adequately explain the temperature data for Mrk 607. For Mrk 79 and Mrk 348, we identify direct evidence of shock-ionization oriented orthogonally to the ionization axis; these shocks are readily detectable because the nuclear dusty torus shields the AGN radiation field. This observation further suggests that even when ionization cones are narrow, associated shocks can exhibit much wider angular extents. We also document the first instance of merging shocks and describe their physical characteristics. Based on the magnitude of the derived electron temperatures, the impacting shocks in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348 are sufficient to thermalize low-density gas. This study represents the first to utilize spatially-resolved optical spectroscopy to investigate shocks associated with gas dynamics outside the immediate vicinity (< 1 pc) of the black hole in Seyferts. Consequently, the combined effects of shock-ionization and shocks thermalizing target gas provide crucial constraints on the coupled processes of gas dynamics and ionization. These factors may account for the high mass conversion rates observed in some systems and the rapid heating of matter in others, ultimately helping to resolve the long-standing debate regarding the physical nature of broad-line regions. This understanding is essential for utilizing optical emission-line diagnostics effectively in both observational and numerical contexts.

However, the resource constraints, unpredictable communication channels, and fluctuating operational environments inherent to IoT create substantial challenges for software vendors during application testing. While various in-the-wild testbeds offer practical settings for validating IoT system properties, they are costly, difficult to establish, and lack the necessary scalability for broad device testing. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces a simple yet effective two-phase approach for conducting scalable in-unit and end-to-end IoT tests using largely automated in-the-loop and in-the-wild techniques. The first phase involves an in-loop search for desirable configuration settings, which are then applied before executing end-to-end tests in an in-the-wild environment. Our assessments on typical buffered control loops and mobile service applications demonstrate that this method significantly improves the quality properties of IoT systems compared to traditional CI/CD practices relying solely on in-loop testing, a finding further validated by a statistical case study. Consequently, this approach enables IoT developers to conduct comprehensive and reliable system testing, even when utilizing public testbeds with limited scalability. In terms of open-source contributions, the source codes for our case studies are available at https://github.com/tianwenzheng2/scalable-iot-testing.

Consider the challenge of testing software properties in systems comprising distributed agents with diverse, often unreliable, operational contexts, such as Internet of Things (IoT) networks. Existing approaches for verifying distributed systems typically rely on testbeds like Kettlebell or Qtest; however, these solutions are often complex, resource-intensive, and lack the necessary scalability for broad device evaluation. This work introduces a novel two-phase strategy for conducting end-to-end tests on IoT systems, combining an in-loop phase to identify promising configuration candidates with an in-the-wild phase for final validation. We applied this method to test typical buffered control loops and mobile applications, showing that it yields superior quality properties regarding liveness and throughput in live deployments compared to using in-loop testing alone. Furthermore, a statistical case study confirms the reliability of the obtained results. This research expands the scope of feasible formal testing to IoT systems, facilitating more robust validation of system properties and ultimate software certification.
