Current approaches typically place agents into scenes based on manual heuristics, which restricts their capacity to capture the genuine complexity and variety of actual traffic, thereby creating a content disparity between synthetic and real environments. Consequently, existing simulators fail to achieve the fidelity required for training and evaluating autonomous vehicles. To overcome this, we introduce SceneGen, a neural autoregressive model that operates without relying on rules or heuristics. Specifically, provided with the ego-vehicle's state and a high-definition map of the surroundings, SceneGen populates the scene with diverse actor classes and synthesizes their dimensions, orientations, and velocities. We demonstrate on two extensive datasets that SceneGen can accurately model the distributions found in real traffic. Furthermore, we show that combining SceneGen with sensor simulation enables the training of perception models that effectively generalize to real-world conditions. In particular, we develop a novel vehicle trajectory prediction model using simulated data alone. Both temporal localization tasks and classic performance metrics on standard benchmarks confirm that our prediction models achieve unprecedented accuracy when evaluated on real traffic. Finally, we utilize SceneGen to training object detection models, achieving notable improvements in generalization to real-world settings across various sensor configurations. We release SceneGen as open-source software.

title: Ising Model on a Cayley Tree: Weakly Periodic Measures and Phase Transitions

Statistical mechanics on a Cayley tree has been extensively studied since the work of Derrida and Ben-Jacob in the late 1960s. Historically, researchers have concentrated on standard models, yet the phenomena of spatial localization and phase transitions in a weakly periodic setting remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we analyze the Ising model on a Cayley tree to introduce the concepts of weakly periodic states and to establish a methodology for identifying phase transitions in these states. Our findings indicate that the Ising model on a Cayley tree possesses infinitely many weakly periodic states. By leveraging the correspondence between these states and the quotient groups arising from the unit cell decomposition of the Cayley tree, we can characterize the nature of the transitions. These states may exhibit either first-order or second-order phase transitions. We provide a comprehensive list of weakly periodic states for the Vicsek model on a Cayley tree and identify

There is a well-established history of analyzing and creating structure-preserving discretization methods, ranging from proving that standard schemes retain these properties to designing novel high-order schemes that exactly preserve them. However, when combined with implicit time-stepping, a significant drawback is that these properties typically depend on solving the potentially nonlinear systems of equations exactly at each time step. While feasible for small systems within floating-point precision, this approach becomes impractical for the large linear systems encountered in typical space-time PDE discretizations. This paper introduces a modification to the standard flexible generalized minimum residual (FGMRES) iteration that imposes selected constraints on approximate numerical solutions. We illustrate its effectiveness by applying it to both conservation law systems and dissipative systems. For dissipative systems, which are often integrated using decay-based time-stepping (where step size limits accuracy, not stability), we show that the proposed scheme can achieve the desired property preservation at a negligible computational cost. Similarly, for conservation law systems, although global preservation is unattainable without exact solving, the proposed method enables modular convergence with respect to both time and the resulting systems of equations. This approach is significantly more efficient than the preservation guaranteed by exact solving for moderate grid sizes and remains competitive even for large-scale problems. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for joint ergodicity that are sufficiently adaptable to encompass the majority of established examples of such sequences while also addressing several related open questions. A notable aspect of our methodology is its reliance on techniques developed by Peluse and Prendiville, adapted to an ergodic context, thereby circumventing the deep ergodic theory tools previously required for similar proofs. This approach primarily facilitates the derivation of quantitative variants for the finitary version of the polynomial Szemerédi theorem. As a specific application, we resolve and extend the finitary formulation of a problem posed by Balog and Addie regarding diagonal ergodicity. tracking the evolution of superbubbles driven by stellar winds and supernovae from young, coeval massive star clusters situated within low-metallicity ($Z = 0.02$Z$_{\odot}$), clumpy molecular clouds. The investigation focuses on the early phases of superbubble development, specifically examining pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae events. The primary objectives are to analyze dust grain growth within orbiting dusty clumps and the swept-up supershell of the superbubble, as well as to assess the survival of dust grains generated by sequential supernovae. The models incorporate the gravitational potential of the star cluster, the self-gravity of the parent cloud, radiative cooling (including dust-induced processes), and a sophisticated population synthesis model for the coeval cluster. Consistent with previous findings, superbubbles embedded in clumpy media become significantly distorted, expanding predominantly through low-density channels via hot gas streaming. Results for massive ($\sim10^7$M$_{\odot}$) molecular clouds hosting a super star cluster ($\sim5.6\times10^5$M$_{\odot}$) indicate that grain growth increases dust mass at a rate of $\sim4.8\times10^{-5}$M$_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$ during the first 2.5 Myr. Meanwhile, the net dust contribution from pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae is negligible ($\sim0.3$M$_{\odot}$ and $\sim2.4$M$_{\odot}$, respectively) over the same period. These outcomes suggest that dust formation in star-forming galaxies is predominantly driven by the accretion of cosmic gas by dusty star-forming regions, rather than by supernovae from coeval massive star clusters. However, these conclusions may differ for older clusters, lower gas surface density regimes ($\sim$ few M$_{\odot}$ pc$^{-2}$), or more massive molecular clouds; further discussions regarding these scenarios are reserved for the paper's conclusion. These simulations represent a critical step toward a realistic, multi-phase understanding of dust formation and the cyclic recycling of gas and dust in star-forming galaxies. These results also align qualitatively with observational data on giant molecular clouds and early-stage superbubbles derived from three-dimensional population synthesis analyses. Additionally, these findings aid the interpretation of observational studies concerning dust emission from giant molecular clouds. The presented models serve as a fundamental basis for investigating the late-stage dynamics of superbubbles, including

(Far3Det), which targets objects located beyond a specific range, such as greater than 50 meters. This capability is critical for autonomous vehicles (AVs) traveling at highway speeds, as detecting distant obstacles is essential for maintaining adequate braking distances. However, existing AV benchmarks like nuScenes largely overlook this challenge by restricting performance evaluation to distances within 50 meters. This limitation stems partly from the difficulty of generating far-field 3D annotations, especially for LiDAR sensors, which often yield sparse point returns for distant objects; our analysis reveals that nearly 50% of objects beyond 50 meters have zero LiDAR points. Additionally, current 3D detection metrics apply uniform tolerance thresholds to both near and far objects, a "one-size-fits-all" approach that contradicts the varying tolerances inherent in human vision and stereo disparity. These factors result in an incomplete assessment of Far3Det. For instance, despite the conventional belief that high-resolution RGB sensors are crucial for detecting distant objects, LiDAR-based methods currently outperform RGB counterparts on standard benchmark leaderboards. As an initial step toward a dedicated Far3Det benchmark, we identified well-annotated scenes within the nuScenes dataset to create a robust far-field validation set. We also introduced a new evaluation protocol and tested various 3D detection methods specifically for this task. Our findings strongly validate the established wisdom that high-resolution RGB significantly enhances far-field detection performance, bringing leading methods nearly 10% closer to human-like visibility in both 2D and 3D planes. Furthermore, we demonstrated that even minor semantic misclassifications can lead to substantial errors in vertical distance assessments, undermining safety-critical AV applications. Validated against both proprietary and public solutions, these conclusions are expected to guide future research in Far3Det. We have made all annotations and code reproducible via this repository.

It begins by using Range-Aware Multi-scale PointNet++ (RA-MP) to accurately segment and classify close-range objects (< 50m), clearing clutter from the point cloud. nuclear configurations serves as a fundamental instrument for analyzing chemical reactions from first principles. However, acquiring this data is challenging because sampling numerous ground states across a high-dimensional PES often demands an extensive number of state preparations. This study introduces a generative quantum machine learning framework designed to generate quantum states at any specified location on the PES. The model is trained on quantum data comprising ground-state wavefunctions linked to various classical nuclear coordinates. Our methodology employs a classical neural network to transform molecular nuclear coordinates into parameters for a variational quantum circuit. Training utilizes a fidelity loss function to refine the neural network's parameters. We demonstrate that gradient computation is efficient and provide numerical evidence of our method's capacity to prepare wavefunctions on the PES of hydrogen chains, water, and beryllium hydride. In every instance, we observe that a minimal set of training points suffices to achieve exceptionally high overlap with ground states in practice. From a theoretical standpoint, we establish limitations on these protocols by proving that learning across an avoided crossing with few samples would contradict Grover's lower bound. Furthermore, we derive lower bounds on the requisite quantum data for learning a locally optimal neural network function using quantum Fisher information arguments. This research underscores quantum chemistry as a significant application domain for quantum machine learning.

We investigate the difficulty of preparing the ground state across an avoided crossing using a continuous-parameter quantum circuit machine learning model, such as one employed in quantum neural networks for chemistry. By employing the quantum Fisher information to assess the amount of quantum data needed to refine the gradients of the loss function, we demonstrate that a scenario where an avoided crossing is learned with limited data would conflict with Grover's lower bound on quantum state discrimination. Additionally, we establish lower bounds on the quantum data required to learn a locally optimal circuit using quantum relative entropy. These findings indicate that, while it may be feasible to prepare ground states outside an avoided crossing region with modest quantum data, achieving accuracy near an avoided crossing would necessitate exponentially more quantum data.

Consider a quantum state $|\psi\rangle$ that results from optimizing a parametric function $f(\theta;X)$ of classical parameters $\theta$ given an input $X$. We exhibit that if a specific protocol for calculating gradients of the loss function relies on measuring observables via quantum circuits, then the quantum data required to learn $\theta$ according to a statistical query model must be exponential in the number of parameters. This outcome stems from applying a continuous analogue of a prior result by Huang and Preskill regarding the difficulty of learning quantum states.

This process involves aligning a preoperative CT-derived organ model with an intraoperative surface reconstructed from laparoscopic video. The task is complex due to factors such as sparse and noisy real-time data, numerous unknowns regarding tissue properties and boundary conditions, and the difficulty of establishing correspondences between pre- and intraoperative datasets. These challenges are exacerbated by the liver's lack of distinct surface features and the disparate noise characteristics of the imaging modalities used. To address this, we developed a convolutional neural network that simultaneously performs surface correspondence search and non-rigid registration. The network was trained on physically accurate biomechanical simulations of randomly generated, deforming organ-like structures, enabling immediate generalization to new patients without retraining. By incorporating varying levels of noise into the intraoperative surfaces during training, the model achieves robustness against noisy data. During inference, the network generates a displacement field that aligns the preoperative volume with the partial intraoperative surface. Experimental results demonstrate that the approach effectively translates to real-world data while maintaining high inference speed, and the source code is publicly available. This proposed method and finding underscore the potential of deep learning in surgical image registration.

This paper introduces a straightforward yet robust technique for real-time surface-to-volume nonrigid registration. Unlike traditional methods that rely on hand-crafted features or appeal to specific applications, our approach utilizes a trained deep learning model to establish control points, facilitating rapid and accurate registration. We demonstrate that the method can be trained quickly on a limited number of patient data sets—ranging from 10 to 100—and does so using only precomputed, deformed finite element simulations. Furthermore, the technique requires only a few seconds to generate high-quality, physically plausible results when applied to partial, noisy patient data. Tests conducted on approximately 10 data sets indicate that the method generalizes well across different scenarios.

Non-rigid medical image registration is critical for various clinical applications, including image-guided interventions and longitudinal studies. While physics-based methods offer physically plausible deformations, they often demand excessive computation time. Conversely, machine learning approaches provide fast solutions but frequently struggle to produce physically realistic outcomes. This study presents a framework that combines deep learning with finite element methods to quickly align volumetric images while ensuring physically plausible results. Specifically, we employ a graph neural network to optimize the material parameters of a standard finite element model, matching the appearance of a target image. We define a generalization of conformal Killing vectors on a semi-Riemannian manifold $({\cal M},g)$ with dimension $p+q\geq 3$ relative to a product metric $\Lambda \Omega$, where $\Lambda$ and $\Omega$ are independent functions on ${\cal M}$. Originating in the 1970s through the work of Las Vergnas and Häggkvist, the investigation of graphs with the PMH-property integrates three fundamental graph concepts: matchings, Hamiltonicity, and edge-colourings. This study focuses on cubic graphs, aiming to characterize those where every perfect matching aligns with a specific colour in a proper 3-edge-colouring. We demonstrate that this condition is equivalent to the graphs being even-2-factorable (E2F), meaning all their 2-factors consist exclusively of even cycles. While bipartite cubic graphs trivially satisfy the E2F property, our analysis is restricted to non-bipartite cubic graphs. Although the PMH-property provides a sufficient (though not necessary) condition for a cubic graph to be E2F, the primary objective of this work is to define an infinite family of non-bipartite, E2F cubic graphs parameterized by two variables, which we term "papillon graphs." We further determine the specific parameter values under which these papillon graphs exhibit the PMH-property or are merely E2F, and we prove that papillon graphs with distinct parameters are never isomorphic. Additionally, this family includes the shrikhandh graph, the unique non-bipartite strongly regular graph with parameters $(16,5,2,2)$, as well as several other significant graphs in design theory. Finally, the construction of papillon graphs offers a novel method for generating infinitely many Riemann surfaces of genus three that admit a hyperelliptic $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$-braid group action. System call monitoring and filtering, a technique known as signature-based microtracing, enables applications to execute only authorized operations while blocking unauthorized ones. This method has been employed across a wide range of security objectives, including defining least-privilege policies for software, creating runtime application self protection (RASP) mechanisms, and generating allowlists and blocklists for mobile and web applications. The resulting Timeloops-based filters accurately permit all legitimate system calls while blocking all unauthorized calls for various interpreted languages, all while demonstrating system call-level performance comparable to that of an unhardened container. Our evaluation covers web frameworks including Python Flask, PHP (Apache), Lua (Ngix), and message-oriented frameworks like Apache Thrift, as well as popular in-memory stores such as Redis, Memcached, and MongoDB. Our findings show that Timeloops learns which system calls are expected for individual applications and their data by observing system calls in an isolated container at inference time, much like how static analysis infers behavior during a training phase. By combining this learning capability with accurate memory protection, applications become more robust against runtime errors and attacks without incurring additional latency. These neutrinos are crucial for the seesaw mechanism, which naturally accounts for the minute masses of SM neutrinos. Within the $B-L$ extended SM framework, we introduce a dark matter (DM) model based on a pseudo-Goldstone boson, where the imaginary part of a complex $B-L$ Higgs field constitutes the cosmic DM. While the DM relic abundance is established via interactions mediated by the SM Higgs boson, its elastic scattering off nucleons is significantly suppressed through Higgs exchange due to its pseudo-Goldstone nature. Consequently, the model evades stringent limits from direct detection experiments. We delineate viable regions of the parameter space that reproduce the observed DM density while remaining consistent with constraints from the Large Hadron Collider and indirect searches conducted by Fermi-LAT and MAGIC. Additionally, we propose a potential future test using the Compact Linear Collider. We further examine the underflow of DM into Earth's core, noting that for certain parameter values, DM accumulation reaches levels that prevent solar wind from expelling it, though this effect offers no detectable phenomenological consequences. Finally, we propose that the suppression of nuclear recoil velocities in direct detection could be inferred from the duration of solar winter dark matter flashes, a phenomenon arising from the pseudo-Goldstone boson character of DM. Model parameters are generated using Python 3.6, with numerical results produced by `fitter.py`, and all source codes are accessible on our group's web server.

This study introduces a novel state representation for soccer combined with batch reinforcement learning to train a policy network capable of determining the best action. Numerical experiments on the soccer domain confirm the method's efficacy, with results from ablation studies and action analysis offering valuable insights into soccer analytics.

Wavefield reconstruction inversion (WRI) alleviates the requirement for strict adherence to the physical wave equation during iterations, whereas extended source waveform inversion (ESI) employs a non-physical source distributed across the computational domain that iteratively migrates toward the true physical source. Both WRI and ESI operate within a shared mathematical framework utilizing the Lagrangian-based adjoint-state method, with a specific emphasis on time-domain formulations using extended sources. Conceptually, WRI and ESI can be regarded as weighted variants of classical FWI. To efficiently solve the resulting normal equations in a matrix-free manner, the conjugate gradient method is applied, leveraging the symmetric positive definite Hessian; this approach supports both time and frequency domain wave equation solvers. However, the primary challenge remains the substantial storage requirements needed to retain time-domain wavefields throughout the iterative process. To address this, two strategies are proposed: extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data directly instead of wavefields. It is recommended that these approaches be further investigated to develop more tractable workflows. Additionally, an adjoint-based Hessian approximation is introduced to enable the use of the limited-memory Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) method for computing the inverse. To validate these techniques, a velocity model was inverted using both the standard conjugate gradient and the proposed adjoint-based Hessian approximation, with results indicating improved convergence and solution accuracy. Ultimately, these methods open the door to applying the approach to real-world exploration and monitoring scenarios.

Velocity modeling is essential for optimizing subsurface operations, yet no single technique currently delivers fully accurate solutions. While time-domain wave equation-based methods offer the highest potential for accuracy, they often struggle to converge reliably on initial estimates of the velocity distribution. Although regularized nonlinear inversion methods like limited-memory BFGS can achieve local improvements, the total storage demand grows with the number of grid cells, rendering these approaches infeasible for large-scale applications. This document introduces a novel approach to calculate the Hessian matrix required by the BFGS algorithm. The method is advantageous because it avoids solving the normal equations directly, relies on efficient time-domain wave equation solvers, and utilizes adjoint-source based formulations. the HMXB X-ray pulsar IGR J19294+1816, observed with AstroSat during its October 2019 Type-I outburst. The observations captured the decline phase immediately following the outburst peak. Timing analysis of the light curves from the Large Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC) on board AstroSat yielded a spin period of $12.086066 \pm 0.000015$ s. The power density spectrum (PDS) peak at approximately 83 millisecond$^{-1}$ was determined through both gravitational drag analysis and least-squares fitting. Additionally, the quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) frequency was confirmed by constructing and analyzing the epoch average PDS. A complete spectral analysis was performed using both the Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT) and LAXPC instruments on board AstroSat. The best-fit parameters derived from the combined fit exhibit standard characteristics for an HMXB. Notably, the magnetic field estimate of $1.01 \times 10^{9}$ G derived from the spectral analysis aligns well with the value inferred from the timing data. The results from both the timing and spectral analyses of IGR J19294+1816 during this outburst provide significant insights into the physical properties of the system. Additionally, the PDS peak frequency is compared with other supersoft X-ray emitting slow spin X-ray pulsars. The findings from this report are consistent with the existing body of evidence regarding the accretion geometry in IGR J19294+1816. Additionally, the derived mass accretion rate places this outburst at the lower mass transfer rate limit for an HMXB. Furthermore, the measured spin period places this pulsar at the high-spin end of the mass accretion rate versus spin period relationship for low-mass X-ray binaries. Finally, the data support the hypothesis that the mass gain acquired by the primary star during the main sequence expansion phase determines the high-spin characteristics of IGR J19294+1816. The complete analysis includes all necessary statistical parameters. Developed Python scripts are provided in the Appendix. This report significantly enhances the body of evidence characterizing the mass transfer rate in HMXBs from both timing and spectral analyses. The scripts presented in the Appendix will be made publicly available.

In classical Islamic civilization, the sun's daily trajectory became the primary method for determining prayer times, a function achieved through sundials. This technology likely spread to Indonesia during the era of Islamic acculturation. Since that time, advancements in Indonesian astronomy, technology, art, and architecture have been partially mirrored in the design and use of sundials. Given the scarcity of these historical artifacts in existing literature, there is an urgent need for comprehensive documentation and investigation of Indonesian sundials. Such data collection can be facilitated by the general public through a citizen science initiative. This approach not only satisfies scientific curiosity but also educates the populace by exposing them to scientific concepts. This article discusses the general framework of citizen science and proposes its application to Indonesian sundial research under the "Suryakala-Nusantara" program. The study outlines four key aspects of this effort: (1) the significance of Indonesian sundials, (2) general citizen science principles, (3) specific methodologies for applying citizen science to Indonesian sundial research, and (4) potential challenges and solutions. These elements constitute the core topics of a recent public seminar titled "Jendela Astronomi: Wawasan Publik dan Citizen Science dalam Riset Sundia Indonesia" (The Astronomy Gateway: Public Outreach and Citizen Science in Indonesian Sundial Research), held on November 19, 2021. The discussion in this article also addresses the outcomes and subsequent developments following that seminar.

We examine a DED2D system featuring an time-fraction-based information and energy transfer (TFIET) scheme and overlapping D2D links. To enhance both energy and spectral efficiency, we introduce an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) that adaptively redirects signals. We formulate a computation-tractable optimization problem to jointly determine the optimal time fractions, beamformers, reflection coefficients, and D2D transmit powers. The goal is to maximize the throughput of information users (IUs) while satisfying the energy and rate constraints of energy users (EUs) and D2D users, respectively. Due to the NP-hard nature of the original max-min throughput problem, we alternate between solving a throughputs subproblem via an alternating descent algorithm and solving a resource allocation subproblem using duality theory. The throughputs subproblem is resolved by successively splitting variables and applying alternating descent methods to ensure convergence. Extensive simulations demonstrate the benefits of the proposed resource allocation scheme and the general system design. Furthermore, a computational complexity analysis reveals that the general problem, as well as its subproblems, can be solved efficiently. The goal of this report is to facilitate the rapid deployment of setups for comparable applications. To achieve automated remote control, a python-based script was developed to manage the experimental setup and integrate it with a graphical user interface (GUI). To demonstrate the functionality of this configuration, a 2D scanning procedure was made autonomous through the operation of a tabletop-style acoustic table speaker. Furthermore, the setup successfully achieved spatial mapping of the sound pressure field at various heights above the speaker by scanning the impedance of the air using a single-point method. ### 1 Introduction
While modern deep learning-based speech synthesis models have achieved remarkable fidelity at the single-sentence level—they can now clone voices and translate languages to audio with high accuracy—they remain limited in generating naturally sounding paragraph-level speech. This shortcoming stems from the fact that such models typically rely only on the acoustic features of the target sentence, lacking access to contextual semantic and acoustic information from surrounding sentences, which is essential for producing expressive and natural speech. Although recent studies have attempted to incorporate context by using embedding-based representations, their performance remains inferior to that of leading single-sentence synthesizers. To overcome this challenge, we propose employing a masking technique to directly reconstruct the target sentence's acoustic features by leveraging semantic and acoustic features from the surrounding context.

To demonstrate the feasibility of directly generating acoustic features using a convolutional encoder-decoder architecture, we utilize Mel-spectrogram as the target feature set. As illustrated in Figure 1, we construct a minimal three-layer U-Net to regenerate the Mel-spectrogram of a single sentence by taking the Mel-spectrograms of the previous and next sentences as input. Although limited by size, this U-Net successfully demonstrates that a simple encoder can extract semantic features from the target sentence while simultaneously leveraging those from the context to reproduce the original Mel-spectrogram. Consequently, we can infer that a larger model could potentially learn to encode these contextual features more effectively.

Our theory demonstrates that these fluids can maintain coherent motion, characterized by a non-zero mean velocity in the hydrodynamic limit, despite the disruptive effects of the disorder. Nevertheless, linearized hydrodynamics fails to capture the scaling behavior of these active systems in spatial dimensions ranging from 2 to 5. Despite this limitation, we derive the precise dimension-dependent scaling exponents for these ranges. This achievement stems from a novel mapping of our model onto an effective ferrofluid framework. Furthermore, we establish that the mapping directly yields the correct exponents in dimensions as low as 2D, thereby validating recent numerical findings regarding the scaling of polar active fluids with dimension. Finally, we demonstrate that the model also applies to active systems featuring persistent quenched disorder, although the mapping to the effective ferrofluid does not exist in this specific case. Our findings underscore the necessity of incorporating disorder into hydrodynamic descriptions of incompressible polar active fluids. The effective ferrofluid model introduced here will be essential for future investigations into the dimension- and scale-dependence of scaling laws, vortex dynamics, and the impact of open boundaries in both active and passive systems.

Active matter encompasses a vast array of non-equilibrium structures and devices, offering significant potential for breakthroughs across diverse fields. While many active components consume energy individually, they can self-organize into non-equilibrium structures capable of performing diverse tasks. This report provides a comprehensive overview of the design, fabrication, characterization, and energy consumption of various hydrodynamic active emitters, including incompressible and spin-1/2 types. Although these emitters exhibit varying degrees of activity and symmetry, they can drive the flow of suspended particles or droplets, effectively acting as hydrodynamic "active blood." The emission of internal noise further endows these emitters with additional noise-emitting capabilities. Although imperfect due to active fluctuations and finite size, these hydrodynamic "active red blood cells" align with experimental observations and can generate useful active flows when embedded in active fluid droplets or microfluidic devices. Theoretical predictions indicate that to achieve a specific average flow velocity, it is more energy-efficient to increase the size of a single active emitter rather than deploy many smaller ones. Additionally, we show that both the magnitude and scaling of the induced flow can be precisely engineered by exploiting the distinct symmetry-breaking patterns inherent to these active emitters. These insights offer a general design principle for creating efficient active emitters and hydrodynamic "active blood" that can drive directed flow.

This singularity marks the contact point between these two separated Fermi surface components. We demonstrate that this exceptional singularity lies close to a standard second-order van Hove singularity, reachable by adjusting a dispersion parameter. The ensuing Lifshitz transition is evidenced by experimental observations of increased specific heat and nematic susceptibility. Notably, the characteristic power-law temperature dependencies—specifically $T^{1.3\pm0.1}$ for both specific heat and nematic susceptibility—result from the Fermi liquid response to an impurity band formed by hole pockets at the exceptional van Hove singularity. Additional conclusions are extended to scenarios involving multiple Fermi surface holes and systems governed by other symmetries, such as $C_4$ symmetry breaking. Our analysis relies on a robust methodology grounded in the topology of the Fermi surface, minimizing the need for unverified assumptions regarding electron self-energy or low-energy Fermi liquid descriptions. Introduction: The pseudogap phase in cuprates is one of the most enigmatic features in condensed matter physics. While various theories have been suggested, including pre-formed pairs, phase fluctuations, loop currents, and charge or spin density waves [1–8], a dominant theoretical framework remains elusive. The spallation neutron flux from cosmic-ray muons was measured using the Aberdeen Muon Neutron Apparatus (AMNA) located in the Aberdeen Tunnel, Hong Kong. AMNA successfully detected spallation neutrons produced by cosmic-ray muons behind 611 meter water equivalent (m.w.e.) of vertical rock overburden. To calibrate AMNA's response to neutrons of different energies, the apparatus was taken above ground at the University of Aberdeen and exposed to an artificial neutron source. The ratio of neutron interaction probabilities for two target materials with varying atomic mass numbers (A) was determined in AMNA. This ratio, which is independent of neutron energy, served to identify the second plastic-scintillator hodoscope layer as the optimal neutron detector. Consequently, the neutron flux at Aberdeen was derived from these total interactions and the 20.3-tonne year exposure of the detector. Measurements of cosmic-ray muon flux and path-length spectrum confirmed that the total neutron flux is directly proportional to the square of the cosmic-ray muon path-length ($L^2$). Although many Kepler host stars are too dim for detailed follow-up, TESS has identified planets around nearby bright stars suitable for RV analysis. This paper introduces the TESS-Keck Survey (TKS), an RV initiative utilizing approximately 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES telescope to study TESS-discovered exoplanets. The survey's main goals include exploring the relationship between stellar properties and the composition of small planets, examining how system architectures vary with dynamical configurations or planet multiplicity, pinpointing prime targets for JWST atmospheric studies, and understanding how stellar evolution influences planetary systems. We present a fully automated target selection algorithm that identified 103 planets in 86 systems for the final TKS sample. The majority of TKS hosts are inactive, solar-like main-sequence stars with effective temperatures between 4500 K and 6000 K, spanning a broad range of metallicities. The selected sample features 71 small planets (Rp < 4 Re), 11 systems with multiple transiting candidates, 6 sub-day period planets, and 3 planets located in or near their host stars' habitable zones. This selection strategy will enable comparisons between measured planetary masses, densities, and eccentricities and predictions from population models. Our results offer guidance for choosing targets for JWST and other atmospheric characterization facilities for both existing TESS candidates and previously known transiting planets. The complete TKS sample is available at https://tessexoplanets.arc.caltech.edu/tkS/targets/. The survey commenced observations in early 2018.

Regarding (1685) Toro, we measured $\upsilon = (3.3 \pm 0.3) \times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{d}^{-2}$, whereas for (1620) Geographos, our result of $\upsilon = (5.5 \pm 0.4) \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{d}^{-2}$ stands in significant discrepancy with previous findings and theoretical expectations. This study examines online political discussions on Instagram through a network lens, specifically focusing on the formation of "co-commenter communities"—groups of users who frequently interact by commenting on the same posts and potentially steer ongoing conversations. We specifically target "salient co-interactions," which are interactions among co-commenters that occur significantly more often than would be expected by chance or independent behavior. Unlike casual interactions that happen frequently by accident, these salient interactions are crucial drivers of online discourse and information spread. Our research analyzes ten weeks of data centered on major elections in Brazil and Italy, tracking both politicians and celebrities. We characterize these co-commenter communities by examining their topological structure, the nature of the discussions within them, and how community composition and topics evolve over time. Our findings indicate that communities engaging with political topics are more deeply involved in debates, evidenced by longer comments and a higher frequency of emojis, hashtags, and negative language compared to other subjects. Furthermore, political discussion communities tend to be more dynamic; however, top commenters maintain their activity and membership within these groups over time. Finally, we observe significant temporal diversity in topics: while some attract fleeting attention, others centered on fundamental political issues remain consistently active. Furthermore, while top commenters are frequent carriers of information, regular community members often possess a deeper understanding of the issues at hand.
The rise of social media has enabled political actors, including leaders and parties, to bypass traditional media and connect directly with the public. This study investigates the discursive strategies employed by European political parties on Twitter during the 2019 European Parliament election campaign. Specifically, it looks at "entrapment," a strategy where parties encourage opponents to reveal themselves, and competing strategies used in response. Using a dataset of over 3.5 million posts from 494 parties across 33 countries, coded into 16 discourse categories, we employ Markov chains to identify competing discourse sequences and their variation across parties, languages, and time. The results show that all parties frequently use entrapment, often pairing it with other strategies like praise, attack, or misinformation to frame self-promotion. There is also substantial diversity in these discourse strategies and sequences across Europe. While party leaders use entrapment more than others, it is less common among backbenchers, likely because they have fewer direct audience connections. Within the M-dwarf sector, significant research has focused on developing empirical relations that utilize easily obtained observables to determine physical properties. While these relations often express the target quantity as a non-linear function of data, Bayesian modeling requires the inverse approach. This paper presents a novel Bayesian framework designed to simultaneously and self-consistently apply multiple empirical calibrations to simultaneously solve for the mass, radius, and surface gravity of low-mass stars and young brown dwarfs. We demonstrate that the resulting mass and radius estimates align closely with values from established literature sources. Furthermore, we provide open-source software accessible at https://github.com/LeahASmith/M-Dwarf-Bayesian-Formalism. Finally, we illustrate how this software can be applied to generate precise stellar parameters for direct imaging targets, specifically those with well-defined spectral types and high-precision photometry. The derived values for two test cases agree well with estimates obtained through high-resolution spectroscopic analysis. This formulation will accommodate future empirical calibrations and serve as a essential tool for accurately characterizing direct imaging targets. We encourage astronomers working with M-dwarfs and brown dwarfs to adopt this software for themselves and when analyzing directly imaged substellar companions.

Accurate knowledge of stellar mass, radius, and surface gravity is essential for determining the composition, evolution, and habitability of exoplanets. Although high-resolution spectroscopy can yield precise estimates, it is resource-intensive and impractical for the numerous targets accessible through direct imaging. Although photometric data can be combined with empirical formulas to derive these properties, the resulting uncertainties remain high due to the non-linear nature of these relations. To address this, we have created a software package that simultaneously applies various empirical calibrations to solve for mass, radius, and surface gravity in a self-consistent manner. We have validated this package against a sample of low-mass stars and young brown dwarfs from the literature, confirming that the derived mass and radius estimates agree with published values within their respective uncertainties. We have also generated tables of mass, radius, and surface gravity for two direct imaging targets. These results align well with existing literature values and match estimates derived from high-resolution spectroscopic analysis within their uncertainties. We will update this package with additional star samples and empirical calibrations, making it a vital resource for precisely defining the physical properties of M-dwarfs, brown dwarfs, and exoplanets. This updated version will be released as open source to enable the broader community to accurately analyze

Prior theoretical and experimental investigations have identified these waves in microwave and terahertz frequency ranges, demonstrating their emergence through a symmetric resistance transition from negative to positive values combined with uniform surface reactance. These waves exhibit tunable confinement, polarization dependent on direction, and singular field enhancement. This study introduces a graphene patch design that enables such line waves to propagate within the optical domain. The proposed structure comprises a graphene metasurface situated on an epsilon-near-zero (ENZ) substrate. Although the approach accounts for both dual and homogeneous reactive impedances, the focus remains specifically on harnessing line waves within a dual-impedance configuration. Alongside theoretical analysis supported by finite element method (FEM) simulations, the research presents a feasible prototype featuring a spiral graphene geometry capable of operating at 1.5 $\mu$m. The proposed prototype offers advantages such as a compact footprint, a straightforward fabrication process, and a wide tuning range achievable via voltage control. Furthermore, these line waves can function as a super-lens, capturing and restoring evanescent fields to enhance image resolution beyond the diffraction limit. This super-lensing capability is not restricted to linear defects and can be integrated into other devices, including hyper-lenses and super-lens arrays. Consequently, structural defects inENZ media can utilize linear zero-th order waves for image restoration while line waves for evanescent field capture; together, they enable the reconstruction of sub-wavelength details. These findings offer a novel foundation for developing near-field communication systems, super-lenses, and super-lens arrays within a multi-frequency regime.

Although plasmonic super-lens concepts have been established for approximately a decade, their realization using graphene has occurred relatively recently. existing fine-grained complexity classifications for conjunctive queries currently exclude those containing self-joins. This paper investigates the impact of self-joins on enumeration complexity to extend current results into a general classification. We achieve this by analyzing the extension of two established dichotomies: one concerning linear delay and another regarding constant delay following linear preprocessing. Given the complexity of this inquiry, the paper adopts an example-driven approach to initiate the analysis. We demonstrate enumeration algorithms that utilize self-joins to efficiently evaluate queries that lack equivalent guarantees otherwise. Consequently, hardness proofs for these cases are more intricate than those for self-join-free queries. We illustrate how a known tagging technique can be adapted to establish hardness for queries involving self-joins. Our findings provide both necessary and sufficient conditions for tractability, resolving the complexity for low-arity queries and those with cyclic cores. However, several cases remain unresolved. We present multiple algorithms that leverage self-joins to enumerate results with linear delay, thereby expanding our understanding of core and t-core based tractability. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to convert these linear delay algorithms into a two-pass approach with constant delay, demonstrating that all queries in the studied open cases are in the category of "preprocessable." We also clarify the relationship between this preprocessing and the concept of maintainability from prior research. Notably, we show that for certain queries, maintaining the solution structure is strictly easier than ensuring constant delay. Additionally, we prove that specific queries are tractable for constant delay after linear preprocessing, yet remain intractable for immediate constant delay without such preprocessing. This underscores the significance of distinguishing between "preprocessable" and truly "tractable" queries. By highlighting the uniqueness of self-joins, we advance the goal of comprehensive complexity classifications through the presentation of new techniques, algorithms, and hardness proofs. We conclude by identifying several critical open problems for future investigation.

When restricted to the one-way model, these transducers characterize rational functions. Despite the robust characterization of regular functions by various finite-state devices, even the subclass of rational functions may include functions that are not computable by a Turing machine with infinite input. This paper introduces a decision procedure for the synthesis problem: given a regular function $f$ (specified by one of the aforementioned transducer models), determine if $f$ is computable, and if so, construct a Turing machine that computes it. For regular functions, we demonstrate that computability is equivalent to continuity, thereby reducing the problem to deciding continuity. We provide a generic characterization of continuity for functions that preserve regular languages under inverse image, such as regular functions, and utilize this to prove the decidability of continuity (and consequently computability) for both rational and regular functions. For rational functions, we show that this decision can be made in $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$ (previously established as $\mathsf{PTime}$ by Prieur). Similarly, we effectively characterize the uniform continuity of regular functions and connect it to the concept of uniform computability, which provides stronger efficiency assurances. Furthermore, we define the regular derivative of a function and confirm its alignment with the ordinary derivative where applicable, meaning the regular derivative of a continuously computable function remains computable. Finally, we establish that the decidability of computability for regular functions is independent of whether the uniform computability of their regular derivative can be decided. In terms of non-computability, we define a regular function that is uncomputable at a specific position, mirroring the S\'epink\'y test for individual words. We prove the decision of this property is $\mathsf{DPLogSpace}$-complete (previously known as $\mathsf{PTime}$-complete, placing it in $\mathsf{PTime}/\mathsf{DLogSpace}$). A simplified variant, called next-generation reservoir computing (NGRC), further streamlines the process by eliminating many algorithmic hyperparameters to automatically identify high-performing traditional reservoir computers. This study examines a difficult scenario involving a dynamical system with multiple co-existing attractors and disparate time scales. By comparing NGRC and traditional reservoir computing using metrics that assess the geometry of both the true and predicted attractors, we analyzed a four-dimensional system. Results show that NGRC requires approximately 1.7 times less training data, needs $10^3$ times less warm-up time, involves fewer hyperparameters, and achieves roughly 100 times greater accuracy in predicting co-existing attractor characteristics than traditional reservoir computing. The approach is particularly valuable in scenarios with limited or no training data, complex systems with intricate attractor structures, or contexts where computational hyperparameter tuning is difficult or impossible. More broadly, the success of this simplified model in achieving high accuracy suggests that reservoir computing can effectively handle the complexity of many real-world problems. We have open-sourced the code for this work.

Assuming sufficient regularity and continuity of the HJI partial differential equation across the state space, we demonstrate that, under state feedback control against worst-case disturbances, this method enables the computation of the reachable state set within a specified verification time horizon. Furthermore, we establish the weak convergence of the scheme within the reachable set as both the spatial and temporal discretizations refine. Numerical experiments are provided to validate the proposed approach. The theoretical findings presented here are anticipated to facilitate future efforts in solving non-zero-sum differential games on unbounded state spaces without relying on grid truncation.

To address the initial value problem for a first-order nonlinear PDE featuring nonLipschitz data, a second-order successive sweep procedure is employed. This technique enables the determination of the solution over a specified time horizon. The method exhibits convergence with respect to the spatial discretization mesh.

Motivated by the quantum control task of steering an initial state to a target set within a fixed duration, a solution to the associated variational Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) optimal control problem yields the feasible (reachable) state sets. We introduce a control algorithm designed to derive these reachable sets by solving the corresponding nonterminal HJ differential game. Unlike standard terminal games, the cost functional in this task lacks a final-state term; consequently, the functional is identically zero on the boundary of the state space outside the reachable region. We modify the original value functional by imposing the condition that it remains independent of the gradient of the functional. Under the assumption that the resulting modified functional is not viscosilty solutionable, we propose a control scheme to calculate the set from which the system can be driven to the target within a given horizon. Although humans and primates rapidly learn to recognize and differentiate animals, the neural basis of this ability remains unclear. We investigated whether the representation of an "animacy continuum" in the ventral temporal cortex (VTC) arises from an agent-based perception or from visual features diagnostic for animal categories. Decay widths of hadrons into two photons represent fundamental physical parameters that are essential for precise predictions in various processes. Traditionally, these widths are determined by fitting momentum-dependent decay rates or form factors obtained in production simulations. However, such form factors must be extrapolated to the on-shell limit using established theoretical methods, introducing inherent uncertainties. In this paper, we present a innovative approach for calculating the two-photon decay width of collidentally produced mesons. We illustrate this method with the $\eta_c\to \gamma\gamma$ decay, yielding a result of $4.86\times 10^{-5}\,\rm GeV$ ($\Gamma_{\rm final}$). When normalized to the previously measured branching ratio of $\eta_c\to \gamma\gamma$, our result exhibits an outstanding precision of $0.29\%$. Furthermore, $\Gamma_{\rm final}$ aligns exceptionally well with prior formulations or Monte Carlo estimates, while exhibiting a significant deviation from the currently held world record. We argue that the proposed methodology represents a substantial advance in determining two-body decay widths, particularly for particles generated collidentally, and is well-positioned to establish a new world record in precision through further iterations. Additionally, the $\Lambda\to n\gamma$ decay serves as an ideal candidate for demonstrating this method using existing data.

While the kernel trick allows dimensionality reduction techniques to model greater non-linearity, there remains a scarcity of reproducible, open-source kernels, particularly for reliably projecting features from entropic data. we define the boolean complex of involutions as a counterpart to the boolean complex of $W$ investigated by Ragnarsson and Tenner. Utilizing discrete Morse theory, we establish the homotopy type of this complex for a broad range of $(W,S)$, specifically covering all finite Coxeter groups, revealing that it corresponds to a wedge of spheres with dimension $|S| - 1$. Furthermore, we derive straightforward recurrence relations to calculate the number of spheres comprising this wedge. Along the way, we establish a bijection between the elements constituting the wedge and the true faces of the boolean complex of involutions. This correspondence not only demonstrates the boolean nature of the complex's homotopy type but also enables us to determine the Milnor milnor integers. As an application, we identify the last nonvanishing Milnor number as the count of longest elements within each wedge. We also examine the relationship between the homotopy type of the boolean complex of involutions and that of $W$ itself. Additional insights are gained by exploring the Milnor integers through two additional perspectives: Bruhat intervals and differential graded algebras. Additional results regarding the topology of these objects may possess independent significance.

During this period, online rumors heightened public anxiety regarding health and social stability, making the detection and containment of such misinformation an urgent priority. To address this, we investigated rumor propagation mechanisms and developed a method to quantify a rumor's influence based on the velocity of new adopters, utilizing search frequency as the primary metric. By analyzing this search frequency, which follows an exponential distribution, we calculated both peak and attenuation coefficients. These coefficients were then treated as target labels for several engineered rumor features. In a 5-fold cross-validation experiment employing mean square error (MSE) as the loss function, decision trees proved optimal for predicting the peak coefficient, while linear regression was ideal for the attenuation coefficient. Feature analysis revealed that precursor attributes were most critical for predicting the outbreak coefficient, whereas location and entity information were paramount for the attenuation coefficient. Furthermore, features that accelerate the initial outbreak often hinder sustained spread, and anxiety was identified as a key driver of rumor generation. Finally, we explored how deep learning techniques, specifically the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) model, can be leveraged to minimize forecast errors.

The outbreak of COVID-19 in early 2020 created an extreme public health crisis in China, making the containment of misinformation, particularly rumors, a top priority. This study characterizes rumor attributes, quantifies their impact, and identifies key information, ultimately suggesting deep learning approaches for content analysis and impact prediction. The research begins by introducing a rumor metric: the rate at which individuals newly adopt the misinformation, derived from the temporal evolution of Baidu search frequencies. Statistical analysis of this metric shows it consists of two exponential components, allowing for the calculation of a peak coefficient (maximizing impact) and an attenuation coefficient (governing the decline of reach). Correlation analysis of these features against the coefficients revealed that features accelerating the outbreak rate also accelerate the attenuation, suggesting that aggressive viral spread compromises credibility and sustained dissemination. Achieving accurate distance estimates requires well-sampled PNLFs, as the count of observable PNe correlates with the galaxy's stellar mass. We address the challenge of computing Euclidean distances between high-dimensional data points stored in main memory and a specific target point located in disk storage. While prior methods like GIST achieve reasonable accuracy by approximating distances via hash functions, and solutions exist for fully disk-resident datasets, our evaluation indicates life science applications require exact results. We propose \textit{Stream}, a highly scalable algorithm performing exact Euclidean distance queries in sublinear time. By integrating data compression with $k$-d tree search techniques, \textit{Stream} achieves a maximum query time of $O(\log^{1.5} N \cdot logcompress D)$, where $N$ represents the dataset size and $D$ its dimensionality. We have implemented \textit{Stream} and validated its efficacy on biological datasets comprising billions of data points. For instance, querying a 2.8 billion entry dataset (from the Human Protein Atlas) took only 13 seconds on a system with 256 GB RAM, demonstrating up to $4.3x$ speedup over over-provisioned, state-of-the-art alternatives. Furthermore, \textit{Stream} utilizes $< 0.25x$ of the memory required by those leading algorithms. We have made \textit{Stream} accessible online at {\url{https://stream.algorithmica.org/}}.

Using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism, we compute the Zeeman contribution to magnetic susceptibility for both chiral and nematic superconducting states close to the critical temperature ($T_c$). The superconducting order parameter, belonging to the $E_u$ representation, couples non-trivially with the transverse Zeeman field, generating a paramagnetic response to magnetization. Furthermore, the Fermi surface topology significantly impacts magnetic susceptibility; a Lifshitz transition shifting the Fermi surface from closed to open drives a phase transition from the nematic to the chiral state, causing the magnetic susceptibility to diverge at this critical point. Additionally, we analyze how electron-electron interactions influence the competition between these phases, finding that in real systems, such interactions can only induce a transition from nematic to chiral states near $T_c$. Finally, our findings are compared against available experimental data.
This work addresses the reaction of an E_u spin-triplet nematic superconducting state to magnetization and offers insight into the superconducting phases of $T_c$-doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$. While previous calculations on $s$-wave and isotropic spin-singlet superconductors attribute the paramagnetic response to normal electrons, we demonstrate that in Bi$_2$Se$_3$, the effect originates from the Landau level $n=0$ on the helical boundary of the topological surface states. Consequently, the evolution of magnetic susceptibility under doping can serve as a probe for the ground state of these materials. These conclusions remain valid even if the $E_u$ nematic state is not the true ground state, provided it is accessible under a magnetic field. We also discuss the implications of our results for other spin-triplet superconductors.

In robotics, for instance, kinesthetic teaching demands that a human simultaneously manage multiple degrees of freedom, a task that restricts the range of problems where high-quality feedback can be delivered. Rather than relying on these optimal demonstrations, instructors can offer corrective feedback, such as preferences or reward signals. Although previous research has developed algorithms for specific types of noisy feedback, diverse teaching scenarios and tasks often necessitate different feedback formats. To address this, we propose a framework capable of learning from a heterogeneous mix of feedback sources. Our central insight is that an instructor's underlying cost function is latent; consequently, a sequence of feedback can be modeled as a sequence of loss functions. By applying any online learning algorithm to minimize the aggregate of these losses, we can effectively learn from diverse feedback that is only weakly correlated with the true cost function. This approach unifies existing methods into a general meta-algorithm for corrective feedback, guaranteeing consistent regret bounds regardless of the feedback type. We validate this method by training a robotic racecar for household navigation, demonstrating its ability to rapidly acquire skills from various forms of noisy input. Furthermore, we show through simulations that the framework can also acquire policies that avoid certain states. This research offers a step toward robust skill acquisition from practical and scalable sources of human feedback. The code is available at https://github.com/yjiong2/CorrecTive_Robotic_Imitation_Learning.

While differential detection provides robustness against channel impairments and a simple implementation, it suffers from a 3 dB performance loss relative to optimal coherent detection. This study proposes a scheme that achieves superior error rate performance for certain CPM formats by using a delay interval shorter than the minimum distance between different data sequences but longer than one symbol period. The approach is generalized to support any delay period, with specific implementations for selected formats, and is supported by error rate simulations.

The finding is illustrated with examples of practical CPM waveforms and confirmed by error rate simulations.

Nevertheless, these techniques experience a marked decline in performance when applied to real rain, largely due to the substantial discrepancy between simplified synthetic rain patterns and the complexity of actual rain. This study posits that rain generation and removal are intrinsically linked processes that must be tightly integrated. To achieve this integration, we introduce a unified disentangled image translation framework that simultaneously learns real rain generation and removal. Specifically, we develop a bidirectional disentangled translation network where each direction incorporates two coupled loops for handling both real and synthetic rain. Concurrently, we enforce a disentanglement strategy by separating rainy images into clean backgrounds and rain layers during the removal phase. This approach, supported by cycle-consistency and adversarial losses, better preserves background identity and enhances rain layer diversity. Conversely, the generation phase employs a similar bidirectional disentangled structure in the opposite direction, which improves the variety of the rain module through the cycle-consistent loss in the removal phase and adheres to the real data distribution via the adversarial loss. Furthermore, we utilize a mean module to aggregate the 3D variations of rain layers and rain modules from both directions, enabling a more effective distribution of real rain. Experimental outcomes indicate that our method not only effectively generates and removes real rain but also outperforms existing state-of-the-art image translation techniques.

Our method utilizes a differentiable search over policies to directly optimize a metric that measures the likelihood of a given state being "good," using localized human labels. Extensive experiments confirm that the algorithm is both sample- and time-efficient, effectively scaling to high-dimensional tasks with sparse labeling.

This report explores whether improving the representation of the state space can enhance these methods. We show that introducing a simple, yet powerful, interactive graphical user interface allows users to label the state space more efficiently, yielding significant gains even with a small amount of additional human time.

To address this, an online survey was conducted to gather data on Big Five personality traits (NEO-FFI-R), impulsivity (BIS-11), sensation seeking (ImpSS), and demographics, alongside usage information for 18 central nervous system psychoactive drugs. Correlation analysis revealed distinct groups of drugs with strongly linked consumption patterns, categorized into three pleiades named after their central substances: ecstasy, heroin, and benzodiazepines. An exhaustive search identified the optimal combination of input features and data mining techniques to classify users versus non-users for each specific drug and group. Various classification algorithms were tested, including decision trees, random forests, k-nearest neighbors, linear discriminant analysis, Gaussian mixture models, probability density function estimation, logistic regression, and naïve Bayes, with the most effective model selected for each case. Classification quality proved unexpectedly high, with leave-one-out cross-validation showing sensitivity and specificity exceeding 70% for nearly all tasks. Notably, sensitivity and specificity surpassed 75% for cannabis, crack, ecstasy, legal highs, LSD, and volatile substance abuse (VSA). However, results were less satisfactory for heroin, benzodiazepines, gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHF), phencyclidine (PCP), and opioids, where sensitivity and specificity remained below 50%. Concept extraction from decision trees proved difficult due to the complex, interdependent nature of risk factors. Despite these challenges, the study successfully defined functional clusters of users and non-users for each substance and group, effectively characterizing the risk profile associated with drug consumption. The derived classification models can serve as a foundation for creating a personalized risk assessment test for each drug.

Despite the computational power of parallel and distributed systems, search-based software engineering tasks still rely too heavily on randomization, which limits the scalability of current solution quality. To overcome this, we replaced randomization with a systematic, deterministic approach in our population-based algorithms. This algorithmic ensemble not only matched or exceeded the solution quality of randomization but also offered predictable performance. Furthermore, by eliminating randomization, we can place population-based algorithms on leading exact solvers like ILOG and CPLEX to solve instances that were previously intractable. For example, a 24-variable problem, which took 15 hours to solve with randomization, was solved in just 11 seconds using our deterministic algorithm. Additionally, the ensemble identified problems that could not be solved by the commercial solver CPLEX

Unlike existing resources that primarily focus on taxonomic information, ATOMIC emphasizes inferential knowledge formatted as typed if-then relations involving variables (for instance, "if X pays Y a compliment, then Y will likely return the compliment"). To differentiate between causes and effects, agents and themes, voluntary versus involuntary events, and actions versus mental states, we define nine distinct if-then relation types. By generatively training neural models on the rich inferential knowledge within ATOMIC, we demonstrate that these models can acquire basic commonsense abilities and reason about unseen events. Furthermore, experimental findings indicate that multitask models utilizing the hierarchical structure of these if-then relation types achieve more accurate inference than those trained in isolation, a result confirmed by both automated metrics and human evaluation. The ATOMIC dataset is accessible at atomic.cs.cmu.edu.

We present the last version of the large-scale if-then relational knowledge benchmark ATOMIC ("About Commonsense Inference: Taxonomy and Atlas of Concepts"). The ATOMIC dataset encompasses 877 thousand if-then relations spanning nine distinct relation types, covering concepts, attributes, entities, events, and mental states. It is significantly larger and offers greater conceptual diversity than any current benchmark. We illustrate that neural models can perform in-context reasoning on previously unseen events drawn from five categories of inferential knowledge. Additionally, we show that training on last-version ATOMIC enhances models' ability to anticipate new, never-before-seen effects for existing causes. We identify three key advantages of organizing knowledge by if-then relational knowledge: (1) acquiring basic commonsense inference, (2) achieving more accurate new event inference through multitask learning from hierarchically structured models, and (3) achieving greater conceptual accuracy when models learn concepts via structured from-if-then-benchmarks. Finally, we outline several avenues for future research.

Title: Can Models Generalize to Unseen Events Beyond Zero-Shot?
Abstract: Recent advancements in event extraction have enabled the identification of hundreds of event types and the acquisition of robust core arguments. However, can models infer peripheral arguments for new, unseen event types? Can they handle events that are extremely rare in text? And can they manage high ambiguity, such as distinguishing between events with overlapping names but different argu-ments (e.g., attending a lecture vs. a meeting)? In this work, we address these challenges by leveraging the large-scale event knowledge graph, EventKnowledge. We evaluate

Although the mean-variance optimization problem can be formulated as a system of linear equations using Lagrange multipliers—potentially enabling the exponential speedup of the HHL quantum algorithm—many components of HHL are incompatible with current Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) hardware. This paper presents NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid adaptation of HHL designed for end-to-end execution of small-scale portfolio optimization on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL builds upon existing hybrid HHL variants by leveraging new hardware capabilities, including mid-circuit measurement, qubit reset and reuse, and Quantum Conditional Logic (QCL). To our knowledge, this is the first algorithm to implement a QCL-enhanced Phase Estimation on real trapped-ion hardware, specifically the Quantinuum System Model H1-1. Furthermore, the work introduces a novel technique for determining the optimal evolution time for Hamiltonian simulation. Although the primary focus is on portfolio optimization, the proposed methods for scaling HHL are broadly applicable to any problem solvable via HHL within the NISQ era. The main contributions of this study are: (1) the development of the NISQ-HHL algorithm for solving linear systems and its application to portfolio optimization, (2) the demonstration of QCL-enhanced Phase Estimation on trapped-ion NISQ hardware, (3) the presentation of techniques for scaling HHL to more practical problem sizes, and (4) the investigation of swap-isometry strategies for transferring quantum states to classical systems. Finally, the paper offers insights into solving linear systems and optimizing portfolios among risk-averse investors using either zero or non-zero expected returns. Overall, this research demonstrates that HHL can be executed on small-scale portfolio optimization problems across the full HHL pipeline on NISQ trapped-ion hardware. This achievement marks the first end-to-end execution of HHL on real quantum hardware since its introduction in 2019. Although error correction remains essential for applying HHL to larger, economically significant instances, the techniques demonstrated here represent crucial steps toward that goal. These methods support the scalable execution of HHL for applications beyond the current limitations of quantum hardware. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism (BiAM) that utilizes a multi-modal learning approach to jointly train the bottom layers of an ASR encoder and a text encoder. BiAM facilitates the exchange of feature sampling rates, ensuring that transformed features from one modality are accurately evaluated within the other's space using diversified objective functions. To validate the method's effectiveness, we conducted two sets of experiments, both with and without additional unpaired text data. Results on the Librispeech corpus demonstrate a Word Error Rate reduction (WERR) of up to 6.15% using only paired data, and a 9.23% WERR reduction when leveraging unpaired text data. For comparison, our baseline model achieved a 7.56% WERR improvement over the prominent Conformer model. Additionally, we conducted experiments with an end-to-end ASR model based on TSTST, which yielded a WERR reduction of up to 5.41%. These findings confirm the effectiveness of BiAM in learning homogeneous features across different modalities and validate its use for ASR models to leverage vast amounts of unpaired text data. first T-dwarf, GJ 229B has been the subject of more extensive observations than most other brown dwarfs, yet it lacks a complete atmospheric analysis using modern methods. Its spectrum displays unique characteristics, and recent dynamical calculations regarding its mass and orbit have yielded conflicting results, both necessitating further study. Situated tens of AU from its host star, GJ 229B resides near the boundary between planetary and stellar formation zones, meaning its atmosphere may hold keys to understanding the origins of such intermediate bodies. To address these uncertainties, we applied the open-source APOLLO code to published spectra spanning 0.5–5.1 ${\rm \mu m}$ to perform atmospheric retrievals. Our results yield a refined mass estimate of $41.6\pm3.3\, M_J$ and an effective temperature of $869_{-7}^{+5}$ K; these figures align better with brown dwarf evolutionary models and indicate a system age exceeding 1.0 Gyr. Additionally, we derived molecular abundances for the atmosphere, successfully reproducing the previously noted high CO abundance, and explore their implications for the object's formation and evolution. This retrieval study offers valuable insights for analyzing other brown dwarfs and directly imaged planets, including those targeted by JWST and future telescopes. All data, including fitted models, are publicly accessible via the APOLLO website or the Zooniverse Exoplanet Repository.

Focusing on the deep-inelastic scattering (DIS) regime, we derive the moment sum rules for these structure functions. These moments correspond to the thermal expectation values of twist-two operators, which can be calculated from first principles in lattice QCD for the initial few moments. Furthermore, we demonstrate how lattice QCD can determine the necessary photon virtuality for Bjorken scaling to emerge. We also offer a parton-model interpretation within the Bjorken limit and verify its consistency. Similar to DIS on a proton, the kinematic variable $x$ represents the fraction of longitudinal momentum carried by partons, though in this context, $x$ extends from zero to infinity. By parametrizing parton momentum as $x T u$, where $u$ is the fluid four-velocity and $T$ is the temperature in the rest frame, the parton distribution function for a plasma of non-interacting quarks is found to be proportional to $x \log(1+e^{-x/2})$. We illustrate how interactions modify this distribution and show that at large $x$, the proportionality shifts to $x^{1.5}$. Additionally, we provide a parton-image parton interpretation for the $x \gg 1$ region, aligning with the specific power-law behavior observed. Finally, we confirm that the first three moments derived here satisfy the sum rules established by Starinski. This study offers a parton and image-parton perspective on a thermal quantum plasma under deep inelastic scattering, a framework that could potentially be tested experimentally at relativistic heavy-ion colliders in the future. Unlike recent methods that handle only minor viewpoint shifts, our prior-free approach successfully predicts videos across wider angular ranges, up to 45 degrees. Furthermore, the method utilizes solely RGB frames to learn a dual representation comprising both view-dependent and global components; the latter integrates complementary details to facilitate prediction from novel viewpoints.
