Document Q-A understanding represents a novel and challenging field where a model must identify answers within a given document for specific questions. Unlike free-text based question answering, users often prefer structured documents like PDFs. While existing state-of-the-art models underperform when answers span multiple pages, and current solutions rely on heuristic post-processing to force multi-page capability, we propose a cleaner approach. We reveal that state-of-the-art models often fail to utilize provided documents fully, frequently ignoring pages containing the actual answers. By highlighting this limitation and introducing a dedicated multi-page evaluation set, we demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms baselines by accurately locating answers across multiple pages. Additionally, we release a large-scale, openly available Document QA dataset named MultiPageDocQA, available at https://github.com/wjx99/MultiPageDocQA. Our code achieves a 19.8% relative improvement over baseline systems.

We introduce a straightforward yet potent framework for super-resolution (SR) that relies exclusively on adjacent image patches, eliminating the need for external information such as semantic labels or 3D priors often used in video SR. This two-stream network learns to encode features for visible frames and extrapolate from neighboring frames, achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) results without target frame priors. Evaluated on various natural image and video SR tasks including KITTI, Scene-12, and bAbAR, our method delivers SOTA SR performance

This study investigates airborne infection risks on an urban bus by employing unsteady Reynolds-Averaged Navier--Stokes equations alongside a passive-scalar model for virus-laden aerosol concentrations. The simulation outcomes are contrasted with the commonly used well-mixed model, revealing marked discrepancies in both the spatial distribution and temporal evolution of aerosol concentrations, as well as in the numbers of aerosols deposited on surfaces. Furthermore, the influence of ventilation rates, air filtration efficiencies, and the orientation of air supply outlets on an infected passenger was evaluated. It was determined that a minimum ventilation rate of 12 air changes per hour is necessary to reduce the risk of infection to no more than 1%, even if the air filter is ineffective, whereas a functional filter can lower this threshold to 4 air changes per hour. Finally, varying air supply orientations were examined for an infected passenger seated in different locations within a poorly ventilated bus; in all scenarios, aligning the supply outlet perpendicular to the bus's longitudinal axis was found to yield the lowest risk of infection.

Wind farms situated along coastlines can substantially alter the exchange rates between the ocean and atmosphere for heat, carbon dioxide, and other substances. This investigation utilizes a high-resolution numerical model to examine the impact of wind energy extraction on coastal exchange processes under varying weather conditions. By employing a control simulation without wind farms and two additional simulations with wind farms located in two distinct offshore regions, the study demonstrates that these structures can modify the along-coast carbon dioxide flux by up to 20% to 40%. These alterations stem from wind farms situated along convex coastlines, which obstruct alongshore airflow, thereby accelerating onshore return flows on their leeward sides and accelerating subsurface carbon dioxide upward from the ocean. Specifically, when the mean flow is aligned parallel to the coastline, the maximum increase in carbon dioxide flux from the ocean to the atmosphere was 43% for wind farms in region A and 27% for those in region B, with the higher value associated with winds blowing from a headland. These findings indicate that the placement of wind farms can significantly influence the efficiency of coastal exchange processes.

the Helmholtz International Beamline for Extreme Fields (HIBEF) within the European X-ray Free-Electron Laser (XFEL) facility, we compute x-ray birefringent scattering occurring in the combined field of two optical or near-optical lasers, evaluating multiple scenarios. To aid the experimental observation of quantum vacuum diffraction and birefringence, our analysis prioritizes cases where the initial and final x-ray photons exhibit differences not only in polarization but also in propagation direction—corresponding to scattering angles within the milliradian range—and potentially in energy. Achieving quantum vacuum birefringence in observation requires the initial x-ray photon to be circularly polarized, and the effect becomes most pronounced when the magnetic field intensity is minimal. We identify viable parameter configurations and offer guidance for future experimental designs. Furthermore, we extend the discussion to include non-vacuum cases, specifically scattering off electrons and atoms. In the electron interaction scenario, circularly polarized x-ray photons experience a flip in polarization upon scattering; however, this circular-to-circular transition probability drops quickly as the photon energy gap increases. When the energy difference is significant, the likelihood of the final photon becoming linearly polarized is even lower, though this conclusion is contingent upon the target being a free electron. Conversely, for circular x-ray photon scattering off atoms, the resulting linear polarization probability is extremely low. This conclusion relies on two key assumptions: circularly polarized atomic polarization and x-ray energies that are not excessively high. We address these assumptions and clarify that the first condition is far more difficult to satisfy than previously stated in certain literature.

*   **Reusability:** The original constructions by Broadbent and Lord suffer from limitations: they either ensure one-time security (where the key is usable only once) in the plain model or rely on the random oracle model for security. We propose unclonable encryption schemes that achieve semantic security. Specifically, we offer two constructions—one for public-key and one for private-key settings—based on minimal cryptographic assumptions.
*   **Lower Bound and Generalized Construction:** We re-examine the information-theoretic one-time secure scheme by Broadbent and Lord. In their construction, the adversary's success probability was bounded at $0.85^n$, where $n$ denotes the message length. We investigated whether the theoretical ideal success probability of approximately $0.5^n$ was unattainable. By generalizing their approach to a wider range of monogamy of entanglement games, we demonstrate a cloning attack with a success probability of $0.71^n$ against a class of schemes that includes theirs. Furthermore, we present a specific cloning attack with a $0.75^n$ success rate targeting their scheme exclusively.
*   **Extensions:** We also explore the adaptation of unclonable encryption to secret-sharing and quantum data obfuscation. We establish schemes for unclonable secret-sharing and provide a method to "hide" any quantum state within a larger quantum state such that only a single recipient can retrieve it. Additionally, we devised a protocol for quantum data obfuscation that mirrors a classical result by Brassard, Høyer, and Tapp (STOC'04). Notably, the success probability of this protocol is independent of the dimension of the quantum state being hidden.

*   **Preliminaries:** Our cloning attacks achieve a success rate of $0.75^n$, surpassing the $0.5^n$ bound that applies to attacks against a generic class of cloning attacks. In the main construction, a key step involved selecting an attack from a set of $0.^n$ options, where $n$ represents the number of encryptions; this step contributed to the $0.25^n$ gap between the cloning and anti-cloning success probabilities

The framework involves an encoder, a decoder, and an adversary who possesses the message, a non-causal noisy view of the transmission, and unlimited transmission power; conversely, the decoder receives a noisy observation of the sum of the encoder's and adversary's outputs. The authors propose a technique to adapt generic existing channel codes for authentication purposes. They prove that this adaptation incurs an asymptotically negligible reduction in coding rate and ensures authentication as long as the adversary's observation is not noiseless. Notably, this modification does not depend asymptotically on the statistical properties of the adversary's channel and requires no secret key, thereby facilitating robust practical deployment. Based on these findings, the channel-authenticated capacity is computed and found to match the capacity of the non-adversarial channel. Although this modular approach is tailored for the specified channel model, it remains applicable across a broad spectrum of scenarios. However, the approach relies on the adversary's non-noiseless observation and their lack of omniscience. If the adversary were to possess an unlimited transmission power and an noiseless observation, they could intercept and replace the signal with an arbitrary one. Despite these limitations, this method offers significant potential for future extensions, such as handling delayed messages, addressing computationally weak adversaries, or operating in unstructured untrusted quantized environments. The paper concludes with suggestions for determining optimal parameters to ensure short-delay authentication and calculating computationally feasible thresholds. Furthermore, the study does not address scenarios where the adversary is omniscient of the specific channel code used; addressing this would constitute a notable theoretical advancement, to be explored in future work. Additionally, the approach is adaptable to scenarios where the adversary is computationally weak. This research extends the authors' prior work published in IEEE ISIT 2020.

This work investigates lower and upper bounds for the secret key rate in point-to-point key agreement systems, focusing on scenarios where the adversary possesses non-trivial side information about the honest parties' data. Unlike many studies that assume the adversary observes any function of the honest parties' data, this analysis accommodates more nuanced adversarial contexts. Specifically, the authors establish that the smooth min-entropy of the joint distribution of the messages and the adversary's data provides a tight bound on the achievable secret key rate. Leveraging this finding, the study derives a novel protocol for point-to-point key agreement that remains secure against adversaries with unbounded computational power. Notably, this

This study examines flat-band plasmons in hole-doped twisted bilayer MoS$_2$ (tb-MoS$_2$) using a comprehensive tight-binding model combined with the random phase approximation. When lattice relaxations are accounted for in tb-MoS$_2$, the flat band remains distinct from remote valence bands, leading to a significantly different contribution from interband transitions to plasmon dispersion and energy. Specifically, considering only intraband transitions within the doped flat band yields low-damped, quasi-flat plasmons, while including interband transitions between the flat band and remote bands results in a $\sqrt q$ plasmon dispersion. Additionally, plasmon energies can be adjusted via twist angles and doping concentrations. Conversely, in rigid samples without lattice relaxations, lower-energy quasi-flat plasmons and higher-energy interband plasmons may coexist; however, in highly doped rigid tb-MoS$_2$, strongly enhanced interband transitions suppress the quasi-flat plasmons. Based on the influences of lattice relaxation and doping, we conclude that observing the low-damped, quasi-flat plasmon mode in twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides requires two key conditions: an isolated flat band and an appropriate level of hole doping. We anticipate that our findings on flat-band plasmons will provide valuable insights into the potential for plasmon-mediated superconductivity in these materials. Furthermore, our results offer critical level of detail for interpreting experimental data on plasmon spectroscopy in twisted bilayer MoS$_2$.

In moiré superlattices, varying doping levels can activate both intra- and interband transitions, potentially resulting in quasi-flat plasmon modes. Additionally, we prove a sufficient condition for an almost conformal Ricci soliton to qualify as an almost conformal gradient Ricci soliton and provide a classification of such solitons based on whether they are shrinking, steady, or expanding. First, on a Sasakian paracosymplectic manifold, if the Ricci tensor is proportional to the metric, the manifold is either flat or the Ricci tensor is proportional to the metric, yielding either a steady or shrinking soliton. Second, on a Sasakian semi-Einstein manifold, the soliton is steady when $r = 2n(n+1)$, and the Ricci tensor is proportional to the metric if $r = n(n+1)^2$ or $r = n(n+1)^2$. Third, on a Sasakian KENMSS soliton, the soliton is always steady. Finally, if the Ricci tensor is conformal to the metric, the manifold is Sasakian flat, or the Ricci tensor is proportional to the metric, resulting in either a steady or shrinking soliton. We also establish sufficient conditions for the existence of non-trivial Ricci solitons and confirm that the Sasakian sphere $S^{n+2}$ supports both non-trivial Ricci solitons and non-trivial non-Sasakian solitons. The paper begins by defining almost conformal Ricci solitons, then examines the implications of the soliton being non-trivial, a Ricci flat manifold, or having a closed conformal factor. Subsequently, it explores the conditions under which the manifold is Sasakian, cosymplectic, or the Ricci tensor is proportional to the metric, alongside the existence of non-trivial non-Sasakian solitons. Finally, the paper investigates the relationships among the dimensions of the distribution $D$, the scalar curvature $r$, and the parameter $\theta$. , often guided by surrounding magnetospheres formed by magnetic fields. The powerful outflows from massive stars are believed to be powered by the line-scattering of radiative momentum, whereas the Sun and lower-mass stars experience significantly weaker mass loss driven by the thermal expansion of a mechanically heated corona. For exoplanets orbiting these low-mass stars, the interaction between radiative heating and stellar winds can cause their atmospheres to expand thermally or undergo mechanical ablation. While stellar magnetospheres arise from the internal trapping of wind outflow, planetary magnetospheres are generally shaped by the external pressure of the stellar wind. In both scenarios, this stress can trigger magnetic reconnection, producing observable phenomena such as X-ray flares and radio bursts. This review provides an overview of the underlying physics of these mechanisms, focusing on the distinct outflow regimes of stars and planets, the formation of their magnetospheres, and the origins of high-energy emissions. We conclude with a lookahead at upcoming observational results from the SKA, ngVLA, JWST, Euclid, and ATLAS, emphasizing how high-resolution observations of chemical signatures in stellar winds and exoplanet atmospheres, alongside high-time-resolution measurements of radio and high-energy flares, will advance understanding of the co-evolution of low-mass stars, planets, and their magnetospheres in the era of multi-messenger astronomy.

As direct images of exoplanet atmospheres near maturity, scientists can now measure the total mass loss of objects like hot Jupiter HD 21913 b. This planet experiences intense stellar irradiation (~10<sup>6</sup> times the solar flux) and loses mass at a remarkable rate of ~10<sup>-7</sup> Msun yr<sup>-1</sup>. This represents the first instance where "stellar aeronomy"—the study of stellar outflows—has been applied to an extra-solar body, offering unique insights into planetary evolution and validating models of high-mass loss using the new James Webb Space Telescope. Although dominated by thermal expansion, the atmospheric outflow of HD 21913 b may also exhibit signs of magnetic ablation. Combining atmospheric mass-loss measurements with constraints on its magnetic field will allow researchers to explore these possibilities. Furthermore, analyzing smaller, more massive worlds is essential for confirming or ruling out magnetic ablation as a significant mechanism. If both mechanisms operate on exoplanets, they could potentially drive the complete evacuation of an object's interior on gigayear

the enhancement of spin-orbit coupling in a layer situated adjacent to an interface with a material possessing strong spin-orbit interactions. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, including graphene and ferromagnetic layers. Manipulating spin-orbit coupling offers a potential route to uncover novel and exotic phases within superconducting and semimetallic systems. In this study, we investigate the magnetoelectrical transport properties—specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect—in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers to identify signatures of the spin-orbit proximity effect and determine its origin. Our findings suggest an increase in the spontaneous magnetic anisotropy of both resistivity and anomalous Hall resistivity at very low Cobalt thicknesses. Furthermore, the analysis of anomalous Hall resistivity indicates that the Bismuth layers alter the Hall effect scattering mechanism to the extrinsic skew-scattering type, implying that the spin-orbit proximity effect may arise from the elastic scattering of Cobalt free carriers by Bismuth sites at the interface. Additionally, we observe a similar increase in anomalous Hall resistivity in Ferromagnetic Semiconductors/Antiferromagnetic Semiconducting quantum wells, which is attributed to the Koshino effect rather than the spin-orbit proximity effect. Consequently, we conclude that the proximity effect in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers stems from electron scattering, whereas in Ferromagnetic Semiconductors/Antiferromagnetic Semiconducting quantum wells, it is caused by the Berry Curvature. These results may aid in developing strategies to manipulate spin-orbit coupling and associated magnetic parameters in hetero- and multi-layers, potentially enabling the creation of new quantum phases.

Multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) exhibit anomalous magnetoresistance (MR) when embedded in superconducting lead, whereas single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) display an anomalous anomalous Hall effect (AHE). This work investigates whether an anomalous MR exists in MWCNTs with doping by antiferromagnetic manganese. Fabricated via electron beam evaporation, these nanocomposites covered approximately 50 nm thick amorphous silicon. Transport measurements reveal that while pure MWCNTs show giant negative MR upon proxemicity to superconducting lead, Mn-doping induces anomalous MR and AHE even at higher temperatures. We introduce a straightforward method for calculating an upper bound of the Lipschitz constant across various $p$-norms for feedforward neural networks comprising standard layer types. This approach allows us to frame the training of a neural network with a bounded Lipschitz constant as a constrained optimization problem, solvable via projected stochastic gradient methods. Our experimental results indicate that these models outperform those trained with other common regularizers. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the hyperparameters are intuitive, explore how the choice of norm influences the model, and highlight that the performance improvements are especially significant when training data is limited. In conclusion, we regard explicit Lipschitz regularization as a potent and versatile tool for enhancing model performance.

However, their linear architecture prompts inquiry into how well they can implicitly grasp the hierarchical structures characteristic of human language and which grammatical phenomena they can master. This study examines agreement prediction in Basque as a case study, a task demanding an implicit grasp of sentence structure and the ability to handle a complex yet consistent morphological system. By analyzing experimental outcomes from two syntactic prediction tasks—verb number prediction and suffix recovery—we observe that sequential models underperform on Basque agreement prediction relative to expectations derived from prior work on English. Preliminary findings from diagnostic classifiers indicate that these networks rely on local heuristics as a substitute for representing the sentence's hierarchical structure. Consequently, we propose the Basque agreement prediction task as a rigorous benchmark for models aiming to learn the regularities inherent in human language. Empirical evidence from our study is presented as a dataset available for download.

Basque, a non-agglutinative European language, serves as a robust case study for syntactic prediction studies. Our investigation reveals that sequential neural networks heuristically predict a default value (often the most frequent morpheme) when facing unseen sentence lengths or when trained and tested on disjoint length ranges. This baseline performance of 63.3% (measured via token accuracy) remains unchanged regardless of input context window size. As a standard baseline, this task can assist researchers in uncovering the connections between language science and deep learning.

We introduce a method to automatically generate a controlled corpus for Basque that exhibits a gap of more than two orders of magnitude in sentence length. This corpus enables the training of models that encode a simpler, linear grammar, which then fails to generalize to new sentence lengths at a level never before observed for Basque. We demonstrate that these effects are not limited to specific architectures, as they persist even when the model is trained exclusively on sentences of a single length. We also discuss how Basque's rich morphology offers a unique perspective on how models handle the compositionality of language. Finally, we present a baseline for morphological reanalysis, a phenomenon where a form is interpreted as having one of multiple possible underlying morpheme sequences.

We present a task called Basque agreement prediction that functions as a difficult benchmark for evaluating how well neural networks can learn to represent the compositional structure of language. Our analysis of prediction results on this task suggests that sequential neural networks utilize a direct mapping from input to output that aligns loosely with a bag-of-words representation of Basque grammar, rather than a hierarchical structure. transiting planet with a highly eccentric orbit (e=0.93), experiences a 1000-fold surge in insolation over its 111-day cycle. Its effective temperature rapidly spikes from 400K to more than 1400K within hours as it swiftly approaches its host star to within 0.03 AU at periapsis. Scheduled James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations during the eclipse—timed just hours before periapsis—aim to leverage this extreme variability to investigate diverse atmospheric characteristics, such as composition, chemical and dynamical timescales, and large-scale atmospheric dynamics. Precise orbital data is essential for planning and interpreting these studies. This report details observations of two complete transit events: one captured by TESS on February 7, 2020, and another monitored by a global network of small telescopes on December 7–8, 2021. Additionally, we present new radial velocity measurements that, when integrated with a coupled transit model, significantly refine the planet's orbital ephemeris. Our updated orbital solution decreases the uncertainty in JWST-era transit and eclipse timing from tens of minutes to just a few minutes. Combined with upcoming JWST data, this enhanced precision could potentially reveal non-Keplerian effects in HD 80606b's orbit. Furthermore, we slightly adjust the planet's radius from prior studies and confirm it remains below the hydrogen–helium separation limit.

This paper introduces a method utilizing a statistical model of baseline gameplay to determine design configurations that mimic behaviors consistent with standard, unmodified play. We demonstrate this approach through a case study of upper limb rehabilitation using a custom controller for a Pac-Man game. In a participatory design workshop, occupational therapists established two interaction parameters to balance gameplay and rehabilitation needs. These parameters' impacts were then evaluated experimentally with twelve participants. Our findings show that a low-latency model, incorporating both user input behavior and internal game state, can identify interaction parameter values that replicate baseline gameplay even under degraded control conditions. Finally, we discuss how this methodology can be applied to systematically resolve gamification challenges by balancing physical constraints with subjectively engaging experiences.

These models account for fracture energies proportional to the $(d-1)$-Hausdorff measure of cracks, where $d\geq 2$ represents the dimension of the reference configuration. The proposed approximation preserves the original models' key characteristics, including high-energy scaling, nonconvexity, and the distinction between fractured and unfractured regions. Numerical experiments demonstrate its effectiveness, and it is shown that the approximation converges to the limit energy under standard Gamma-convergence conditions. This work offers a practical tool for numerical simulations and supports the development of variational fracture models for more complex, realistic materials. The primary technical achievement of the paper is a representation theorem for a newly defined total variation type functional on spaces of bounded variation functions with values in the special orthogonal group. While representation results are evident in the Euclidean setting, they required proof in the nontransitive context of the special orthogonal group; such findings may hold broader independent significance. In the appendix, we apply the representation theorem to derive a $\Gamma$-convergence result starting from a potentially complex approximate functional. Although the main development focuses on the linearized elasticity case, the work is variational in nature, and the authors believe the results have meaningful applications in the nonlinear setting as well. For related recent research, see [17].

We introduce a stochastic extension of the balanced torus code (BTC), termed the stochastic balanced torus code (SBTC). We prove that a maximum likelihood decoder can successfully decode the SBTC on average for rates below the critical rate of the Parry-Seneta spin glass model on a torus, a model closely linked to the SBTC's energy landscape. Additionally, we establish large deviation principles for the spin glass model and its associated spin measures. These principles are relevant not only to SBTC decoding performance but also generally, given the nontrivial nature of the principles themselves. Specifically, we show that the specific heat of the spin glass model exhibits a weak discontinuity at a temperature $T^*$. A similar behavior is observed in the specific heat of the ferromagnetic $O(2)$ glass, which applies to the SBTC's landscape in the high-dimensional limit ($d\to\infty$). The decoding success of the BTC was first demonstrated in [1], and its connection to the Parry-Seneta model was established in [2]. Related recent work

Within the framework of models featuring third-generation gauge vector leptoquarks (LQs), we compute the full ${\cal O} (\alpha_s)$ corrections for the $pp \to \tau^+ \tau^-$ process, attaining next-to-leading order (NLO) accuracy augmented by parton showering (NLO$+$PS) through the POWHEG technique. We have developed a specialized Monte Carlo tool that calculates NLO QCD corrections dynamically during event generation, employing it to assess the quantitative effects of NLO$+$PS corrections on kinematic variables relevant to current experimental searches for non-resonant ditau signatures. Utilizing these phenomenological findings, we establish NLO-precise limits on the masses and coupling strengths of third-generation gauge vector LQs, based on the most recent LHC ditau data from approximately $140 \, {\rm fb}^{-1}$ of proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13 \, {\rm TeV}$. This newly presented NLO$+$PS generator facilitates enhanced signal modeling, serving as a critical resource for upcoming ATLAS and CMS investigations into vector LQs in $\tau^+ \tau^-$ channels. Additionally, the described NLO$+$PS algorithm is readily adaptable to other scenarios involving non-resonant ditau production.

In concurrent work, we address the computational challenges of computing NLO QCD corrections to biquark processes.

Many current claims of leptoquark discoveries are based on limited datasets or uncorrected cross sections, potentially undermining their validity. We calculate the total cross section for same-sign di-lepton production via leptoquarks at the LHC to NLO QCD, showing that the true cross section is 10 to 30 times smaller than previously reported. We offer an explanation rooted in the fundamental definition of NLO cross sections and correct prior errors. We also examine other current leptoquark claims, noting that several are already excluded by non-detections of associated di-jet or lepton-jet signatures. Lowering the radiotracer dose or scan duration to mitigate this risk reduces photon counts, thereby compromising image quality. While recent deep neural network (DNN) techniques can translate low-quality PET images—acquired with reduced doses—into high-quality results by leveraging corresponding MRI data, these methods often struggle with out-of-distribution (OOD) data that differs significantly from their training sets. This study introduces a novel DNN approach that incorporates (i) the fundamental sinogram physics of PET imaging and (ii) uncertainty quantification via per-voxel heteroscedasticity in the residuals between predicted and reference images. The first element ensures validity when applied to OOD data, while the second enables the model to interpolate between training extremes and accurately handle very low dose levels. Experiments were conducted using [18F]NaF bone scans and [11C]raclopride dopamine scans, covering a 200-fold dose reduction, with (if available) co-registered T1 bone and gray matter MRI data. The proposed method outperformed state-of-the-art approaches on test sets ranging from 25% to 100% OOD, achieving (i) a 2.9-fold improvement in mean absolute error, (ii) a 1.7-fold reduction in negative log-likelihood, and (iii) a 1.5-fold enhancement in structural similarity index. These findings indicate that integrating fundamental imaging principles with uncertainty quantification can substantially boost generalization in medical image reconstruction, especially with out-of-distribution data. Finally, the technique is expected to be equally effective for other cross-modality translation tasks.

Recently, deep neural network (DNN)-based super-resolution (SR) methods have been widely employed to convert low-dose CT (LDCT) images into diagnostic-quality contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) images. Although existing single-domain SR models demonstrate strong performance, they often fail to generalize to out-of-distribution (OOD) data. To develop more robust and reliable SR models that handle OOD datasets, this paper utilizes the uncertainty of the translation process to train models on such data. Specifically, we present a novel end-to-end SR framework using conditional generative adversarial networks (GANs) that incorporates uncertainty into the adversarial training to improve generalization for OOD data. as increasing concern grows over excessive data collection under the guise of personalization and its use for questionable purposes. Our experience developing privacy-safe personalization tools for publishers prompted an investigation into how users perceive the intersection of privacy and personalization. Through a survey examining individual experiences and perspectives across various age groups, this paper presents key findings for the publishing community and developers. These insights aim to guide the design and implementation of next-generation news recommender systems that prioritize human-centric approaches, striking a necessary balance between personalized experiences and privacy to maximize the benefits of both. Consequently, this work serves as a crucial reference for practitioners, researchers, and system developers aiming to create effective and privacy-preserving news recommender and personalization systems. Furthermore, it offers a human-centric perspective on personalization to enhance system design, alongside a set of principles to ensure that personalization does not become a privacy invasion. Finally, we propose the term "privatization" to describe a new class of systems where the experience degrades from personalization to privatization. These findings also establish a foundation for future studies, which should integrate the views expressed in this paper to advance human-centric news recommender and personalization principles and frameworks. In summary, the insights from this work on human-centric privacy and personalization in news consumption will enable the creation of next-generation systems that deliver superior personalization without compromising privacy. The code associated with this study is available at https://github.com/aherronr/Perceiving_Privacy_and_Personalization.

This study explores the relationship between Centering Theory and contemporary coreference resolution systems. We propose an operational definition of centering and employ a search-based methodology to systematically evaluate whether neural coreference resolvers comply with CT rules through various discourse metrics. Our information-theoretic analysis indicates a positive correlation between coreference and centering, yet demonstrates that high-performing neural resolvers gain little advantage from explicitly modeling centering concepts. Furthermore, we find that contextualized embeddings encapsulate much of the necessary coherence information, explaining why CT yields minimal improvements for modern neural systems utilizing pretrained representations. Finally, we address coreference factors unmodeled by standard CT, such as world knowledge and recency bias. By formulating an enhanced version of CT that incorporates recency, we show it captures coreference information more effectively than the original formulation. Overall, our work provides an empirical examination of CT's role in coreference, clarifying what the model learns, where it struggles, and the complex nature of coreference itself. We hope this research encourages future studies on other under-explored coreference characteristics. We release our datasets and models at https://github.com/Microsoft/Modeling-Centering-Theory-for-Coreference-Resolution.

We present a general framework for formulating coreference evaluation metrics that operates without requiring annotated gold-standard predictions. Using this framework, we developed two evaluation metrics for coreference resolution that significantly outperform existing methods. We also demonstrate how the framework can be applied to measure coreference in low-resource settings.

In this study, we examine zero-shot coreference evaluation, a problem where models assess unfamiliar texts without prior training exposure. We introduce the ZeroShotCoreEval dataset to facilitate research in this area. Our findings reveal that state-of-the-art systems suffering from domain shift on this dataset also exhibit coreference bias, a form of token bias where models incorrectly assume all mentions of the same entity are equivalent. We measure this artifact and observe that even trained evaluators struggle with it. To mitigate such biases, we propose a novel multi-task evaluation dataset, IndirectCoreEval, which tests a model's ability to link mentions of the same entity to different center sentences. Models evaluated on both DirectCoreEval and IndirectCoreEval achieve superior zero-shot performance compared to those trained solely on DirectCoreEval. To further reduce coreference bias, we introduce anti-bias techniques including data re-weight

The findings encompass a new fixed-parameter algorithm based on the count of sources, an XP-algorithm defined by treewidth, and another fixed-parameter algorithm utilizing treedepth. All three methods stem from an innovative framework that integrates SPQR tree-decompositions with parameterized techniques. This approach not only unifies but also extends prior tractability results for series-parallel digraphs, single-source digraphs, and outerplanar digraphs. Furthermore, the work offers a fixed-parameter algorithm for treed width, extending the established XP-algorithm in that specific context. Additionally, the research presents a new fixed-parameter algorithm for a generalization of planar digraphs known as almost planar digraphs. Notably, this digraph extension is not a subclass of planar series-parallel graphs. The problem under investigation generalizes the embedding of outerplanar and planar digraphs, as well as the orientation of undirected planar graphs. The stated contributions represent the initial fixed-parameter algorithms for this broad class of problems. The methodology described here further extends to related problems, such as testing if a digraph is almost series-parallel, although those extensions are left for future investigation. The presented algorithms are also applicable to generalizations of the upward planar drawing problem, including x-upward planar drawings (where x is a real number), 1.5-planar drawings (allowing one edge crossing per edge), and k-layers. However, these extensions remain unexplored in this paper, with their results reserved for future work. The underlying SPQR tree decomposition-based framework is relevant to other drawing problems, though this study focuses exclusively on planarity and related constraints. The work on x-upward planar drawings references prior fixed-parameter algorithms, yet those methods do not currently have a unified framework. The discussed problems are deeply rooted in drawing digraphs with minimum area, a challenge known to be NP-hard even for bipartite graphs. While there are many related area minimization problems, this research does not align with those that rely on grid minor exclusions. The findings extend to planar digraphs with bounded out-degree, although no fixed-parameter algorithm exists for that specific case. The problem also relates to other planar digraphs concerns, such as the longest path problem, which is NP-hard for planar digraphs with maximum out-degree exceeding two. This automation not only boosts development cycle agility but also facilitates the rapid, automated integration of decoupled workflows. This paper introduces a novel framework designed for the automated configuration of systems modeled as state machines. By utilizing model checking and satisfiability modulo theories (SMT), the framework is applicable to any domain that can be expressed via SMT formulas. Our method supports modular application, thereby enhancing scalability. Additionally, we demonstrate how optimization techniques can generate configurations that are optimal according to specific metrics and more amenable to human comprehension. We illustrate the framework's versatility and capabilities by employing it to configure a CGRA memory tile for diverse image processing tasks.
In summary, our contributions are threefold: (1) we identify gaps in current configuration methods and propose a framework to address these issues; (2) we develop and demonstrate a technique for optimizing configured system performance; and (1-3) we illustrate the framework's utility and efficacy through its application to the configuration of a composite, reconfigurable computing device and the optimization of the arithmetic logic unit within that system.
'Config5' addresses the challenge of automatically determining valid configurations for configurable systems or components, a task that is often complicated and time-consuming when done manually.
We present a method for the automated configuration of systems modeled as sets of SMT-expressible state machines. Our approach employs collaboration graphs to facilitate modular configuration and integration. Furthermore, we illustrate the method's application in configuring a composite computing device, demonstrating optimizations that improve both performance and usability.

Findings from the second half of the first year are reported, highlighting (1-2) progress on developing collaborations graphs for modular configuration, and (3-4) the application of this work to configure a sensor node for an in-ground vehicle, specifically a collaboration module and a processor module, respectively.

by applying quantum information theory. Specifically, we examine Krylov complexity, entanglement negativity, von Neumann entropy, and entanglement capacity for systems with SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetries. Our primary methodology relies on two-mode coherent states, which enable the analysis of operator growth and its entanglement structure across any system within the discrete series representations of these groups. Our findings confirm that the investigated quantities display specific universal characteristics consistent with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of leveraging symmetry, as it substantially streamlines the computation of metrics related to operator growth. Notably, we contend that the reliance on the Lanczos algorithm—the predominant tool previously used in this field—is unnecessary, since essential insights can be derived directly through symmetry arguments. Ultimately, our work underscores the efficacy of utilizing special states, such as those enabled by symmetry, for investigating dynamics in quantum many-body systems. By employing quantum information theory and special states, we believe deeper and more intuitive insights into the phenomena of operator growth and quantum scrambling can be achieved. We further propose that our approaches are applicable to other problems in this and related domains. Based on our findings, we advocate for future research into general definitions of kinetic quantities for symmetric systems, which we contend are essential for a comprehensive understanding of operator growth and quantum scrambling across all quantum many-body systems. Based on our approaches and results, we suggest that different kinematic and dynamical quantities can be investigated using special states, offering a field-renewing methodology for advancing the study of operator growth, scrambling, and related topics in quantum many-body systems. Additionally, we contend that a diversity of special states should be examined to derive deeper insights into the universal nature of operator growth and quantum scrambling. Additionally, we contend that the principles of symmetry and quantum information theory must serve as foundational frameworks for investigating kinetic phenomena in quantum many-body matter. Finally, we contend that the utilization of special states offers a superior methodology for researching operator growth and quantum scrambling compared to the predominant approach relying on the Lanczos algorithm. By utilizing special states, we can more efficiently examine kinematic and dynamical processes, including their universal traits, while providing a clearer intuitive understanding of kinetic phenomena and their symmetries. We further contend that our methodologies can be applied to investigate kinematic and dynamical processes, as well as their universal properties, for other symmetries and special states, thereby deepening our comprehension of operator growth and quantum scrambling in quantum many-body systems. We also maintain that our methods must serve as

dominant method for indoor person and device localization. WiFi fingerprinting, which involves gathering Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) measurements at known locations, is a prevalent technique in various positioning algorithms found in existing literature. However, accurately calculating the spatial distance between users and access points is essential for effective fingerprinting, a task that is currently not addressed sufficiently in research. Since there is no universally standard approach for converting RSSI into spatial distance, this paper reviews and analyzes multiple open methods for this transformation. Leveraging these existing solutions, we developed a machine learning algorithm that estimates spatial distance from RSSI using data from both indoor and outdoor settings. This algorithm serves as a critical module in a signal-based localization system that also incorporates a machine learning module for signal mapping to 2D coordinates. To validate the proposed approach, we designed and executed a validation experiment at the "Electrical and Computer Engineering" faculty building at Alexandru Ioan Cuza University in Iasi, Romania. The results demonstrate that the proposed spatial distance estimation method is robust, effectively generalizing to new access points and environments that were not seen during training. Finally, we show how this estimation enhances the overall accuracy of the positioning system. Specifically, estimating spatial distance improved the median accuracy from 3.15 meters to 2.41 meters in the signal-based localization algorithm tested. These findings confirm that the estimated spatial distances are reliable for enhancing overall localization accuracy. In the future, this method could be extended to estimate other key parameters, such as the orientation of signals relative to access points.

The rapid advancement of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has made sensor-based monitoring a common practice in both personal and professional settings. While the goal of existing signal-based localization algorithms is to determine the exact 2D or 3D coordinates of a user, this paper argues that for many IoT applications, such precision is unnecessary and often excessive. Instead, a coarser granularity, such as quarter-circle sectors, is often sufficient and more cost-effective. This suggestion is particularly relevant for IoT sensors that do not require real-time updates or frequent user interaction. To achieve this lower-precision, energy-efficient localization, we propose using Random Forest (RF) algorithms to classify IoT nodes into four sectors based on their angle of arrival (AoA) relative to an access point (AP). These sector estimates then inform an energy-efficient signal mapping function that translates AoA into actual angular position. This study investigates the feasibility of constructing such a structure around a black hole. We examine six potential energy sources: the cosmic microwave background, Hawking radiation, an accretion disk, Bondi accretion, a corona, and relativistic jets. To support a Type II civilization, an output of $4\times10^{26}\,{\rm W}$ ($1\,{\rm L_{\odot}}$) is required. Among the sources listed from (iii) to (vi), an accretion disk offers the highest luminosity, reaching $10^{5}\,{\rm L_{\odot}}$, which is sufficient to sustain a Type II civilization. Furthermore, if the Dyson Sphere captures additional energy forms, such as kinetic energy from jets alongside electromagnetic radiation, the total harvested energy could be roughly five times greater. Based on the resulting emission from such a sphere, we find that a Dyson Sphere around a stellar-mass black hole in the Milky Way (located 10 kpc away) should be detectable via waste heat radiation in the ultraviolet (10–400 nm), optical (400–760 nm), near-infrared (760 nm–5 μm), and mid-infrared (5–50 μm) bands. Similarly, thermal radiation from a supermassive Dyson Sphere around a Milky Way-type black hole (10 kpc distant) would be observable through these same channels. Based on these findings, we recommend searching for near and mid-infrared emissions as a method to identify Dyson Spheres around black holes. Additionally, we note that the emission from an accretion disk around a supermassive black hole differs from that of a standard stellar accretion disk. Finally, we conclude by investigating the feasibility of Dyson Spheres around other celestial bodies.

are governed by Service Level Agreements (SLAs), necessitating rigorous monitoring to ensure compliance. A common approach utilizes active measurement mechanisms that deploy probes throughout the network to inject synthetic traffic and assess performance; however, this method is resource-intensive. Consequently, it typically covers only a subset of the network, risking missed SLA violations. Furthermore, the selection of this subset relies on human administrators, a process that lacks scalability and fails to adapt to rapidly evolving network dynamics. This article investigates the advantages of leveraging Peer-to-Peer (P2P) technology to enhance SLA violation detection. Initially, we outline the principles of P2P-driven active measurement steering, characterized by decentralized decision-making within a self-organizing overlay. Subsequently, we introduce measurement session activation strategies derived from these principles. These strategies operate without human intervention, dynamically adapt to fluctuating network conditions, and remain independent of the specific active measurement technology employed. We validate our proposals using ns-3-based active measurement applications. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed strategies yield significant gains in both performance and cost compared to current human-centric methods. Specifically, we report up to a 4.3-fold increase in detection sensitivity for active measurement sessions, alongside a measurable boost in operator revenue. Additionally, we reveal that P2P can be effectively employed for active measurement steering despite the presence of self-generated traffic loads. This work opens avenues for further research into SLA violation detection, offering the potential to transform active measurement into a scalable, decentralized service. The proposed solutions are already deployed in production environments. We released the measurement session activation code under the GNU General Public License (GPLv3) on GitHub, while the measurement application itself is utilized by a commercial operator. The study relies on GreenICM modeling for performance and sensitivity analysis. We encourage readers to contact us for additional details regarding the proposed solutions.

We address the challenge of detecting Service Level Agreement (SLA) violations in carriers by moving from currently used, inefficient active measurement strategies to more effective ones. Our methodology comprises three key components: 1) Formulating a mathematical model to calculate the minimum probability of violation detection; 2) Developing activation strategies for these measurement sessions that require no human input; and 3) Verifying the approach's validity through simulation. Our results indicate that the proposed methods significantly outperform existing techniques in both sensitivity and network resource efficiency. We have implemented and deployed this solution commercially. All source code for the application and activation strategies is available on GitHub. We suggest that this work inspire future developments in active measurement technologies

precision long-baseline experiments depend on accurate models of neutrino-nucleus interactions, which currently represent a significant source of systematic uncertainty due to the historical inability of detectors to observe final-state neutrons. Three-dimensional projection scintillator trackers, integral to the near detectors of next-generation long-baseline facilities, offer a solution. Their fine granularity and excellent timing resolution enable the measurement of neutron kinetic energy on an event-by-event basis, providing crucial data to refine interaction models and neutrino energy reconstruction methods. Two prototypes were exposed to the neutron beamline at Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL) in 2019 and 2020, covering neutron energies from 0 to 800 MeV. To validate neutron detection capabilities, the total neutron-scintillator cross section was measured and compared against external data. The resulting total cross section for scintillator in the 98 to 688 MeV range is determined to be 0.36 ± 0.05 barn. To demonstrate the capability for neutron reconstruction, the neutron energy spectrum was measured using both the total cross section and neutron direction as inputs, yielding a mean energy of 16.4 ± 0.7 MeV for neutrons with total energies between 200 and 400 MeV. micrometer-sized chondritic grains vary with temperature, revealing a fivefold reduction in surface energy as temperature rises. This study investigates the influence of surface water. While ambient lab conditions feature multiple water layers, protoplanetary discs at low pressure and moderate temperatures likely retain only a monolayer, which evaporates entirely as dust migrates inward into hotter zones. To model this, we measured the tensile strength of chondritic material using two new preparation techniques alongside our previous methods: air-dried cylinders and vacuum-heated cylinders (super-dry). For temperatures up to 1000 K, dry samples exhibited sticking forces approximately ten times greater than wet ones. Super-dry samples mirrored the dry samples' behavior up to 900 K, but beyond that point, their sticking forces rose exponentially, reaching another factor of ~100 near 1200 K. This enhancement from wet to dry conditions extends a trend previously observed in amorphous silicates and multimineral mixtures. Consequently, super-dry dust findings suggest that aggregate growth is significantly amplified in a narrow high-temperature region around 1200 K, potentially representing an optimal zone for planetesimal formation. These results aid in determining the initial conditions for numerical models of planetesimal formation. Our statements regarding wet sticking forces apply strictly to low-pressure, relatively cool (T < 1200 K) environments within protoplanetary discs. Multimineral aggregate models should incorporate the strong temperature dependence of both dry and wet sticking forces. For wet aggregates, models must also account for the temperature-dependent number of water layers. Given that super-dry sticking forces increase sharply around 1200 K, we developed a simple fit function to describe this relationship. When disc temperatures exceed 1200 K, larger aggregates are expected to pull in more super-dry grains, resulting in sticking forces closer to the measured values for those high-temperature experiments. Finally, we present evidence that the 1200 K phenomenon is driven by specific chemical changes occurring within the material.

A pivotal step in this process is how dust properties, particularly surface surface forces, change with temperature and pressure. We conducted experiments to measure the sticking forces of super-dry chondritic dust up to 1200 K. For dry dust, sticking forces increase by a factor of ~1

This work examines two methods for regularisation path computation in lfda: a novel closed-form approach and a traditional numerical technique. Standard discriminant analysis effectively separates high-dimensional data into classes, but it requires prior knowledge of class labels, which is often unavailable. `semi-lfda` addresses this by enabling lfda with incomplete label information. This package implements both the standard and semi-supervised variants, including semi-supervised kernel and lfda. This paper introduces a user-friendly application for solving lfda that supports label-annotated datasets and allows users to adjust regularisation parameters via a visual interface.

Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic/dynamic limitations, recent advancements in constrained imitation learning enable the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings, thereby expanding the method's applicability. Although various constraints such as joint limits, obstacle avoidance, and planar restrictions have been explored, nonlinear hard constraints remain insufficiently addressed. This paper introduces Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) to tackle core challenges in imitation learning, particularly nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP learns probabilistic patterns from multiple demonstrations, adapts skills to arbitrary target joint positions and velocities, avoids obstacles at the link level, and satisfies both linear and nonlinear equality and inequality constraints. Furthermore, the paper examines the relationship between EKMP and current state-of-the-art motion planning techniques and provides evaluations, including 7-DoF robotic arm trajectory planning, to validate the framework's effectiveness. Experimental results demonstrate that EKMP successfully acquires skills from multiple noisy human trajectories, achieving high accuracy in following desired states and limits while effectively avoiding obstacles. Overall, this research advances EKMP to a new level, establishing it as a promising direction for future research in imitation learning.

The paper outlines the necessity for such research, highlighting that while EKMP offers a robust solution for many constraints, it does not fully address all aspects of kernelized learning, optimization, and noise handling found in competing methods.

Although extensive work exists on self-supervised learning for robotic manipulation, data acquisition remains a significant challenge. We present a novel self-supervised learning framework that facilitates EKMP application in imitation learning, enhancing performance under uncertain conditions and across 6-DoF and 7-DoF task spaces.

In this study, we employ quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation to investigate the superconducting behavior of a doped two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model incorporating Rashba spin-orbit coupling and an external Zeeman field. Our results generally indicate that Rashba coupling promotes s-wave superconductivity, whereas the Zeeman field has a suppressive effect. Specifically, in the regime of strong Rashba coupling and moderate Zeeman coupling, we observe that the spin-glass phase induced by the Zeeman coupling is eliminated upon entering the superconducting state. Notably, we detect an emergent long-period spatial modulation of the superconducting gap whose wavelength increases as the magnetic field strength decreases. We attribute these modulations to a competition between Fermi surface nesting and Zeeman splitting. Furthermore, our analysis of spectral functions reveals that quasiparticle excitations within the superconducting state possess finite bandwidth. To our knowledge, this is the first time that both spatial modulations and the bandwidth of quasiparticles have been observed in this specific lattice model. Additionally, we find that the spin susceptibility remains finite within the superconducting state, indicating the presence of Canted spin-s-wave pairing. Finally, the calculated bipartite spin correlation functions suggest that the preceding spin-glass phase persists but is weakened by the onset of superconductivity. We also discuss the implications of our findings for CuBa$_2$O$_3$, a doped two-dimensional narrow-band system. We contend that the longitudinal spin excitations observed experimentally in CuBa$_2$O$_3$ can be attributed to the coexistence of spin glass and superconducting phases, and that the enhancement of spin excitations with increasing magnetic field stems from Pauli spin splitting. Additionally, we propose that the magneto-OR effect observed in CuBa$_2$O$_3$ can be explained by the combination of spin glass and superconductivity.

This transition, occurring at doping levels of $x=p=0.17$ and in conditions characterized by magnetic fields above 35 T and temperatures well below the zero-field $T_c$, is manifested in the vortex lattice's compression modulus. Our analysis, grounded in the Eilenberger theory of vortex lattices, indicates that this event represents the anticipated 45-degree rotation of the square vortex lattice—a long-predicted phenomenon in $d$-wave superconductors occurring near a van Hove singularity. The triggering of this rotation at $p=0.17$ is attributed to an electronic transition involving a partial filling of the singularity. This finding offers fresh perspective on the evolution of the superconducting gap function in LSCO and clarifies the behavior of thermodynamic quantities in the mixed state, including prior observations of kinks in vortex viscosity and a 50% reduction in thermal conductivity. We have additionally pinpointed two earlier, reportable transition in the mixed state at $p=0.17$ as a consequence of this electronic event. Finally, we propose that a similar, though less distinct, electronic transition at $p=0.19$ is responsible for previously documented experimental results in LSCO. Our findings significantly advance the understanding of the superconducting state in LSCO and offer valuable insights for interpreting the behavior of emergent phenomena in other cuprate materials. La$_{2-x}$Sr$_x$CuO$_4$ (LSCO) stands out for its unusually complex energy landscape, marked by multiple electronic transitions in the normal state and various phenomena in the mixed state. Recent data from specific heat, thermal conductivity, and NMR have revealed two additional transition in the mixed state at $p=0.17$ and  $p=0.19$.

We attempted to synthesize a one-year ASM from a short-exposure, one-week observation dataset using three ML-based image processing techniques: dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise. Although ML inference yields less clarity than standard likelihood analysis, it generally enhanced the quality of the ASM. Notably, these algorithms successfully replicated the complex diffuse emission along the galactic plane from one-week data, effectively mimicking a ground truth (GT) derived from a full year of observations. These methods can be implemented with relative ease to produce sharper images without relying on specific emission model assumptions. However, significant discrepancies were observed between the simulated ML maps and the GT map, attributed to the substantial temporal variability of blazar-type active galactic nuclei (AGNs) over the year. Consequently, the proposed ML methods are not only viable for improving ASM image quality but also capable of algorithmically detecting variable sources like AGNs without human bias. Furthermore, this approach is deemed widely applicable to ASMs from various missions, offering the potential to investigate giant structures and transient events that are often missed in pointing observations. Finally, the algorithms developed here may serve as a valuable educational resource for future ML researchers in astronomy.

Various machine learning (ML) methods have been applied to convert short-term Fermi LAT all-sky maps (ASMs) into long-term representations. These methods outperform point-estimate approaches, such as Li & White's likelihood analysis, in reproducing the emission morphology of the ASM, including the galactic plane, while also identifying variable sources without human intervention.

In this work, we introduce a deep learning framework utilizing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to transform Fermi LAT ASMs from approximately 10 days of exposure into approximately 1 year. We trained a CNN on about 10,000 pairs of 10-day maps using a supervised learning scheme where the "ground truth" was a 1-year map. The model was further fine-tuned using 10-day maps from different time periods. Our results demonstrate that the Fine-tuned CNN successfully reproduced the emission morphology of the ASM, successfully distinguishing between steady sources and transient ones.

choice theory, we investigate its application to diverse combinatorial optimization challenges. We propose an abstract framework where agents act sequentially according to a specified order. Each agent selects an action to maximize her own value, conditioned on the choices made by preceding agents. Our objective is to identify action sequences that achieve a total social welfare close to the optimal solution. We assume the ability to query the value $v_i(S)$ obtained by agent $i$ when acting after the set of agents $S$. We derive tight bounds on the social welfare achievable with a polynomial number of queries. While these general bounds indicate only a marginally sublinear approximation of optimal welfare, significantly better approximations emerge when valuations originate from specific combinatorial structures. For instance, when valuations correspond to bipartite matchings, directed graph arborescences, or Boolean satisfiability, simple query-efficient algorithms achieve a $2$-approximation. We also address truthfulness concerns, demonstrating how certain algorithms can be made truthful via VCG-like payments. Furthermore, we define and analyze the "price of serial dictatorship," a metric offering an optimistic assessment of the solution quality produced by action sequences in combinatorial optimization. We provide general upper and lower bounds for this metric and establish tight bounds for several common valuation types. Notably, we show that even in the most structured scenarios—such as when valuations come from additive functions like scheduling—price of serial dictatorship can exceed $2/\pi$. We provide explicit constructions for these and other cases involving polynomial approximations. Ultimately, our work aims to bridge the gap between social choice theory and combinatorial optimization. Although serial dictatorship is known to guarantee an additive approximation for additive valuations, we demonstrate that in related settings, it can yield arbitrarily poor approximations. We offer bounds and constructions for the solution quality of serial dictatorship in scenarios involving knapsack, vertex cover, set cover, set packing, subset sum, and knapsack with multiplicities. We also examine the impact of limiting the number of items available to each agent. As with combinatorial problems, the algorithmic price of serial dictatorship is often close to $2$. Additionally, we define and analyze "fractional" and "round-robin" variants of serial dictatorship. We show that for scalar functions, the price of serial dictatorship is at most $n^{1/2}$, with this bound being tight for specific functions and scenarios. Finally, we discuss lower bounds for the price of serial dictatorship in submodular and convex valuations cases.

Massive MIMO enhances mobile data rates by deploying a large number of transmit antennas, yet it often struggles with interference management due to channel reciprocity. SM-MIMO offers an alternative large-scale solution that achieves similar gains while using fewer transmit antennas than conventional MIMO, as it relies on an orthogonal codebook rather than signal superposition, thereby reducing hardware complexity and cost. This paper investigates the asymptotic error rate of a regularized least-squares detector within an SM-MIMO framework. Initially, the study establishes that the asymptotic error rate formula applicable to standard least-squares detectors in large MIMO systems also applies to SM-MIMO, provided the number of users and the number of bits per user scale proportionally with the number of receive antennas. Building on this insight, the document introduces two methods for adjusting the regularized detector in SM-MIMO: a bayesian adjustment and a more practical asymptotic modification. Both approaches require only a scalar parameter, which can be determined via a closed-form expression. Furthermore, the paper addresses spatially modulated delay diversity using a regularized detector and outlines general strategies for tuning such systems to maximize a wide range of performance metrics, including the error rate. The findings are supported by the observation that, in many instances, the asymptotic error rate of the optimal bayesian detector applies beyond its strict asymptotic conditions. While the authors of [1] analyzed the asymptotic error rate of a regularized least-squares detector for large MIMO systems, this work extends that analysis to SM-MIMO and delays. Additionally, the work addresses how to tune the detector to minimize a broad class of convex distortion functions, although it does not cover non-convex functions, as the computational complexity would otherwise become prohibitive.

The paper is structured as follows: Section \ref{sec:sm-mimo} provides an overview of SM-MIMO, including a brief description of spatially modulated delay diversity, and introduces a family of regularized detectors applicable to this system.

We believe that incorporating interactive viewers into astronomical databases will significantly enhance their utility for the research community, and we have deliberately designed this open-source solution to facilitate similar implementations in other domains.

Introduction
Effective and efficient interaction between astronomers and digital repositories of spectral and imaging data is crucial for maximizing the scientific return of major surveys. Recent advancements in web technology have enabled the creation of highly customizable, interactive, and seamless open-source web tools. Although some algorithms for analyzing spectral and imaging datasets (e.g., PyASTRO ALFOSC ToolBox, irsweb, DASH, webDAI, ALFOSC JavaScript ToolBox, ALADIN, and ALADINO) are now available as open-source packages, very few of these solutions support integration as interactive viewers within astronomical archives. Existing strategies typically involve embedding static images or graphs generated by these packages into web forms like Simple Image Search And Download (SISAND); however, this method is inherently limited. Our objective is to develop a contemporary, customizable, and interactive web solution that addresses the broader needs of astronomical communities.

In this paper, we detail the design, implementation, and features of our novel web-based design. We demonstrate its application as an interactive viewer for spectra and imaging data, focusing on the RCESEDv2 Catalog (https://rcsed2.voxastro.org/) as a test case. While our implementation is specific to RCESEDv2, we have engineered the system to accommodate other catalogs as well.

a vast Jurassic-Cretaceous intraplate basin system situated on the southern margin of the South American plate. By integrating quantitative analysis of existing literature with fresh well data, this study reconstructs quantitative estimates for both sediment accumulation and marine transgression and regression cycles across the early to mid-Cretaceous period in the South Atlantic rift basin. Results indicate that total accumulated thickness before the onset of the early Cretaceous ocean flooding varied from 1.85 km to 4.91 km across different areas. A strong positive correlation exists between water depth and the thickness of the alluvial sequence (correlation coefficient r = 0.78), suggesting that the transition from alluvial to marine sediments was governed by the depth of the sediment source area rather than the basin's sinking rate. Furthermore, the ratio of alluvial to marine thickness offers a quantifiable metric to assess the influence of climate on sediment distribution patterns within rift basins; a ratio ranging between 1 and 10 corresponds to the arid-semi-arid climate characteristic of the La Amega arena. Finally, the interval between the maximum alluvial deposition and the maximum marine transgression can serve as a quantitative proxy for the duration of the early Cretaceous southern high latitude aridification event on the South American plate. Overall, the development of the South Atlantic rift basin during the early to mid-Cretaceous was shaped by three primary factors: the evolution of the rift geometry, tectonic structures, and regional climate. Consequently, the alluvial-transgressive model observed in this basin provides a critical case study for comprehending high-latitude ancient fluvial-sea barrier development following desertification in midlatitude intraplate basins.

To facilitate this study, we utilize Dungeons and Dragons (D&D) as our experimental platform; this role-playing game involves multiple player characters and a Dungeon Master (DM) who work together to reach shared objectives beneficial to the players. In this context, each player character represents a student with unique personas and capabilities, while the DM acts as the teacher, serving as the rule arbiter and guide responsible for helping students reach a global objective. We develop a theory-of-mind-inspired approach to train such a DM using reinforcement learning (RL). This methodology involves two key steps: first, the DM learns to anticipate player reactions to its statements by analyzing a dataset of D&D dialogue transcripts, and second, it employs these predictions as a reward function to evaluate how effectively its utterances guide players toward their goals. Both human and automated evaluations demonstrate that training a DM with RL to incorporate a theory-of-mind perspective significantly enhances the players' capacity to achieve goals grounded in their shared world. We believe this work advances the state of the art in controlling large language models (LLMs) for tailored applications and provides a comprehensive framework for systematically evaluating them. This paper advocates shifting the focus from mere detection to discovery, specifically identifying novel word senses emerging over time across the entire vocabulary. By extensively fine-tuning both token-based and type-based approaches on recently published German data, we demonstrate that these models can effectively uncover words undergoing meaning shifts. Additionally, we present an almost fully automated framework for both discovery and evaluation. Our results show that even simple models can successfully identify these changes. However, we also highlight the significant additional challenges involved in moving from identification to proper disambiguation. Final evaluations, conducted alongside human experts, reveal that while models correctly flag the majority of selected cases, they fail to capture many other valid instances of changing word usage. ### 1 Introduction

While the capacity to recognize shifting meanings within specific contexts has been studied for over a decade, and even automatic discovery was demonstrated as early as 2012, the field of lexical semantic change remains largely in its infancy. A primary obstacle has been the scarcity of high-quality, manually disambiguated corpus data. With recent releases of extensively fine-tuned German text resources, we can now overcome this barrier and evaluate the potential of currently state-of-the-art techniques for discovering lexical semantic change across a full corpus.

Our approach involves identifying an subset of text pairs consisting of historically adjacent sentences (e.g., five years apart), leveraging their labels from existing annotations to uncover instances of evolving meaning. We offer a comprehensive framework for this methodology, utilizing two recently released, manually Fine tuned German corpus resources.

However, the scientific community has not yet reached a consensus on whether EDE can simultaneously alleviate this tension while adequately fitting Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) and large-scale structure data. This study deconstructs existing constraints from Planck CMB observations and full-shape clustering data from the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS) to clarify the sources of conflicting conclusions found in previous literature. By employing two distinct analytical methods—grid sampling and profile likelihood—we investigate whether current constraints are skewed by volume effects during marginalization or biased toward specific values of the EDE fraction, $f_\mathrm{EDE}$. Our results indicate that the data-allowed range for $f_\mathrm{EDE}$ is highly sensitive to the choice of other model parameters, with certain parameter configurations favoring larger $f_\mathrm{EDE}$ values than those derived from standard Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analyses. This sensitivity suggests that volume effects are the primary cause of the discrepancies in the field. Consequently, we apply a profile likelihood approach to the EDE model to calculate a volume-effect-free confidence interval for $f_\mathrm{EDE}$, determining $f_\mathrm{EDE} = 0.072\pm 0.036$ ($68\%$ C.L.). Because this interval avoids volume biases, our method can be applied to other cosmological models; a comparison with the $\Lambda$CDM model yields a p-value of $0.19$, indicating that the $\Lambda$CDM fit is not statistically disallowed. Finally, applying profile likelihood to the EDE model with Planck + BOSS full-shape clustering data allows us to conclude that the $\Lambda$CDM fit is disallowed at the $3\sigma$ level. We note that this work does not address the impact of Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAO) and Cepheid distance measurements, which are expected to further constrain $f_\mathrm{EDE}$. In a forthcoming paper, we will utilize the profile likelihood method to examine final constraints from all available datasets. Our approach represents a systematic framework for analyzing the viability of the EDE model and can be extended to investigate other novel cosmological models.
