Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem, which violates the standard counting law for NG bosons found in the normal NG theorem within nonrelativistic and Lorentz-symmetry-violated relativistic frameworks. The investigation focuses on mathematical foundations spanning Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The basis of the NG boson counting law in the anomalous context is explored through both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. A quasi-Heisenberg algebra is identified as a generic feature across various symmetry-breaking schemes of the anomalous NG theorem; this algebra suggests a violation or modification of the Heisenberg uncertainty relation within the NG sector, a phenomenon that is potentially verifiable experimentally. The formalism of the effective potential is introduced to elucidate the mechanism of the anomalous NG theorem using the derived Lie algebra results. Following an examination of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential as an explicit Lorentz-symmetry-breaking parameter, a general model Lagrangian approach to the anomalous NG theorem is proposed. This analysis not only determines the conditions for the counting law of true NG bosons but also reveals the mechanism for generating the mass of massive NG bosons. Furthermore, the emergence of a massive mode in the NG sector is interpreted through the quantum uncertainty relation of the Heisenberg algebra, which arises from Lie algebra symmetry breaking and is realized within the effective potential of the kaon condensation model. Additional predictions from the general Lagrangian model are discussed, including the verification of the anomalous NG theorem in heavy ion collisions and cosmology, specifically within the context of early universe chemical imprints. Finally, the violation of the Heisenberg uncertainty relation within the NG sector is proposed as a viable method for detecting chemical imprints from the early universe at future experiments such as LHC Run 3, Run 4, and the Forward Physics Factory (FPF). The work concludes with a summary and an outline of future research directions. The introductory section of this paper includes a pedagogical review of the derivation of the anomalous NG boson counting law through Lie algebra methods. Following the introduction, the "Methods" section presents the Lagrangian formulation of the anomalous NG theorem, detailing the violation of the NG boson counting law, the general mechanism for generating massive NG bosons, and the breaking of the Heisenberg uncertainty relation within the NG sector. Nevertheless, definitive experimental proof of this remote mechanism has remained absent. Frequently, contaminants at the graphene/substrate interface allow alternative processes, such as pinhole-seeded lateral or van der Waals epitaxy, to account for the formation of exfoliable single-crystalline films. In this study, we demonstrate that growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene atop sapphire substrates yields a 30-degree superstructure that corresponds to the geometric stacking of multiple, pinhole-free, 3-x-monolayer thick supercells. Because the epitaxial strain energy is concentrated along the graphene layer, these observations confirm that remote epitaxy is the operative growth mechanism. Furthermore, we establish that growth via van der Waals epitaxy is not energetically favorable and that pinhole defects at the graphene/substrate interface can actually hinder remote epitaxy by creating local strain fields that distort the expected superstructure. Heusler films with various chemical stoichiometries were generated by altering partial source deposition times; the most successful films, those with a Pt:R rare-earth ratio of 2:1, exhibited a 45-degree superstructure indicative of pseudo-substrate epitaxy. Notably, these 10-nm thick, 3-x-monolayer films can be mechanically exfoliated to produce thick, single-crystalline membranes featuring atomically sharp interfaces with both graphene and sapphire (Al$_2 O$_3). Additionally, we show that the superstructure energy is localized at the graphene film, enabling the creation of Heusler films with lower-energy 3-x-monolayer periodicities on both pinhole-clean and contaminated graphene/substrates. This is evidenced by the presence of contaminants within the central regions of the 30-degree superstructures observed on clean graphene, a phenomenon attributed to migration from substrate impurities. These superstructure configurations correspond to previously unreported hexagonal stacking sequences. Finally, we discuss how heptagonal superstructures indicate the presence of pinhole defects and explain why they preclude remote epitaxy. Heusler films were characterized using low-energy electron diffraction, atomic force microscopy, and scanning tunneling microscopy. We contend that this work provides the first clear experimental evidence of remote epitaxy. The paper examines the universal and particular aspects of mathematical structures, their relationships, and morphisms, framing these elements as the components of a 2-category. It illustrates how an adjunction within this 2-category functions as a natural transformation between two monads, thereby linking an abstract mathematical method to the preparation of quantum states via physical measurements. Specifically, we show that both the GNS construction and the representation of an abstract von Neumann algebra are instances of such adjunctions. Based on this 2-categorical formulation, we derive and discuss the physical interpretations of these mathematical phenomena. Additionally, the work includes relevant statements concerning toqral.

A natural transformation between two functors $F, G : \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}$ assigns to each object $c$ in $\mathcal{C}$ a morphism $n_c : F(c) \to G(c)$ in $\mathcal{D}$ in a way that respects the action of morphisms under $F$ and $G$. This respect for morphism action constitutes the universal property of $n$. Given the scarcity—or potential absence—of stable de Sitter vacua, dark energy in string theory is presumed to manifest as a quintessence field undergoing slow roll. As this field evolves, a tower of massive states will generically become lighter, initiating a catastrophic phase transition in low-energy cosmological dynamics within at most a few hundred Hubble times. Consequently, dark energy domination cannot persist forever, and there exists a non-zero probability that we currently reside in the initial Hubble epoch. We employ a simplified model of quintessence interacting with a tower of heavy states to explicitly illustrate the collapse of cosmological dynamics as these states become light; this occurs because a vast number of corresponding particles are produced after a specific duration, overwhelming the quintessence field. Furthermore, we explore implications for inflation in the early universe. If dark energy (quintessence) emerges from generically independent mechanisms from inflation, the associated tower of states will inevitably become light, implying either unstable scalar spectral indices or premature termination of inflation caused by heavy particle production. Even in scenarios where both phenomena stem from distinct towers of tower of states, a sufficiently sparse distribution of branes necessary to prevent dark energy from triggering catastrophic state production would suffice to ensure stable slow roll inflation. We also examine the scenario where dark energy and inflation are governed by the same tower of states. In this case, if the self-coupling of the field driving dark energy is positive, quintessence behavior arises only after a specific threshold of field value, allowing for controlled production of massive states before dark energy dominates, thereby ensuring stable inflationary dynamics. This scenario suggests that the number of e-folds need not be precisely calculated, nor does there need to be a single preferred number of e-folds. However, if the self-coupling is negative, this outcome is unattainable. We conclude by noting the potential relevance of our findings to the Hubble Tension, though this point demands more intricate analysis in future work. We maintain an open stance regarding the validity of single field slow roll inflation, emphasizing that it need not rely on a unique valley in the scalar potential.

This paper addresses an impulse control problem characterized by discontinuous switching costs. This analysis presents significant challenges, with only a handful of existing methods available. Information can be encoded either as time-independent classical expression differences at a single point or as full expression profiles over time. This approach employs a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) to handle the time domain and utilizes relevance learning to pinpoint the most predictive feature dimensions over time. The resulting mapping facilitates the visualization of temporal sequences and enables the prediction of classes for new sequences. By using relevance learning, we identify discriminating masses or gene expressions while pruning dimensions that are irrelevant to the classification task or primarily represent noise, thereby creating a highly efficient learning system for temporal data. Results demonstrate that combining simultaneous supervised learning with metric adaptation significantly enhances prediction accuracy for both synthetic and real-world data compared to standard techniques. Temporal gene expression analysis holds great promise for understanding biological systems and developing diagnostic tools, yet it remains in its infancy. A primary obstacle is the scarcity of samples, a critical factor in many applications. We address this by introducing a learning algorithm designed to extract meaningful information from expression data measured over a small number of time points. The proposed algorithm combines a time-independent supervised learning component with a learning component specialized for temporal sequences. The former identifies predictive variables and provides an initial estimate of the target function, which is then refined by the latter component. This combination allows for the discrimination between diseases and healthy states, as well as the classification of various stages of development or progression. The algorithm was tested on data from a flow cytometry experiment tracking T-cells' response to stimulation and on microarray data from mouse heart development. In all cases, the predictive mass genes identified by our algorithm outperformed those found by classical methods, and the overall prediction accuracy for our algorithm matched or exceeded that of state-of-the-art time-series classification methods.

venshtein introduced the sequence reconstruction problem, which examines a scenario where an identical sequence from a specific set is sent through several channels, with the decoder observing the resulting distinct outputs. Assuming the transmitted sequence lies at a distance $d$ from a code and that each channel introduces no more than $r$ errors, the goal is to determine the minimum number of channels necessary to uniquely recover the original sequence. This number must exceed the maximum overlap between two metric balls of radius $r$, provided their centers are separated by at least distance $d$. This paper investigates the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations using Hamming distance. Within this framework, we define a Cayley graph and calculate the precise value of the largest intersection of two metric balls under Hamming distance for the cases where $r=4$ and $d\geqslant 5$, as well as when $d=2r$. Additionally, we provide lower bounds (which are nearly accurate) for the scenarios where $d=5$ and $r=3$, as well as $d=2r$. These findings rely on novel constructions and analyses of coding problems specific to permutations. We further demonstrate that these problems can be transformed into related challenges involving nonattacking rooks and attacking queens on multidimensional tori. Several open questions are also discussed at the end. The research presented here was funded by RFBR grants \#17-01-00186 and \#18-01-00180.

While numerous machine learning methods have been developed to identify instrument classes from audio, most require large amounts of labeled data for each individual class. We explore a different strategy: using a hierarchy of musical instrument classification to improve flat-classification performance even when trained and tested only on non-hierarchical data. By applying a hierarchical loss function—similar to those used in multi-label music tag recognition—to a few-shot learning algorithm that predicts only flat classes, we enable the model to infer a hierarchy during training. This method allows for the recognition of closely related instruments (e.g., flutes and oboes) using few examples, despite comprising a larger subset of all possible instruments.

We address two main limitations in current deep learning approaches for musical instrument recognition. First, we introduce a technique to learn a taxonomy of instruments during training that can be applied during few-shot classification. Our method involves defining a taxonomy over the target instrument set and modifying the loss function to enforce this hierarchy, requiring no changes to the network architecture, algorithm, or inference process. Second, we demonstrate that learning such a hierarchy naturally leads to improved classification accuracy and reduced ambiguous errors, even when the training and testing datasets have a flat class structure.

Although extensive research exists on automatically classifying musical instruments, models are usually trained and evaluated using "flat" classifications that ignore hierarchical relationships. We show that explicitly incorporating a instrument hierarchy during training enhances performance on few-shot classification tasks, whether the testing dataset is flat or retains its own hierarchy.

We present the FEVER dataset and library, which contain 227,826 human-written claims about entities found in Wikipedia for use in factual verification tasks. The top-performing system achieved a score 1.5 times higher than the average of randomly generated baselines. This paper details the methodology, code, and metrics of that top system.

Unlike previous approaches, our system treats a 20-base-pair PCR primer pair not as a definition for a single object, but as a distinct storage partition managed independently with its own indexing structure. We observe that while the total number of compatible primer pairs is constrained, the internal address space within each partition is virtually limitless. By exploiting the flexibility of this address space, we enable advanced storage semantics, including hierarchical organization and robust, efficient data update mechanisms. Additionally, to maximize the potential of PCR's prefix-based addressing, we developed a method to convert any arbitrary indexing scheme into a PCR-compatible format. This allows primers to be dynamically extended to include specific index segments, thereby narrowing the reaction scope to precisely retrieve individual objects (such as files or directories) within a partition. Our wet lab validation confirms the feasibility of this approach and demonstrates a 140-fold reduction in sequencing costs when retrieving smaller objects from a partition. In summary, we view a fixed 20-bp primer pair as defining a storage partition with a near-infinite addressable region where primers can be effectively and efficiently extended to facilitate nuanced data retrieval. These techniques can be broadly applied to endow DNA storage with sophisticated, efficient, and scalable data structures, even when using longer primers for inter-partition hierarchy or when employing primer pairs of varying lengths. Finally, we demonstrate how to assign unique primers to specific index bits, creating a partial overlap graph that visually represents the full indexing structure. This method is particularly valuable for rapidly visualizing and debugging the storage system and can enhance other indexing methods, for instance, by allowing primers to be progressively extended to retrieve any object in a Trie.

**Introduction**

Since its inception, DNA storage has seen rapid advancement in both methodological techniques and practical utility. Although the total capacity of current DNA storage systems remains relatively modest, the amount of storable data is theoretically unconstrained. The fundamental mechanism of DNA storage relies on the polymerase chain reaction (PCR), which serves as a powerful and adaptable retrieval tool. PCR functions as a prefix-based indexing system: a specific primer pair targets a unique object within a collection, and because primers are inherently hierarchical, a primer derived from an object's full name (e.g., a file path) can be used to fetch any of its prefixes. This principle forms the cornerstone of our proposal for a rich and efficient indexing scheme for DNA storage.

While the Shallow Water Equations (SWEs) are standard for this task, conventional numerical solvers are computationally intensive and depend on high-resolution bathymetry data. This study introduces a two-stage framework: first, we employ the Principal Component Geostatistical Approach (PCGA) to derive the probability density function of bathymetry from flow velocity data, followed by the application of machine learning (ML) algorithms to create a rapid SWE solver. significant and emerging subfield within machine learning, focused on embedding causal knowledge into the highly adaptable spaces of deep learning architectures. Successfully integrating these causal structures promises more robust, generalizable, and informed predictions and inference. However, the field remains nascent, particularly regarding how to evaluate disparate methods that differ vastly in their output formats, encoding mechanisms, and representation strategies. This living paper extends Pearl's ladder of causation by refining its levels and introducing a new dimension to categorize parametric assumptions for both inputs and representations, thereby creating a comprehensive map of causal deep learning. This framework encompasses various machine learning domains, including supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling. Designed as a research tool, the map assists scholars in locating benchmarks, comparing methodologies, and, crucially, identifying gaps in current research. While the volume of published work on CDL grows daily, this map remains static. We have open-sourced the map to facilitate its use by the community, whether for structuring related work sections or more effectively highlighting specific contributions.

Although numerous studies remain unincluded due to the map's early stage, many high-profile papers lie outside its scope for reasons distinct from novelty. A primary distinction of this work is explicitly separating CDL from standard deep learning, a differentiation that is often blurred in the literature. A paper is excluded if it does not address one of three core challenges of CDL: (1) infusing structures representing uncertainty, (2) learning these structures from data, or (3) reasoning with multiple causes. For instance, excluded works often rely on assumptions about data generation, as seen in typical deep learning contexts. Methods that learn structures, such as contrastive estimation or causal representation learning, are also excluded because they specifically target structure acquisition. Furthermore, the map emphasizes that while much recent effort concentrates on learning structures, CDL inherently involves all three rungs of Pearl's ladder; even the simplest model must at a minimum learn a representation of cause and effect.

Additionally, the map excludes papers on other related topics. Works on generalizing across domains, a common challenge in statistics and machine learning, are not covered, nor are those on handling missing data. While these areas benefit from the principles of CDL, they remain distinct research domains. It is important to note that the volume of excluded work far surpasses that included, yet this map is not intended to be exhaustive.

This study addresses this challenge by utilizing real-time magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) alongside the temperature-dependent proton resonance frequency (PRF) shift of water to measure temperatures within a cylindrical fixed bed. We successfully generated three-dimensional (3D) temperature maps while heating the reactor from ambient conditions to 60~$^{\circ}$C using hot air. The findings reveal distinct temperature gradients along both the axial and radial axes, with results aligning closely with optical probe data and an average error of $\pm$ 1.5~$^{\circ}$C. This MR thermometry approach offers new avenues for investigating mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds and holds potential for future application to reactive gas-solid systems. More importantly, this work lays the essential foundation for eventually monitoring temperature in such systems to optimize reaction outcomes. While the current study focused on non-reactive conditions, the methodology is readily adaptable to non-isothermal catalytic tests, potentially enabling the observation of "hot spot" formation. Ultimately, obtaining spatially and temporally resolved temperature and conversion data would allow for direct, in situ verification of the power law model for heat generation in first-order, exothermic reactions. Resonance Decoding was employed to encode temperature into the PRF of water during the 3D MR thermometry acquisition. This research significantly advances understanding of gas-solid fixed bed physics and offers opportunities to explore the influence of key parameters on internal temperature distributions in catalytic reactors. By providing option for 3D temperature measurement in a gas-solid fixed bed, the study highlights the critical role of axial and radial heat transfer (conduction and convection). Although the presented system and method are tailored for non-isothermal, non-reacting tests, they can be adapted for non-isothermal, reacting analyses by integrating magnetic encoding for spatial resolution with appropriate pulse sequences. Such adaptation would facilitate the determination of 3D temperature and conversion distributions, thereby allowing for the direct validation of standard design equations.

This category represents the most fundamental class of maps adhering to a version of the $h$-principle; in two dimensions, it closely approximates oriented submersions, as every such map of dimension 2 targeting a closed, simply connected manifold is bordant to a submersion. Our framework encompasses several established results on limiting spectral distributions, including those for the standard Wigner matrix, the adjacency matrix of a sparse homogeneous Erd\H{o}s-R\'{e}nyi graph, heavy-tailed Wigner matrices, certain banded Wigner matrices, and Wigner matrices featuring a variance profile. While traditionally created by professionals—a process that demands significant time, labor, and resources—the rise of AI-empowered persuasive video generation (AIPVG) has made large-scale content production more feasible. As an interdisciplinary field, AIPVG can be difficult for newcomers to navigate, and to date, no comprehensive survey has addressed it. This paper fills that void by examining essential AI techniques for automatically crafting persuasive videos. We present an original taxonomy categorizing AIPVG into three core stages: 1) visual material understanding, which identifies relevant information from visual assets; 2) visual storyline generation, which selects and sequences high-quality assets to construct a compelling narrative; and 3) post-production, which includes generating background music and animating stills to improve the viewer experience. Furthermore, we outline standard evaluation metrics and datasets used in this area, critique the strengths and limitations of current approaches within these stages, and explore promising avenues for future research. By offering this panoramic view of AIPVG, we hope to assist researchers, practitioners, and industry professionals in better understanding automatic persuasive video generation and fostering further advancements in the field.

Video-based AI evaluations have garnered substantial attention recently, yet a unified overview of the field remains missing. This paper provides a survey of video-based methods for assessing foundational AI models, covering video understanding models, generative models, and algorithmic bias. We begin by examining data representations, including static frames, augmented frames, and motion tokens, followed by a review of evaluation tasks aligned with each representation. We also discuss challenges in building benchmark datasets and training test sets to avoid overfitting. Finally, we offer an original critique of AI video evaluations, propose future research directions, and provide a non-technical summary to make the topic accessible to the broader community. Our comprehensive survey serves as a vital resource for the video-based AI assessment community, facilitating a deeper understanding, better benchmarking, and more effective communication of video-based model evaluations.

We consider a sequence of independent words, each of length $n$, drawn uniformly at random from an alphabet of size $q$. Let $X_n$ denote the count of distinct words in this sequence. It is established that for constant $q$, the distribution of $X_n$ converges to a limit as $n$ grows, a finding with applications to connective diseases where genes function as "words." This paper extends the analysis to two generalizations: (1) a uniform distribution of gene frequencies and (2) a "heavy-tailed" distribution of gene frequencies. In both scenarios, we derive a recurrence relation for the moments of $X_n$. This relation enables the computation of moments for any specific model parameters. Furthermore, we apply these methods to two simplified processes that mirror the first moment's dynamics of the general models. While the first generalization does not yield a Gaussian approximation for $X_n$ as $n$ increases, the second generalization does. When two or more resonators are positioned near one another, their resonant frequencies and field profiles are mutually influenced, causing a pair of initially degenerate modes in an asymmetric system to exhibit anti-crossing behavior as a parameter is varied. Similarly, in a single resonator, two counterpropagating modes become coupled, potentially leading to cross-phase modulation, Kerr frequency comb generation, and other nonlinearity-driven effects. The primary objective of this paper is to present a clear derivation of the solution to Maxwell's equations, building upon the foundational work of T.A. Jefimenko [1]. While previous studies have examined the radiative and non-radiative properties of these solutions [2,3], our focus differs. Previous proof-of-concept studies and certain two-dimensional experiments have demonstrated that spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) maximizes collected field information, thereby achieving resolution that surpasses the Rayleigh criterion. This study examines a two-trophic ecosystem involving two predator species that compete for a shared prey resource, incorporating explicit interference competition. Through appropriate rescaling, the system is modeled as a singularly perturbed setup characterized by rapid prey dynamics and slower predator dynamics. Near a singular Hopf bifurcation, the model exhibits chaotic mixed-mode oscillations (MMOs), which consist of concatenated small and large amplitude oscillations and act as prolonged transients before the system settles into its asymptotic state. To identify the dynamical trigger for a large amplitude oscillation within an MMO orbit, the model is simplified to a normal form near the singular-Hopf point. This normal form includes a separatrix surface that distinguishes between the two oscillation types; a large amplitude oscillation begins when a trajectory crosses from the "inner" to the "outer" side of this surface. Furthermore, specific conditions on the normal form variables are derived to predict whether a trajectory will undergo additional MMO cycles before a regime shift occurs. These derived conditions offer potential early warning signs for sudden population shifts in ecosystems. In the presented model, a regime shift results in the collapse of the prey population, causing predator populations to drop due to starvation and triggering a cascade of fluctuations. The model parameters are derived from a rigorous mathematical formulation based on the underlying stochastic processes. Additionally, simplified models are constructed to demonstrate the necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of MMOs and the specific dynamics involved in approaching the singular-Hopf bifurcation point. To broaden the warning signal beyond the local singular-Hopf neighborhood, modified nullclones are introduced. Derived sufficiently early warning signals indicate that these modified nullclones effectively predict the global phenomenon of MMOs. The paper concludes by deriving the Jacobian matrix near the singular-Hopf bifurcation point to provide a comprehensive description of the observed phenomenon.

We develop a novel approach for action recognition in low-light environments. While recent studies on low-light image segmentation and detection rely on dataset adaptations and reinforcement learning, these methods are not directly applicable to video analysis. We propose a straightforward model that achieves effective low-light action recognition without needing adjustment for a second dataset. Our model, trained and assessed on the ARID dataset, surpasses current baseline models by an 11% reduction in error rate. Furthermore, we analyze several training and inference strategies, demonstrating that our model benefits from training on a smaller dataset and utilizing only dark frames during both training and inference, though it remains capable of operating on well-lit video using camera control mechanisms. In contrast, training on low-light video alone results in a model unable to recognize actions in well-lit conditions.

We introduce a model for action recognition in low-light conditions. Since state-of-the-art models are trained on large datasets with consistent, sufficient lighting, they often fail when applied to low-light video. We assess several training and inference strategies using a dataset of dark video clips and report the corresponding evaluation results. Our model achieves action recognition in low-light conditions with an error rate of 0.13, a significant improvement over the 0.44 error rate of existing models in this domain. Additionally, we demonstrate that the model can achieve an error rate of 0.21 by training on only low-light video or 0.29 by training on only well-lit video. We further explore various training and inference configurations, such as mixing frame counts at different stages, which yield only marginal improvements (0.11 error rate). In contrast, utilizing a large number of frames during training but selecting only dark frames for inference proves highly effective, achieving an 0.05 error rate in our tests. This technique is explained through the lens of transfer learning, where the model learns to identify the absence of light rather than specific actions, as action identification becomes more complex with increased variability. This document outlines the design, development, and testing of a Search Engine on an FPGA, which functions as a specialized, high-speed, hardware-based key-value processor. Unlike traditional computer CPUs, this Search Engine utilizes exact matching for keys while employing prefix matching for values. By leveraging dedicated hardware for addressing and memory, it offers significantly faster performance than software alternatives, delivering O(1) constant time complexity for exact key matches and approximately 3.3us for matching among one million prefixes. The engine supports various data types, including integers, floats, and strings, and performs essential operations such as add, update, remove, and search. These capabilities demonstrate that the Search Engine can serve as a vital component for building more intricate processors, potentially evolving into a parallel processor capable of handling big data applications.

Each galaxy features compact, kiloparsec-scale starburst cores with characteristics indicative of forming bulges, situated within extended, massive stellar disks. Notably, these disks are both distinctly quiescent and severely asymmetric. This configuration suggests that "outside-in" quenching is actively occurring in these group members. We propose a scenario where the significant mass asymmetry in the disks (varying by factors of 1.6 to over 3), likely induced by accreted gas and clumps, suppresses star formation in the outer regions while channeling gas toward the nuclei to fuel central starbursts. The asymmetric side of the disks indicates the impact site of accretion streams, with nearby dust and stellar components directly tracing the inflow direction. Interactions with these accreted clumps, viewed as minor mergers, align the major axes of the three galaxies with external Lyman-$\alpha$-emitting feeding filaments. These findings offer the first observational proof of how cold accretion streams influence galaxy formation and evolution. The first method relies on a variational approach, which requires the background medium to satisfy the Chandrasekhar–Kumar–Narasimhan condition. The second method avoids variational techniques and makes no assumptions about the medium other than periodicity. These results are significant because they enable the application of perturbation theory to demonstrate the existence of large-amplitude solutions in a broad class of cubic Maxwell–Schrödinger systems.

To overcome this limitation, we introduce a neurosymbolic approach that leverages weak supervision from a static program analyzer. This method enables a deep generative model to symbolically identify long-distance semantic relationships within already generated code by invoking static-analysis tools. Title: Teaching Large-Scale Pretrained Language Models to Generate Correct and Efficient Code. Abstract: Existing neural models for program synthesis primarily prioritize semantic correctness while neglecting syntactic validity and performance. We present P3 (Paraphrasing for Performance and Correctness), a technique utilizing a Java interpreter to train a source-code-transformer to rewrite syntactically flawed code. By learning to balance semantic equivalence with syntax and performance, we demonstrate that a compact transformer can outperform larger, specialized models across various programming tasks. P3 achieves state-of-the-art results on method generation, full-program correctness, and performance optimization tasks, as well as on multi-objective optimization benchmarks like DeepMind's Lib2Tensors. Additionally, we demonstrate its application in refactoring existing codebases to modern Java versions and reducing memory usage on C++ programs. P3 represents a initial step toward generating correct and efficient programs and provides a framework for future research in this domain. Notably, no gamma-ray photons were recorded from this event. The findings imply that solar neutron production via pion decay can occur following moderate flares, a process that does not necessarily require the hard gamma-ray spectra often associated with large neutron events. The data support the view that gamma-ray lines are not critical for neutron generation. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that non-thermal (power-law) electron and ion populations are sufficient to produce both neutrons and radio emissions. The paper offers a qualitative analysis of neutron generation through proton-induced photonuclear reactions and provides a quantitative examination of neutron production from the photodisintegration of nuclear protons. Additionally, it explores electromagnetic pair shocks as the source of pair-instability neutrons and their accompanying radio emissions. A summary of the survey's statistical neutron detection rates is also provided. The event's significance lies in proving that moderate solar flares can generate neutrons, emphasizing that while hard gamma-ray spectra facilitate larger neutron events, they are not a prerequisite for neutron production from moderate events. These solar neutrons are distinct from those originating from solar flares' cosmic ray-like X-rays. The observations further reveal that pair shocks can account for all known solar neutron types. Finally, the document discusses the potential for these detections to constrain solar neutron claims made in recent years.

These findings are compared against results obtained from kinetic theory using the relaxation time approximation and from causal first-order theories. Our analysis reveals that all methods yield comparable dynamics for scalar and vector modes; however, the specific divergence-type theory examined here uniquely predicts propagating, damped tensor waves, consistent with kinetic theory. Additionally, non-hydrodynamic tensor modes appear in holographic fluids. These outcomes validate the use of hydrodynamics in scenarios involving fluid-gravitational wave interactions. We also examine the implications of these modes for viscous relativistic fireballs, noting that they could influence particle production and anisotropic flow during the early stages of heavy-ion collisions. Furhtermore, these tensor modes offer a potential physical mechanism for generating gravitational waves through viscous effects in strongly interacting relativistic matter. Finally, we speculate on the application of these findings to the early post-Newtonian stages of stellar collapse and associated supernova explosions within general relativity. Since the sound speed in hot, dense quantum chromodynamic plasma is predicted to be $1/\sqrt{3}$ plus corrections of order $e^2/b^2$, this regime may support the same waves as kinetic theory. Given that transverse stresses are anticipated to be significant in such plasmas, it is reasonable to expect their influence on gravitational wave generation in heavy-ion collisions, provided the system size and duration are sufficient. We term these waves "sound," "vortex," and "shear" waves. Under appropriate conditions, these waves could also impact the fate of a collapsing stellar core, potentially influencing neutron star formation, the generation of knotty jets, or the creation of a black hole.

Current state-of-the-art flow anomaly detection techniques often depend on fixed memory structures—such as hash functions or nearest neighbors—which struggle to effectively constrain high-frequency values akin to moving averages, eliminate seamless outliers, or operate within an end-to-end deep learning framework. This paper introduces a novel incremental anomaly detection approach that utilizes random Fourier features combined with quantum measurement mechanisms and density matrices, effectively functioning as an exponential moving average density estimator. Capable of handling potentially infinite data streams with a constant $O(1)$ update complexity, the method is evaluated systematically against 12 leading streaming anomaly detection algorithms across 12 datasets. Leveraging original legal analysis alongside precise computer science formalisms, we introduce "demonstrability" as a core concept for characterizing compelled acts. Furthermore, we provide a language to assess whether a compelled action meaningfully achieves the government's objectives as effectively as desired. We then apply these definitions to evaluate the compellability of various cryptographic primitives, including decryption, multifactor authentication, commitment schemes, and hash functions. Notably, our framework yields a new conclusion regarding compelled decryption in scenarios involving deniable encryption: while the government may compel the act, the respondent remains free to choose any password.

To ground these formalisms, we present a collection of original legal arguments and perspectives on compelled acts, deniable encryption, and the structure of passwords. These elements together constitute a rigorous, scientific approach to the study of compelled acts in computer security. Following these definitions, we examine the viability of additional cryptographic constructs under this framework, such as key derivation functions, authenticated encryption, and secret sharing, alongside standard functions like logging in, searching, and signing. Ultimately, we aim to advance the field by inspiring further research into computer functions under the foregone conclusion doctrine and their associated cryptographic assumptions.

Baker's method yields a PTAS for planar graphs, minor-excluded classes, and similar structures. Regarding maximization finite-valued CSPs (where constraints are arbitrary non-negative functions), Romero, Wrochna, and \v{Z}ivn\'y [SODA'21] demonstrated that the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation provides a straightforward PTAS for all fractionally-treewidth-fragile classes, representing the broadest known "sparsity" condition for such schemes. We generalize these findings to general-valued CSPs, which incorporate "crisp" (or "strict") constraints requiring satisfaction by every valid assignment. The sole requirement for these crisp constraints is that their domain includes an element at least as feasible as any other, though potentially less valuable. For minimization general-valued CSPs featuring crisp constraints, we introduce a PTAS applicable to all Baker graph classes—a definition by Dvo\v{r}\'ak [SODA'20] that covers every class where Baker's technique succeeds, with the possible exception of fractionally-treewidth-fragile classes. Although this result is typical for problems meeting specific monotonicity conditions on crisp constraints, we demonstrate that this can be weakened to diagonalisability, a property of relational structures linked to logics capable of expressing all natural constraints. This work also establishes a general link between diagonalisability and "local" CSPs. Furthermore, we prove that Baker's method and its extensions are fully general for minimization and general-valued CSPs with "universal" constraints (those definable via first-order logic with limited variable quantification). These problems constitute a vast array of practical CSPs, potentially the most significant collection not already addressed by Romero et al. Title: Detecting Fake News in Emerging Events via Meta-Learning

**Abstract:**
Deep learning models can effectively identify fake news on social media when ample labeled data from a specific event is available. However, these models often struggle when encountering new events with limited verified posts, as structural and distributional shifts occur between events and categories. Existing solutions for emerging events face two main issues: (1) a lack of research comparing adaptation to novel events versus new categories, and (2) the difficulty of achieving effective detection with limited validation data. Current methods generally rely on large event-specific datasets, making them vulnerable to distribution shifts in unseen events. To address these limitations, we propose a framework that integrates Distributionally RobOptimal Transport (DOT) with meta-learning. Our method, named FEND, leverages a small number of verified posts to facilitate efficient fake news detection in newly appeared events. Evaluations across six datasets from Twitter and WeWe confirm FEND's validity and superiority over multiple state-of-the-art techniques. FEND addresses the limitations of current methods, and the associated datasets and codes can be found at https://github.com/yj2000/metaFEND.

As a measure of time, AoI quantifies the recency of data at a destination; lower values indicate more up-to-date information. Unlike conventional performance metrics such as delay, which measure the time a packet spends in the system, AoI is defined as the elapsed time since the most recent data was generated. The paper also details the experimental validation of the framework using five real-world datasets and discusses the potential reduction of dimensionality with structure preservation. Ultimately, the work highlights the substantial potential of the framework for improving both supervised and unsupervised learning tasks. Conducted in September 2022, the research was supported by the University Grant Number 401.62.1.1.4001 of Songkla University, Thailand. The findings were further validated in September 2023 across five datasets.

This research advances the classification initiative launched by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by demonstrating that the star normal quotient twisted wreath category encompasses infinitely many such graphs. Although Group Lasso is a recognized efficient method for selecting both continuous and categorical variables, it often yields distinct estimates for each level of a selected factor, resulting in non-sparse fitted models that are hard to interpret. This study introduces a technique to embed structured knowledge into LLMs by directly training T5 models on factual triples extracted from knowledge graphs. A key benefit of this approach is that it eliminates the need for aligning knowledge graphs with text corpora during data preparation, rendering it especially advantageous for industry-scale knowledge graphs. LLMs have recently attained state-of-the-art results on a wide range of natural language tasks, yet it is unclear if they can leverage knowledge from structured sources such as knowledge graphs (KGs). This paper presents a framework to inject structured knowledge into pre-trained language models (PLMs) through fine-tuning on factual triples. We evaluate the framework using two PLMs fine-tuned on two KGs of varying complexity. To assess Fine-grained factual knowledge, we measured a PLM's ability to answer yes/no questions about factual assertions using the BNIF knowledge base and its derived graph, GraphDB. To assess General knowledge, we evaluated a PLM's performance on four question-answering datasets derived from IMDb and Wikipedia, including QASM (a multi-hop QA dataset) and MetaQA. Fine-tuning on factual triples from a KG enabled the PLM to answer 21% more yes/no questions with high confidence compared to the baseline, while improving exact match scores by 1.75% on the metaQA task.

Pre-trained language models (PLMs) can leverage external knowledge graphs (KGs) to enhance their knowledge representation and reasoning capabilities. However, integrating KGs is difficult because of structural and vocabulary disparities between the graph and the PLM's corpus. This paper proposes a knowledge graph enhancement method to address these challenges. We evaluated the approach on two PLMs fine-tuned on two KGs with differing complexity. Our analysis explores their consistency with analogous inhomogeneous boundary value problems in classical partial differential equation (PDE) frameworks as the nonlocal kernel becomes localized in the limit $\delta \to 0$. Simultaneously, for rescaled fractional-type kernels, we investigate convergence to corresponding inhomogeneous nonlocal boundary value problems of fractional equations in the global limit $\delta \to \infty$. These discussions aim to clarify key issues surrounding nonlocal problems defined on bounded domains with inhomogeneous data. The study encompasses kernels of Green's function type, symmetric kernels, and a specific kernel designed to address inhomogeneous Neumann-type conditions in fractional equations. The problems under examination include inhomogeneous Neumann, Dirichlet, Dirichlet-Neumann, and Neumann-Dirichlet conditions for both local and fractional equations. Our findings indicate that solving inhomogeneous nonlocal problems on bounded domains requires careful kernel selection, particularly when matching the type of inhomogeneous data to ensure consistency. This requirement appears more complex for fractional equations compared to local partial differential equations. We anticipate that these findings will aid researchers in properly formulating nonlocal boundary value problems with inhomogeneous data on bounded domains using kernel functions. The paper concludes with suggestions for future work regarding other kernel types and inhomogeneous data types. The formal analysis in the main text is supported by numerical experiments presented in an appendix. The work is grounded in recent literature from the last five years [15-24].

Building on this assumption, we introduce novel minimal solutions for stitching panoramic images captured by cameras sharing the same optical center, meaning they undergo pure rotation. This work extends their methodology and findings to Eisenstein series formed by inducing two Speh representations, $\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$, for the group $GL(m+n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$, where $\tau$ is a self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation. The extension is achieved by elucidating the combinatorial structure of the associated Weyl group cosets. Furthermore, we clarify how this combinatorics relates to the cancellations of poles. Our primary result provides a necessary and sufficient condition for the cancellation of all poles of a specific type within an Eisenstein series, demonstrating that these cancellations occur precisely under the condition that $m=n$ and $\tau=1$. Title: Cancellation of Poles for Eisenstein Series of Two Speh Representations

Hanzer and Mui\'{c} established a method to produce pole-free Eisenstein series by ensuring the combinatorial cancellation of associated Weyl group cosets. We generalize their approach to a broader context. Our main theorem determines which cuspidal Eisenstein series do not possess poles, extending Hanzer and Mui\'{c}'s original example. Additionally, we explore the implications of these pole-free series for automorphic forms and their cohomology. Specifically, we demonstrate how to construct non-trivial automorphic distributions (and corresponding cohomology classes) by cancelling the poles of Eisenstein series composed of two non-self-dual GL$(m)$ or GL$(n)$ GL$(n)$ representations.

PD is a neurodegenerative condition characterized by the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, which disrupts the normal dynamics of the basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex circuit. While multiple mechanisms contribute to the disease, a comprehensive understanding of its molecular pathogenesis remains elusive, and no cure currently exists. To bridge this knowledge gap, researchers have suggested computational models that mimic neurobiological features observed in animal models. Our approach employs a data-driven method where biologically constrained parameters are optimized via differential evolution. The resulting models accurately replicate single-neuron mean firing rates and local field potential spectral signatures from both healthy and parkinsonian marmoset brains. To our knowledge, this represents the first computational model of PD constructed from simultaneous electrophysiological recordings across seven brain regions in marmosets. Our findings indicate that this model can aid in investigating PD mechanisms and support the creation of techniques for identifying new therapies. Furthermore, the approach is applicable to other computational neuroscience challenges where biological data can be used to fit multi-scale brain circuit models.

Parkinson's Disease affects over 10 million people globally and remains incurable. It is a progressive disorder causing motor and non-motor symptoms that severely impair daily activities and lowers quality of life. Although many mechanisms have been proposed, their relative importance varies among patients, hindering the development of targeted treatments. Early diagnosis and a clear depiction of the disease trajectory are essential for implementing personalized treatment strategies. Consequently, researchers are exploring advanced imaging, electrophysiology, and genetic data within a data-driven framework to identify robust pathophysiological mechanisms and establish patient-specific models. This survey outlines these mechanisms and discusses how such approaches can facilitate the study of PD's pathophysiology and accelerate the discovery of novel therapies.

Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the subthalamic nucleus is a standard treatment for Parkinson's disease patients who do not respond to medication. Although DBS significantly alleviates motor symptoms, it induces complex changes in the electrical activity of the basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex network that are not fully explained. By combining detailed neuron-type models with a data-driven method, we demonstrate that DBS can be represented as a shift in the expression of a low-dimensional attractor within a computational model of the monkey basal ganglia. Because the OpenGL API has limitations, a standard approach involves splicing multiple triangles at different scales to approximate fan-shaped joins, a method that often results in unrealistic artifacts and suboptimal rendering speeds. These targets, selected from the Great Observatories All-sky LIRG Survey (GOALS), represent a broad spectrum of merger evolutionary stages. Our data successfully resolve key emission lines—including H$\beta$, [OIII]$\lambda$5007, H$\alpha$, [NII]$\lambda\lambda$6549,6583, and [SII]$\lambda\lambda$6717,6731—at a spectral resolution of $R$ = 1500–2000. This precision enables the construction of spatially dependent physical plasma parameters, such as electron density ($n_e$) and ionized gas motion ($\mu$cm s$^{-1}$ to km s$^{-1}$). Additionally, we present a novel method for deriving n$e$ and $\vec{v}$ from [SII] ratio maps and line profiles, yielding more accurate results than previous approaches. The median [SII] ratio indicates that n$e$ is generally higher in the stellar bodies of U/LIRGs than in their outer regions or in massively star-forming galaxies. Specifically, the median n$e$ in the stellar bodies is <5000 cm$^{-3}$, rising to >1000 cm$^{-3}$ in the outer regions, with the discrepancy between body and halo n$e$ potentially increasing as mergers progress. Ulrviolet radiation from young stars likely drives these n$e$ distributions, while the presence of kilometric gas motions suggests a role in external galaxy gas accretion or internal accretion onto the starburst region. U/LIRG n$e$ also varies distinctively across different morphological components and phases of merger evolution. The derived gas motions in U/LIRGs are significantly larger than those previously observed in typical LIRGs or star-forming galaxies, and we note that our data constrain the inflow properties of gas onto U/LIRGs. Finally, we suggest that future multiwavelength IFU observations of merging galaxies could help construct models of the dynamical behavior of accreted gas within merger remanents.

Designing a novel radial basis function (RBF) is essential for creating high-dimensional smooth quasi-interpolation operators that exhibit optimal stability constants. This paper introduces a new RBF called the hyperbolic quadratic (HQ) function, which is distinct from existing bases. We establish that the HQ function satisfies the strict necessary and sufficient conditions required to ensure that the associated smooth quasi-interpolation operator is uniformly stable in the infinite norm. Specifically, we derive explicit lower and upper bounds for the singular values of the matrix representing this operator in the Fourier basis, which serve as generalization parameters. These bounds depend on the spacing between grid points and the spatial dimension, rather than being solely functions of the dimension, thus extending previous results from the univariate case. Current approaches typically rely on sensor arrays or in-vehicle cameras to forecast weather, yet these methods incur incremental costs and offer limited scope. To guarantee the uninterrupted operation of all transportation services regardless of conditions, a robust detection system capable of classifying weather in the wild is essential. However, solving this problem is challenging due to the diverse nature of weather conditions and the lack of distinctive features across different scenarios. Existing solutions are often scene-specific and restricted to classifying only two weather categories. This paper introduces a novel open-source dataset named RFS, comprising images of three weather classes: rain, snow, and fog. Additionally, a new algorithm is proposed that employs super-pixel delimiting masks for data augmentation, achieving reasonable performance across ten Convolutional Neural Network architectures. The algorithm's primary objective is to classify four weather types using random forest super-pixel features. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach attains competitive performance with low computational complexity. Notably, the proposed method has been optimized for deployment on Raspberry Pi 4, requiring just 0.033 seconds to classify weather on Test B, whereas Xilinx Alveo AI Accelerator AIU180AI requires 0.0015 seconds. These results indicate that the proposed algorithm and dataset effectively address the open challenge of classifying four weather types across various scenes. The developed solution and open-source code are accessible at https://github.com/roshanz2002/RainSnowFogSnow.

Recent years have seen significant advancements in deep learning-based image classification, largely driven by extensive datasets like ImageNet. Despite this progress, there remains a scarcity of published research and public datasets focused on weather classification. Existing solutions often struggle with generalization when conditions change. To推动 forward research in this domain, we have created a new dataset called Road Frontier Scenarios (RFS), which features four weather categories: clear, rain, snow, and fog. We also present an algorithm designed to classify images from this dataset. The proposed method utilizes over-segmentation techniques to detect weather elements, generating descriptive features that are saved for later use. These methods were evaluated on 12 public datasets across 12 different algorithms, with our results showing that the proposed approach delivers strong performance with high computational efficiency. The datasets and both the optimized algorithm and code optimizations are publicly available at https://github.com/roshanz2002/RainSnowFogSnow.

By comparing the observed slope against these characteristic values, we can rule out $\Lambda$CDM if the distribution becomes less power-law like (slope $>-1$), or favor it if the distribution adheres more strictly to the power law (slope closer to $-1$). This approach is appealing because it relies on fundamental dynamics, thereby circumventing the invalid assumptions found in mass-flux convection schemes at current resolutions. Nevertheless, the optimal closure strategies for multi-fluid equations governing atmospheric convection remain unclear. This study develops a straightforward single-column model featuring two fluids—one rising and one falling—without incorporating additional sub-filter variability modeling. When applied to Rayleigh-Bénard convection, the model demonstrates that minimal closures suffice to predict the correct scaling of heat flux (Nu) across six orders of magnitude in buoyancy forcing (Ra). These findings indicate that even a rudimentary two-fluid model can effectively capture the primary coherent overturning structures of convection. Furthermore, these results offer insights into constructing more sophisticated cliMAtO-conSEnsUs (CLIMCON) models capable of explicitly resolving large-scale convective structures even at relatively coarse grid spacings, ultimately aiding in the improved representation of deep convection in global weather and climate models.

Climate model projections regarding the amplitude and pattern of future changes in atmospheric circulation remain uncertain. Although increased computational power allows for finer grids that better resolve convective processes, it remains unclear whether this yields unique solutions for key phenomena such as the position of the African tropical rain band or the frequency of extreme weather events. We utilize an ensemble of large-eddy simulations (LES) based on CLIMCON, a simplified two-fluid model of large-scale convection, to investigate these issues. Our results show that while the total heat flux (Nu) is uniquely determined, the horizontal flow pattern is not, as multiple distinct large-scale flow configurations can exist for identical boundary conditions. These co-existing states likely account for the uncertainty observed in climate models concerning West African weather patterns. By comparing our findings with observations, LES, and global climate models, we derive simple relationships that capture the dependence of Nu and the root-mean-square (RMS) surface wind speed on the environmental state. These new relationships indicate that the CLIMCON model can be extended to slightly more complex formulations by employing current coarse global climate model grid spacings, potentially offering improved representations of African deep convection and associated weather patterns.

We analyze the conditions required for these three uncorrelated atoms to achieve genuine multipartite entanglement. Our results indicate that this process is unattainable if the cavities interacting with the uncorrelated atoms share classical correlations with any other cavity. However, we observe that the atomic states can become genuinely multipartite entangled if the cavity housing the uncorrelated atom is highly entangled with another cavity. This non-trivial finding offers a potential method for generating multipartite entangled atoms through Jaynes-Cummings interactions and can be implemented using existing experimental setups. Additionally, we show that the proposed protocol enables the preparation of W-state superpositions of excited atomic states with a fidelity exceeding 0.5. Finally, we suggest that the protocol can be enhanced to prepare W-states with near-unit fidelity.

We introduce a cavity quantum electrodynamics scheme capable of generating a specific class of Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states involving the polarizations of three remote atoms. Our approach relies on the resonant exchange of photons between an atom and a microwave cavity non-linear device and does not demand the observation of multiphoton interactions within the device. Notably, the microwave field acting on the atomic system plays a crucial role in determining the exact form of the target entangled state. We propose that the described protocol can facilitate the preparation of the intended class of GHZ states with a fidelity surpassing 0.99.

We investigate the generation of multipartite entanglement among three superconducting qubits via a common mechanical resonator. We demonstrate that qubits, whether prepared in ground or excited states, can become entangled through the coherent exchange of a single phonon with the resonator. We present the necessary conditions for this interaction to yield genuinely multipartite entangled states and illustrate how to prepare these states using current superconducting technology. Specifically, we show that two qubits initially in their ground state can become entangled with one qubit in its excited state. We also propose a method to prepare the Grover state for three qubits with a fidelity exceeding 0.999.

In December 2011, underground tunnels at the LHC were flooded, forcing the LHC operation team to shut down the machine and initiate procedures to expel the water. Data from a flow rate measurement system—installed to monitor the flood—were analyzed using time series analysis and inverse problem techniques. While multiple devices were deployed, this study focuses on the time series from one location and infers the flood source location and volume flow rate via an inverse problem. A simplified model of the tunnel was created, incorporating water flow equations and a linearized Boussinesq equation for shallow water, supplemented by boundary conditions and a parametric description of the source. An optimization algorithm was used to solve the resulting inverse problem. When applied to a specific sensor's data with a source located up to 100 meters away, uncertainties in the shape of the tunnel or the friction coefficient had negligible impact on the solution. # Abstract---Accurate sentiment classification typically relies on semantic labels (e.g., POS tags, coreferences) to enhance performance. This paper presents an end-to-end neural framework for sentiment analysis that employs an attention-based approach to model contextual coreferences. Extensive experiments on two distinct Korean sentiment analysis tasks demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results even in the absence of contextual semantic labels. We release our code and data for reproducibility at https://speechbrain.github.io/blog/2020/05/21/korean-sentiment-analysis-.

We often claim to communicate freely and openly, yet we clearly avoid topics aligned with our dislikes. This phenomenon, formally known as the censorship effect, occurs across all societies, making it essential to understand how individuals decide which information to omit from their messages. This paper investigates the mechanism by which listeners' semantic knowledge influences a speaker's choice of context-relevant but potentially sensitive information. We show that a listener's semantic representation of a topic causes ambiguous activations in the output layer of a feedforward network when trained solely on non-censorship dialogue data. To mitigate this, we propose incorporating sentences that trigger clear activations, a strategy that improves sentiment predictions and yields more robust models for avoiding out-of-bound outputs. We validate our findings using human experiments and support them with evidence from neural network interpretability and a network-based semantic model. Our dialogue dataset is available at https://github.com/SpeechBrain/CS-effect-.

Large-scale pre-trained models have become increasingly influential in deep learning, yet obtaining their predictions for every query is often difficult or costly. While existing query-specific adaptation techniques generally assume access to both the pre-trained network and data, this paper presents a novel transfer learning framework that requires only the network. By formulating adaptation as clustering problem on the query data, we develop a two-step solution that trains a coarse classifier via self-training on queried data and subsequently transfers knowledge from the pre-trained model's decision boundaries to refine its predictions. This approach effectively adapts to out-of-domain queries even when they contain examples of new, unseen classes.

Decision-based learning aims to enhance model performance, particularly in risk-assessment scenarios like medical diagnosis where privacy and security are critical. Unlike recent methods that use perturbation-based queries to infer decision boundaries for computing guidance, our approach directly determines the complete decision boundary of a DNN for all classes through a series of queries, thereby providing more comprehensive learning signals. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) takes a graph $G$ and a positive integer $k$ as input and asks whether a strong geodetic set of size at most $k$ exists; this problem is established as NP-hard for general graphs. This work introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which determines if a specific, given vertex set $S \subseteq V(G)$ constitutes a strong geodetic set. We show that SGR is NP-complete. Furthermore, we examine and contrast the computational complexity of both SG and SGR across various graph classes, presenting polynomial-time algorithms, NP-completeness proofs, and preliminary findings in parameterized complexity. Notably, our analysis provides a resolution to an open question regarding the complexity of SG on chordal graphs. Additionally, we define and explore the related concepts of the strong geodetic kernel and strong geodetic radius. To support practical applications, we also present several heuristics for the SG problem, validated through extensive numerical experiments on well-known graph collections. Our findings provide complexiticity resolutions for multiple longstanding open problems. The complexity analysis of SGR facilitates a distinction between the more intricate SG and the relatively straightforward SGR, offering a polynomial-time algorithm for SG on a broad class of graphs that previously lacked such an algorithm. These complexities analysis of SGR, along with our proposed heuristics, offers researchers an efficient method to investigate strong geodetic sets, complementing the previous difficulty in finding polynomial-time algorithms for the general strong geodetic problem. We propose that these approaches offer valuable insights for practical strong geodetic set applications, such as network monitoring and virus spreading.

Conversely, gathering vast amounts of suboptimal or task-agnostic trajectories is relatively easy; while these do not directly guide imitation, they reveal the environment's dynamical structure and potential actions. This work investigates whether such suboptimal offline data can enable provably better downstream imitation learning. We affirmatively answer this by introducing training objectives that leverage offline datasets to learn a factored transition model, facilitating the extraction of a latent action space. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that this learned space enhances the sample efficiency of subsequent imitation learning, thereby diminishing the reliance on extensive expert datasets by incorporating auxiliary non-expert data. To implement this practically, we propose TRAIL (Transition-Reparametrized Actions for Imitation Learning), an algorithm that employs contrastive learning on an energy-based transition model to reparametrize the action space for more sample-efficient imitation. Experiments on navigation and locomotion tasks validate our theoretical findings, showing that TRAIL can improve baseline imitation learning performance by up to 4x. Overall, we demonstrate how offline behavior cloning can factoredly learn a transition model and a latent action space, leading to significantly enhanced imitation learning results.

We present a general framework for multi-agent reinforcement learning (RL) utilizing self-play, which relies on two contributing elements: a multi-agent communication protocol resembling a game theory mixed strategy and a learning rate adaptation mechanism. We provide a formalization of TRIPLETTE along with implementations of its variants, including TRIPLETTE-H, TRIPLETTE-H2, and TRIPLETTE-H3. Both theoretical analysis and experimental results confirm that TRIPLETTE-H and its extensions can effectively boost the sample efficiency of multi-agent RL. Specifically, TRIPLETTE-H achieves a sample efficiency improvement comparable to four times that of TR2C on complex tasks like Smac. Furthermore, the TRIPLETTE framework enables the direct comparison and interchange of different agent policies outside of neural network function approximators, thereby enhancing the transparency of multi-agent RL.

We examine the simultaneous learning of a reward function and a policy from expert demonstrations, a capability essential for customizing AI systems to specific user preferences and applications. Unlike prior methods that optimize a black-box policy directly, we formulate the problem as learning a reusable reward function. This acquired function can subsequently guide policy optimization, allowing for the incorporation of multiple experts or the adjustment of the resulting policies in a TRIPLETTE-H like manner. reinforcement learning efficiency by leveraging expert demonstrations. However, acquiring such demonstrations is often prohibitively costly or unfeasible in many practical settings. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a new framework named Co-Imitation Learning (CoIL), which utilizes an agent's own historical successful experiences rather than relying on external experts. Specifically, we train two distinct agents by having them alternately explore the environment and leverage the peer's past experiences. Since these experiences may range from valuable to misleading, we propose estimating their potential utility based on the expected gain of the value function. This allows agents to selectively imitate one another, prioritizing useful data while filtering out noise. Experimental results across various tasks demonstrate the significant superiority of the proposed CoIL framework, confirming that agents can mutually benefit without external supervision. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/hjdw8888/CoIL.
In this work, we address the challenge of sample efficiency in deep reinforcement learning by introducing Dual Curiosity (DC). Unlike previous approaches that employ a single intrinsic motivation mechanism, DC utilizes two agents with opposite exploration goals: one maximizes (and the other minimizes) the estimated sparsity of future states. This process forces both agents to select actions that are neither too similar nor too dissimilar, ensuring they explore diverse yet complementary regions of the state space. Consequently, DC enables agents to acquire a robust understanding of the task from these varied perspectives, leading to mutual benefit and significantly reduced data requirements for effective task mastery. We validate DC's sample efficiency and stability across multiple standard tasks, including MuJoCo environments and the Box2D rocket ship. Evidence shows that two agents equipped with DC can achieve performance comparable to a single agent with extensive experience. Furthermore, we present the OpenAI Gym domain visualizer for the DC framework, providing users with unique insights into the distinct exploration regions of two curiosity agents. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/SeungHyunSon/DualCuriosity.

Using this proposed metric, PAC code decoding requires computational effort comparable to sequential decoding of conventional convolutional codes. Simulation results indicate enhanced error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes when employing this metric. We demonstrate that setting the polarized cutoff rate as the metric's bias value exponentially decreases the probability of the sequential decoder traversing incorrect paths, relative to the path depth. Additionally, we prove that the upper bound of PAC code computation follows a Pareto distribution, a finding confirmed by simulations. We also propose a scaling-bias procedure and a threshold spacing selection method for search-limited sequential decoding that significantly lowers average computation. Our findings show that for codes of length 128, search-limited PAC codes achieve error-correction performance nearly matching that of polar codes decoded via successive cancellation list decoding (list size 64, CRC length 11), yet with substantially reduced computational cost. Furthermore, we show that the computational efficiency of search-limited PAC codes exceeds that of sequential termination by more than five times. These results are expected to be validated experimentally. The source code and data are accessible on GitHub. We further suggest that this work contributes to the development of high-performance, low-complexity forward error correction (FEC) schemes for the second phase of the 5th Generation (5G) mobile communication standard and for the satellite links constituting the Starlink very large scale antenna (VLSA) constellations. We have adopted an open-access model for this publication.

Likelihood Estimation (MLE) pre-training is a flexible approach for boosting Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Nevertheless, recent studies suggest that RL's benefits in NMT largely stem from reinforcing tokens that were already highly probable during pre-training. We propose that the extensive action space is a primary barrier to RL's efficacy in machine translation and validate this hypothesis through two experimental series. First, we observe that shrinking the vocabulary size enhances RL performance. Second, we demonstrate that effectively lowering the action space dimensionality without altering the vocabulary also leads to significant gains, as measured by BLEU scores, semantic similarity, and human assessment. Specifically, initializing the network's final fully connected layer—which maps internal dimensions to the vocabulary—with a layer designed to generalize across similar actions results in a substantial performance boost, averaging 1.5 BLEU points. Furthermore, this layer exhibits a remarkable ability to generalize to actions that were not seen during training. These findings offer a novel perspective on why RL underperforms in high-dimensional action settings and provide a practical solution to this challenge. We are ready to deploy this enhanced model for the WMT20 Neural Machine Translation (NMT) Shared Task.

This study introduces a learning-based, markerless extrinsic calibration system utilizing a depth camera that operates without simulation data. Models for end-effector (EE) segmentation, single-frame rotation prediction, and keypoint detection are trained using automatically generated real-world datasets. To derive EE pose estimates, we employ a transformation trick applied to rotation predictions and a matching algorithm applied to keypoint predictions. Additionally, we enhance calibration robustness by integrating the iterative closest point algorithm, multi-frame analysis, filtering, and outlier detection. Evaluations using training data from various camera poses and test data from unseen poses demonstrate sub-centimeter and sub-deciradian average errors in both calibration and pose estimation. Furthermore, we show that a single, carefully selected training pose yields comparable performance. This markerless approach offers a practical alternative to traditional marker-dependent methods for external camera calibration, including end-effector-to-base poses for robotic arms.
